phrases.translation: Alif-Lãm-Mĩm
phrases.explanation:
Alif-Lam-Mim is one of the openings made of separate letters, and the earliest exegetes differed about what it means. Some said it is one of the names of the Quran, others that these are letters with which Allah opens the Quran, others that it is a name for the surah, others that it is the greatest name of Allah, and others that it is an oath by which Allah swore, belonging to His names. Some took each letter to carry a meaning of its own, different from the meaning of its neighbour, some took them to be letters of the alphabet simply placed there, some took each letter to comprise several divergent meanings, and some said that every book has a secret and the secret of the Quran is its opening letters. One further explanation is that the surahs were opened with these letters to make the polytheists listen, since they had agreed among themselves to turn away from the Quran.

An objection is raised to the view that they are names of surahs. Several surahs begin with Alif-Lam-Mim and several with Alif-Lam-Ra, and a name only marks a thing when it distinguishes it. The answer is that names are instituted for distinction in the first place, and where two things share one name, something else is added to tell them apart. Two men both called Amr are distinguished as Amr the Tamimi and Amr the Azdi, and in the same way a reader says Alif-Lam-Mim al-Baqara and Alif-Lam-Mim Al Imran. On this reading the three letters stand in the nominative, each raised by the other, and the words that follow, This is the Book, begin a new statement of their own.

The verdict preferred here is that Allah made these letters separate instead of joining them into ordinary speech because He intended each of them to point to many meanings and not to one. A single letter can carry several meanings just as a single word can. Arabic uses one word, umma, for a community, for an era, for a devout and obedient man and for a religion, and another, din, for recompense, for reckoning, for rule and obedience and for submission. So each of these letters comprises what the exegetes said of it. They belong to the names and attributes of Allah, they open the surahs, they carry the numerical values of the letters of the alphabet, and they mark and name the surahs they stand over. One explanation alone is rejected, the claim of a philologist that the letters stand for the alphabet as a whole and so mean that these letters are the Book. It is set aside because it departs from everything reported of the Companions, the Followers and the exegetes after them, and because the one who held it contradicted himself about what raises the words This is the Book, assigning that raising once to the letters, once to a pronoun inside the verse and once to a later phrase in it.

Two further points settle the matter. If Allah had intended one of these meanings to the exclusion of the rest, the Prophet would have said so plainly, because the Book was sent down to him so that he might make clear what people differed about. His leaving the letters unexplained is itself the strongest evidence that every aspect they can carry is intended. The claim that they fall outside the Arabic language altogether is answered by the Quran's own description of itself as a clear Arabic tongue. Allah addressed the Arabs only in what they knew of their speech, and letters no creature could understand would not be clear. Allah opened some surahs with praise of Himself and some with glorification, so there is nothing impossible in opening others with an oath by these letters.

phrases.translation: This is the Book!
phrases.explanation:
The word for that is used here where a reader might expect this, and most of the early exegetes took the meaning to be simply this Book. The passage explains why both pointings are sound: anything just said and now finished takes on something of the absent, while still counting as present for the person addressed. A listener answering a story says both that is exactly as you said and this is as you said, without difference of meaning. So when the letters Alif-Lam-Mim had been mentioned and their meanings set out, the words that follow point back at them as something just completed and say that this which has been made clear is the Book.

Two other readings are recorded. One takes the Book to mean the surahs sent down before al-Baqara, so that what those earlier surahs comprise is the Book about which there is no doubt. The other takes it to mean the Torah and the Gospel, in which case that is plainly a report about something absent and no difficulty arises. The first explanation is preferred, as the one that fits the Book best.

phrases.translation: There is no doubt about it
phrases.explanation:
Doubt here is the word rayb, which comes from a verb meaning that a matter disquieted someone and made them unsure, so the phrase denies that anything in this Book unsettles the mind or leaves it uncertain. A line of poetry is quoted in which the same word carries exactly that sense.

One further point is made about how the sentence hangs together. The word for guidance that follows can be read as a fresh statement of praise, as something sharing the case of the word that, or as following the position of this phrase. Which of these is allowed depends on how the opening letters are read, and the passage argues that the reading chosen at the start has to be kept consistently rather than abandoned halfway through the verse.

phrases.translation: —a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺
phrases.explanation:
The God-fearing are those who feared Allah in two directions at once. They held back from what He forbade and stood by what He made obligatory, so they avoided disobedience and obeyed Him in carrying it out. The verse describes them with God-fearingness generally, without limiting it to one part of what Allah has a right to, so nobody may narrow it to a single aspect without a proof that has to be accepted.

On that basis one narrower explanation is set aside, the claim that the God-fearing are only those who kept clear of ascribing partners to Allah and of hypocrisy. A person can do both and still be corrupt in his conduct, unless hypocrisy is itself taken to mean committing what Allah forbade and neglecting what He made obligatory.

phrases.translation: who believe in the unseen,
phrases.explanation:
The meaning of belief here is taken from what the word means in Arabic, which is holding something to be true. A person who holds a statement to be true is called one who gives credence to it, and one who confirms his statement by his action is called a believer in the same sense. So belief covers acknowledgment of Allah, of His books and of His messengers, together with the confirming of that by action. The reading preferred here follows from that: these people hold the unseen true in word, in conviction and in deed.

The unseen is everything hidden from a person of any matter. There is a difference of opinion about who the verses at the opening of this surah describe. Some took them to be the believers among the Arabs alone, others the believers among the People of the Book in particular, and others again every believer with these qualities.

phrases.translation: establish prayer,
phrases.explanation:
Establishing the prayer means performing it with its limits, its obligations and everything commanded in it, in the manner prescribed, rather than leaving any of it idle. Reports gloss it as the complete performance of the bowing, the prostration, the recitation and the humble attentiveness that belongs to it, and as the prescribed prayers rather than prayer in some general sense.

The word itself means supplication in the speech of the Arabs. The prescribed prayer is thought to carry that name because the one who prays turns toward the reward of Allah and asks Him for what he needs, just as a suppliant turns toward his Lord with his request.

phrases.translation: and donate from what We have provided for them
phrases.explanation: The exegetes differed over what spending covers here, and the reading preferred is the widest one. These people discharged everything obligatory upon them in their wealth, whether the alms due on it or the support of those whose maintenance fell to them, by kinship, by ownership or otherwise. Allah described them in general terms as spending from what He provided them and praised them for it, and He did not limit that praise to one kind of expenditure, so it takes in every kind a person is praised for giving. What is spent is the good He provided them, the lawful part of their wealth, with nothing forbidden mixed into it.

phrases.translation: and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you,
phrases.explanation: These words describe belief in the whole of revelation rather than in part of it, what was sent down to the Prophet and what was sent down to the messengers before him. Although the opening verses of the surah describe the believers, they carry an allusion that rebukes the unbelievers among the People of the Book. Those people claimed to hold true whatever the earlier messengers had brought, while at the same time calling the Prophet a liar. They claimed to be rightly guided all the same, and claimed that nobody would enter the Garden except a Jew or a Christian. These verses brand that claim a lie, because believing in the earlier Books cannot be separated from believing in the one sent down now.

phrases.translation: and have sure faith in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The Hereafter is an attribute belonging to the Abode, as in the verse that calls the final Abode the true Life. It is described as last only because it comes after an earlier abode that preceded it, as when a speaker says he showed someone favors one time after another and was thanked for neither the first nor the last. A second explanation is that it is called last because it comes after the creation, just as the present world is called the nearer world from its nearness to the creation. Certainty about it is knowledge of a thing that has not arrived yet, held without wavering.

phrases.translation: It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful
phrases.explanation:
The exegetes differed over whom this verse means by they. Some took it to cover the people of the two qualities mentioned before, the believers in the unseen among the Arabs and the believers in what was sent down to the Prophet and to the messengers before him. Others took it to mean the God-fearing who believe in the unseen, and held that these are the same people. Others again took it to mean the believers among the People of the Book, who held the Prophet and what he brought to be true.

The reading preferred here is the first. They refers to both groups together, the God-fearing and those who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet. The grammar was worked through to reach that result, since the second those can stand in the genitive by two routes and in the nominative by four, including as a fresh statement opening a new verse.

Following the guidance of their Lord means that they are upon a light from their Lord, upon a proof, and upon steadiness and correctness. Success itself is explained as continued existence, so the successful are those whose good lasts with them rather than ending where this world ends.

phrases.translation: As for those who persist in disbelief,
phrases.explanation:
The verse opens by naming a group whose disbelief is settled, and the scholars of interpretation differed about who is meant and about whom it came down. One explanation takes it to be the Jews around Medina at the time of the Prophet, rebuked for denying his prophethood even though they knew him as they knew their own sons. Another takes it to be particular people among the disbelievers, named and known, since some of those who disbelieved did come to believe later.

Disbelief here means denial. The rabbis among the Jews of Medina denied the Prophet and concealed him from the people, keeping his affair secret while they found his description in their own books.

phrases.translation: it is the same
phrases.explanation: The word for the same means being in equilibrium, and it comes from the same root as the word for equality, so a speaker says these two matters are equal to me and they are the same to me with one meaning. The Quran uses it that way elsewhere when it tells the Prophet to throw a treaty back to a people on equal terms. A poet uses it of the night and the day running level for a woman, with no slackening in either of them, and another of eyes that see equally well in a darkness so deep that the sound-eyed see no better than the one-eyed.

phrases.translation: whether you warn them or not—they will never believe
phrases.explanation: The two halves of the sentence are put in the form of a question but mean a statement, since the particle here stands in place of the word for which of the two. A speaker says it makes no difference to us whether you stand or sit, and asks nothing by it. Some grammarians held that the particle is simply attached to the word for the same with no question intended, because a real question seeks to settle which of two things is so, and nothing is being sought here. The sense is that warning these people and leaving them unwarned stand level, and they will not believe.

phrases.translation: Allah has sealed their hearts
phrases.explanation:
Sealing here comes from the word for impressing a stamp, and a signet is called by the same root, so to seal a document is to put a stamp upon it. Hearts are described as vessels for the knowledge entrusted to them, and hearing is what perceives sound. Sealing them is therefore comparable to sealing any other vessel, and nothing is left open for what would have entered.

The exegetes differed over how that sealing is to be described. Some said the verse is only a report of their arrogance and their refusal to listen to the truth they were called to. The view preferred here is the one a reliable narration from the Prophet supports, which takes the sealing as a real act rather than a figure for their attitude. The sins, when they pile up upon the hearts, shut them off, and when they envelop them the sealing and stamping come from Allah, and then there is no path for faith toward them.

The argument put to the other side is direct. Their arrogance and their turning away from belief, are they their own act, or an act of Allah toward them? Whichever answer is given, what the verse describes stands. Some took the people meant here to be the leaders of the confederates who were killed at Badr.

phrases.translation: and their hearing, and their sight is covered.
phrases.explanation: The report about sealing ends at their hearing, and what follows about the eyes is a fresh statement begun after it. The proof given is that the word for covering stands in the nominative, which makes it the subject of its own sentence rather than something governed by the verb of sealing. An early exegete made the same point and supported it from the Quran, with the verse saying that if Allah wills He seals upon your heart. A covering in the speech of the Arabs is what envelops a thing entirely, as a poet used the word of something that enveloped a man and mingled with him. The reciters and the scholars agree on the reading followed here, and whoever departs from it stands alone against what they established together.

phrases.translation: They will suffer a tremendous punishment
phrases.explanation:
The punishment is mighty, and the explanation of the phrase is that it belongs to them on account of their opposition to the Prophet, and that it concerns the scribes among the Jews. Others connected these two verses with the people who exchanged the favor of Allah for disbelief and settled their own folk in the abode of ruin, and said that of the leaders among them none was saved and none was guided.

The verse is also one of the clearest proofs against those who deny that a person can be charged with what he cannot bear except by the help of Allah. Allah reported that He sealed the hearts and the hearing of a group of His unbelieving servants, and He did not lift the obligation from them.

phrases.translation: And there are some who say,
phrases.explanation:
Two views are recorded about the word for people itself. One takes its original form to have begun with a hamza that was dropped because the word is used so constantly, after which the definite article was added. The other holds that it is a different form altogether, because the Arabs build its diminutive on the letters as they stand.

The exegetes agree that this verse came down about a group given to hypocrisy. The occasion given for it is that when the Prophet's position was established in the land of his migration, and Allah's word prevailed there, the learned among the Jews showed the Prophet their rancour and open enmity, except for a small group whom Allah guided. Belief in what they say with their tongues means holding something to be true.

phrases.translation: “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers
phrases.explanation:
A day is called a day among the Arabs only because of the night that precedes it, and without a preceding night the daylight is not called a day. The Day of Resurrection is therefore a day after which no night comes, except the night whose morning the Resurrection breaks in.

Allah then denies these people the name of belief even though He has reported what they said with their tongues. That is a flat contradiction of what they claimed about their own conviction and their acknowledgment of the Resurrection, and it tells the Prophet that what they show him with their mouths is the opposite of what lies hidden in their hearts and the reverse of what their souls are set on.

phrases.translation: They seek to deceive Allah and the believers,
phrases.explanation: The deception of the hypocrite is that he shows with his tongue words and assent contradicting the doubt and denial living in his heart, so that what he displays protects him. Some who knew the language held that the verb here carries the plain sense of deceiving rather than of trying to deceive. The view preferred is the opposite. The form belongs to the reciprocal action that only happens between two parties. So the hypocrite tries to deceive Allah by the lie on his tongue, and Allah is his deceiver, in that He leaves him without sight of what would save him at his return. The point is made plainly that the deceiver is himself deceived, and that the show of faith is used to ward off a judgment that would otherwise fall on him.

phrases.translation: yet they only deceive themselves,
phrases.explanation:
Arabs do call a man a deceiver toward someone he has escaped, when he shows with his tongue something other than what is inside him. On that usage the hypocrite is a deceiver of Allah and the believers, because what he displays saves him while he carries something else within. Yet that very act deceives himself, since he seems to give himself what it wants while leading it to destruction.

It would be wrong to say they deceived the believers, since that would grant them a deception actually carried off. The comparison given is a man who fought another and killed himself but not his companion, where the fighting is affirmed, the killing of the other denied and his own affirmed. A deceiver is one whose deception succeeded, and theirs did not.

phrases.translation: but they fail to perceive it
phrases.explanation: To perceive something means to know it and recognise it, so that no one knew it and no one recognised it. What these people do not perceive is that Allah is the one deceiving them, by the respite He gives them and the gradual way He leads them on, which they take for a good thing granted to them when it is the opposite. A man may shoot up an arrow while nobody notices it, then turn back and say how delicious the milk is, and so it is with them. They count the respite among the favors granted to them, when in truth it is the opposite.

phrases.translation: There is sickness in their hearts,
phrases.explanation: The disease in the heart is not an illness of the body. It sits in the conviction these people hold to in religion, and in their position toward the Prophet and what he brought from Allah. What that disease consists of is doubt about his affair and confusion over it. They are neither certain of it with the certainty that belongs to belief, nor have they come out against it openly, and the unsettled state between the two is the sickness named here. They are in the position of one who neither confirms nor denies. The interpreters reinforced one another in this explanation, so it is not the reading of one school only.

phrases.translation: and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase.
phrases.explanation: The increase is of the same kind as what was already there. The disease Allah reports having increased for them is the doubt and confusion in their hearts before the increase, made greater rather than replaced by something else. The means of that increase is what Allah brought into being of prescribed limits and obligations, so that every fresh command and every new revelation gave their doubt something further to fasten on, and the sickness grew by what should have cured it. Some of those who explained it held instead that the growth came from their own acts, the dissembling and the lying that made the disease in them greater.

phrases.translation: They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies
phrases.explanation: Painful here means causing pain, the active sense carried by a form that looks passive, in the way Arabic speaks of a painful blow for one that causes pain. The word for the reason they are punished was read in two ways. Most of the reciters of Kufa read it as lying, while others read it as denying, holding that the punishment falls on them for calling the Prophet a liar rather than for ordinary falsehood, which would not by itself bring such a threat. The reading preferred follows the shape of the passage. These verses opened by naming the shameful deeds of the hypocrites, so the threat that closes them answers what was opened, and the punishment is tied to the falsehood they were actually practising.

phrases.translation: When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”
phrases.explanation:
The scholars of interpretation differ over the interpretation of this verse. One takes it to be about the hypocrites of the Prophet's own time, and another about the people who came after them with the same trait until the Day of Resurrection. The one preferred is the first. It is chosen because the scholars agree that this was the character of the hypocrites among the Prophet's companions.

Their claim to be reformers is then examined. Whatever their reform amounted to, whether reconciling the Jews and the Muslims or managing their own religious position while lying to the believers about what was in their hearts, they believed themselves to be doing good, and in the sight of Allah they were doers of evil who went against His command.

phrases.translation: Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it
phrases.explanation: This saying of Allah is a refutation of the hypocrites with respect to their claim. They were commanded to obey Allah in what He commanded and forbidden to disobey Him in what He forbade, and their reply was that they were only reformers and not corrupters, that in the very thing they were blamed for they stood on righteousness and guidance, and that they were by no means the ones astray. The correction is therefore not about what they did but about who was blind to it, since they did not perceive that the corruption was theirs, and that blindness to their own condition is what kept them from seeing it.

phrases.translation: And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained as an instruction to give credence to the Prophet and what he brought from Allah in the way the people have given credence to it. The people meant are the believers who accepted him and his prophethood, so the hypocrites are told to believe as those believers believed.

Their answer turns on a word worth explaining. Fools is the plural of a term for someone ignorant and weak in judgment, with little knowledge of where benefit and harm lie. So the insult the hypocrites throw at the believers is the language of someone who thinks he sees consequences others cannot. The verse returns it on them. They are the fools and do not know it, and ignorance of one's own condition is what makes the foolishness complete.

phrases.translation: When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates
phrases.explanation: The verse describes two audiences and two speeches. With the believers these people say that they believe, and when they are alone with their own instigators they tell them the opposite. Much of the discussion here is about the small word translated as with. Some grammarians of Basra held that the phrase means withdrawing to someone for a particular need, so that the preposition can only carry the sense of drawing apart to confer. Others among the grammarians of Kufa read it as directing their seclusion toward their devils, taking the preposition to give direction rather than mere company. Either way the point of the verse survives, since what matters is that the second speech is made away from the believers and to the people who lead them.

phrases.translation: they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”
phrases.explanation: The people of interpretation agree, with no disagreement among them, that we were only mocking means we are only mockers, so the form of the words reports what they habitually are rather than a single act. The verse is set alongside the earlier one describing them as saying they believe in Allah and the Last Day while they do not believe, and as trying to deceive Allah and the believers. Taken together, what they tell their own people when they withdraw with them is that they are on their side, and that the profession of belief they made in front of the believers was mockery of it. The wording is examined too, why it says they withdrew to their devils rather than with them.

phrases.translation: Allah will throw their mockery back at them,
phrases.explanation:
Mockery in the language of the Arabs is that the one who mocks shows the person mocked something outwardly pleasing in word and deed while intending through it what harms him. The question raised is how such a word can be used of Allah at all. The answer is that this is an announcement of requital in the wording of the deed requited, the same pattern that runs through the Quran, where they seek to deceive Allah but He is their deceiver.

The working out of it for the hypocrites is that Allah gave them in this world the rulings that follow from what their tongues showed, so they were counted and treated as Muslims are treated. In the Hereafter they are gathered with the same people, and there their mockery is returned on them. Play and folly may not be ascribed to Allah, while mockery, scoffing, scheming and deception may, because in the second group the word can carry the sense of answering a deed with its like.

phrases.translation: leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance
phrases.explanation:
The word translated as leaving them was read in two senses, and the most correct is that it means He increases them, by granting them respite and leaving them in their insolence and rebellion. That is how Allah described His dealings with people like them elsewhere, turning their hearts and their sight away. The other reading, that He grants to them, has no ground, because the Arabs and those who know their language allow the verb to take its object directly, as when one river is said to have increased another.

Defiance comes from a root meaning to exceed one's limit and behave outrageously, and the Quran uses it of the person who transgresses because he sees himself self-sufficient. So the respite described here is not a favor. Allah leaves them to behave badly in their error and disbelief, wandering bewildered. That wandering is the last word of the verse, and it means error and going astray, as when a poet uses it of losing the way in wasteland. The plural form describes people astray and bewildered, and the sense of the whole is that in their error and disbelief, whose stain has flooded over them, they wander about without direction. The exegetes explained the word in the same way.

phrases.translation: They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance.
phrases.explanation:
An objection opens the discussion. How can these people be said to have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance when their hypocrisy was never preceded by faith, so that they had no guidance standing behind them to trade away? The scholars of interpretation differed, and one reading takes the purchase simply as taking misguidance and letting guidance go, since buying means taking the thing bought in place of the price paid for it.

That reading is possible but is not the one preferred here, because the verse goes on to say that their commerce brought no profit, which points to a real transaction rather than a bare exchange of positions. What is chosen is the explanation that they took misguidance and let guidance go, since the account given of these people from the start shows only the displaying of falsehood with their tongues and never any light of faith. Every unbeliever exchanges faith for unbelief in that he acquires the unbelief coming from him in place of the faith he was commanded to hold, and the Quran says elsewhere that whoever exchanges unbelief for faith has strayed from the right path. So the hypocrite and the unbeliever have exchanged guidance for misguidance.

phrases.translation: But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation:
Through that purchase the hypocrites lost and gained nothing. A merchant makes a profit only when he exchanges what he holds for something more valuable than it, and these people gave up the more valuable for the less. A question is raised about the wording, since profit and loss belong to merchants rather than to commerce itself, but the verse attaches them to the trade because the trade is what the traders did.

The closing words explain why the loss was unavoidable. They were not rightly guided in preferring misguidance to guidance, in exchanging faith for unbelief, and in buying hypocrisy in place of assent and acknowledgment, so nothing in the transaction could have come out well for them.

phrases.translation: Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see
phrases.explanation:
A difficulty is raised about the shape of the comparison. The word for their example carries a plural ending, since it refers to a group, while the one who kindles a fire is a single person. How can a group be likened to one individual? The answer is that comparing a group of hypocrites with one individual made into a likeness for their deeds is permissible and correct. The ruling turns on the difference between comparing deeds and comparing names. Where a group and an individual share one and the same deed, the deed of the group may be likened to the deed of the single person.

The people of interpretation then differed about what the likeness itself means, and several statements are reported on that. An objection is answered about the reading that when the fire lit up what was around him it went out and was extinguished, since no such words appear in the verse. The reply is that omission of this kind is ordinary in Arabic speech.

So the shortening in the report about the hypocrites matches the shortening in the report about the one who kindled the fire. The sense of the whole is that these people were given light enough to see by, in the profession they made, and it was taken from them when it mattered most, leaving them in darkness with no way to see.

phrases.translation: They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind,
phrases.explanation:
These three descriptions follow from the similitude of the fire that has just been given. Since the light was taken away and the people left in darkness where they do not see, the verse now reports what they have become. It is a statement about the hypocrites that, having bought misguidance in place of guidance, they were not guided to the truth, and are deaf to it, silent about it and blind in it.

Some space is given to how the three words are to be read. They admit the nominative in two ways and the accusative in two. The reading chosen is the nominative rather than the accusative, on the ground that nobody may depart from the written copies of the Muslims, which settle the matter against a reading that would be grammatically possible but is not attested.

phrases.translation: so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺
phrases.explanation:
Not returning is reported of the same people, tied to what has just been said of them. Having bought misguidance in place of guidance, they do not go back to looking for the guidance they let go. The sense of it is that they show no repentance and do not let themselves be admonished, so that the believers need no longer hope that these will come upright, speak the truth, or hear a caller to guidance.

A saying from one of the companions runs against this report, holding that they do not return to Islam. It is set aside, because the plain wording of the recitation points the other way. The verse says they do not return, a statement about their condition rather than a return they might make.

phrases.translation: Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning.
phrases.explanation:
A second similitude is set beside the first, and a question is raised about the word or that joins them. Are both similitudes about the hypocrites, or only one? If both, why does the verse say or, when that word can carry doubt?

The answer is that the matter is not what the question supposes. Although or sometimes expresses doubt, it also occurs with the sense carried by the plain and, either from what precedes it in the utterance or from what follows it. Here the word simply adds a second picture to the first. The word for similitude is also left out of this phrase, because the earlier phrase about the one who kindled a fire already supplied it, and Arabic omits what the context has made plain.

The parts of the picture are then explained. Darknesses is a plural built on a singular meaning one darkness. Thunder is a matter on which the scholars differed, some holding that it is an angel driving the clouds. Taken together the similitude is of the light the hypocrites gave themselves by saying with their tongues to the Messenger and the believers that they believed in Allah and the Last Day, and of the darkness, noise and terror mixed into it.

phrases.translation: They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺
phrases.explanation:
The disagreement about the storm continues. Some held that thunder is a wind stifled beneath the clouds which then rises, and that its voice comes from that. If thunder is what the early authorities described, then the verse means a rainstorm from the sky in which there are darknesses and the voice of the thunder. Lightning too was explained in more than one way, some calling it a whip of light with which the angel drives the clouds. It is suggested that what several of them reported may amount to one meaning, the whips named by one being the same as those named by the others, and the word for striking is discussed, since it is the thunder that contends with the angel rather than the clouds.

The similitude is then applied. The rainstorm stands for the outward profession and affirmation the hypocrites show with their tongues. The darknesses in it stand for the darkness of the doubt, denial and disease they hide. The thunder and lightning stand for what frightens them in it, and their fingers in their ears are how they try to escape. The phrase for fear of death stands in the accusative as a reason, in the way Arabic says I visited you as an honouring to you. The verse closes by reporting that although these people shelter themselves from Allah's punishment and worry over it, Allah encompasses the disbelievers, so nothing they do to avoid it puts them beyond it.

phrases.translation: It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation:
The similitude is carried through to its movement. The lightning all but snatches their sight, and whenever it gives them light they walk in it, while when it darkens over them they come to a standstill. That is the picture of a people whose profession of belief lights up only as far as this world requires and then fails them.

A question about the threat that follows is answered. Allah singled out hearing and sight, rather than naming the rest of the body, because of what the similitude had turned on, the clap they fear and the flash that nearly takes their vision. The verse ends on Allah's power over everything, which is what makes the threat more than a figure of speech, and nothing in the storm they stand in is beyond Him.

phrases.translation: O humanity! Worship your Lord,
phrases.explanation:
The command is addressed to the two groups the verses have just described, both those whose hearts are sealed and those who are guided, so nobody is excluded from it. Worship is reported from one of the companions here in the sense of acknowledging Allah alone, which is the first thing the word asks of a person.

The verse is then used as an argument. It is treated as one of the strongest proofs against the claim that a person may only be commanded to do what he can already manage on his own, since Allah commands the worship of the Lord here before any such condition is stated.

phrases.translation: Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation:
The reason given for the command is creation. The Lord to be worshipped is named as the one who made them and made the people before them, so the obligation rests on something everybody in the address shares.

The purpose is then explained as becoming God-fearing through worshipping the Lord who created you, through obeying Him in what He commanded and forbade, and through leaving off error. A difficulty is raised about the wording, since the particle used can mean perhaps, and it cannot suggest that Allah was unsure how things would turn out. The answer is that this particle carries purpose and expectation rather than doubt in ordinary Arabic. The verse therefore states what the worship is for, not what Allah is waiting to find out.

phrases.translation: ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy;
phrases.explanation:
This clause is tied grammatically to the one before it, so the relative word here refers back to the Lord who created you, and the two descriptions together specify who is to be worshipped. A resting place is what is spread out to be settled on, and the earth answers to that description for human beings. The sky is named from loftiness and rising above, which is why it stands over the earth as a canopy does over what it shelters.

The heaven and the earth are counted among the favors listed here because both of them supply food, sustenance and the means of existence, and because life in this world depends on them. Naming them first is what makes the command to worship rest on something the hearers can see for themselves.

phrases.translation: and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you.
phrases.explanation: The water sent down from the sky is rain, and what is brought out by it is the fruit of what people themselves planted and sowed in the earth, their crops and their plantings. It is called provision because it is nourishment and food. The favor lies in the joining of the two. The rain comes from above where no human effort reaches it, and the produce comes out of the ground where their effort does, and neither half of that arrangement is theirs to supply. So what the people eat is traced back to the one who sends the rain down and gives the increase, and not only to the labor of the sower.

phrases.translation: So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺
phrases.explanation:
An equal is anything that stands as the counterpart of a thing and resembles it, and the prohibition is against setting up such counterparts to Allah in worship. The people addressed were divided in the explanations recorded, some taking the words as aimed at all who associate partners with Allah, and others at the people of the Torah and the Gospel in particular.

What follows in the verse settles the address. The knowledge mentioned is what these people already held, that Allah is one, that He originated creation and created it and provides for it. The prohibition is therefore not addressed to ignorance. It is addressed to people who grant the creator and provider in argument and then worship something alongside Him, which is why the verse closes by naming what they know.

phrases.translation: And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true
phrases.explanation:
This verse is an argument put by Allah on behalf of His Prophet against those who opposed him, the polytheists among his own people and the unbelievers among the People of the Book. The challenge is framed as a conditional. If the doubt you carry about what has been sent down to Our servant is genuine, then settle it by producing something like it, and the inability to do so answers the doubt.

The exegetes differed about what the likeness required consists in. Some took it to mean a surah like the Quran in eloquence and clear statement. Others took it to mean a surah brought by someone like Muhammad among human beings. The first explanation is preferred, and it is supported by another verse which puts the same challenge. An objection is answered along the way, that the demand is not for one matching the Quran in composition and in the meanings that set it apart from other speech, but only in eloquence.

The helpers called on are explained from the word itself, a plural that can mean those who bear witness for something or those called on to give support. The reading preferred is that these are the people they would gather to help meet the challenge. The verse is finally set beside the fuller form of the same challenge elsewhere in the Quran, where mankind and the jinn are told that even gathered together they would not produce its like.

phrases.translation: But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—
phrases.explanation: The first half of the verse restates the challenge as a failure to meet it. If you do not do it, meaning if you do not produce a surah like it even after you and your associates and helpers have strained together to manage it, then what follows applies. The point is that through your testing and trial your own incapacity and the incapacity of all creation to do so becomes clear to you, and you come to know that it is from Him. The second half is then given its own explanation, that you will never produce a surah like it. So the inability is not a matter of trying harder later. It is a settled fact about what these people are able to do, and the warning that follows rests on it.

phrases.translation: then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones,
phrases.explanation: The fear commanded is fear of entering the Fire, and the reason for it is the denial of the Messenger concerning what he brought from Allah, namely that it is revelation from Him. The Fire is then described by what feeds it, people and stones, and a question about why the stones were singled out and joined with the people is answered by the report that they are stones of sulphur. These are said to be the hottest of stones once they are heated, so the fuel named is of a kind that burns beyond ordinary fire and cannot be put out, and the fuel is described to make plain how terrible is the thing being warned against.

phrases.translation: which is prepared for the disbelievers
phrases.explanation:
Being prepared means the Fire already exists for this purpose rather than being made when the person arrives. The word for disbelievers is explained from its root, since one who covers a thing is called by this name in Arabic, and Allah named the unbeliever with it because he covers and denies what he knows.

The verse is then read back against the ones before it. The Fire is prepared for those who deny that Allah is their Lord, the one who created them and created the people before them, who made the earth a resting place and the sky a canopy, who sent down water and brought out fruit by it. That is the denial in question, so the punishment answers the specific refusal described in the verses leading up to it.

phrases.translation: Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow.
phrases.explanation:
To give good news is to inform, and the root of the word means a report of something that makes the hearer rejoice, given before any other bringer of news gets there. The command is to the Prophet to carry this report to those who believed in Allah and in him and in what he brought from his Lord, and who made that belief true by their deeds.

The gardens named are explained as what is in the garden of trees, fruit and planting, not its ground, since the rivers are said to flow beneath it. The verse is then set beside the one before it, which warned by naming what is prepared for those who disbelieve, while this one encourages by naming what is prepared for those who obey.

phrases.translation: Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,”
phrases.explanation:
The pronoun in from it goes back to the gardens, but what is meant is their trees, so the fruit comes from the trees each time.

The exegetes differed about the saying that follows. Some took it to mean that this is what we were given before in the life of this world. Others took it to mean what they were given before of the fruit of the Garden itself, arguing that whenever fruit is plucked another like it returns in its place, so what comes back matches in every respect what was picked and eaten. The plain wording of the recitation is held to rule out the second reading and to point to the first, that the comparison is with the fruit of this world.

An objection is then answered. How can they say this is what we were given before when what was given earlier has already gone, eaten up, and how can the people of the Garden say something that is not true? The answer is that the meaning is this is of the kind we were given before. It is compared to a man told that so and so has prepared various dishes for him, who answers that this is the food in my own house, meaning the kind of it and not the identical items.

phrases.translation: for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺.
phrases.explanation:
The pronoun in it returns to the provision, so the fruit provided for them is brought to them resembling one another. What that resemblance consists in was explained in several ways. Some said the whole of it is excellent with nothing inferior in it, unlike the fruit of this world. Some said the resemblance is in color while the taste differs. Some said it is in color and taste together. Some said it is the resemblance between the fruit of the Garden and the fruit of this world in color, though their tastes differ. And some said nothing in the Garden resembles anything here except the names.

The explanation preferred is that the fruit is brought resembling in color and appearance while taste and smell differ. Whoever denies that anything in the Garden can be like anything in this world is asked whether the names of its fruit, food and drink are like the names of those things here. If he denies that he contradicts the text of the Book, since Allah made known what is with Him in the Garden only by the names those things carry here.

phrases.translation: They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever
phrases.explanation:
Spouses is the plural of the word for the wife of a man. Purified is then explained as purified from every impurity, filth and defect that occurs in the women of this world, and the list given covers menstruation, bleeding after childbirth, waste, mucus, saliva and the like, with childbearing added in one report.

The pronouns are fixed so that for them returns to those who believe and do good and therein returns to the gardens. Abiding forever is then explained as the continuance of their existence there, with the joy and lasting bliss Allah has granted them, so the promise closes on permanence rather than on any particular pleasure.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller.
phrases.explanation:
The exegetes differed about what this verse was sent down concerning. One report says that when Allah set forth the two parables of the one who kindled a fire and of the rainstorm from the sky, the hypocrites said that Allah is too exalted and too mighty to set forth such parables, and this verse came down in answer. Another says the verse is itself a parable of the life of this world, since the mosquito lives as long as it is hungry and dies once it grows fat.

The report preferred is the first, since the announcement comes right after the parables set forth in this surah for the hypocrites, not after those in other surahs. The verse is then read as an announcement that Allah is not ashamed to set forth parables in the truth, small as well as great, as a trial separating the people of faith from the people of error. He did not mean to inform about the mosquito itself. It is the weakest of creation, chosen for its lowness, and the point is that Allah is not ashamed to set forth the lowest parable or the highest, without limit in loftiness.

A parable is a likeness, and the particle standing with it carries the sense of that which, so the meaning is that Allah is not ashamed to set forth as a parable that which is a mosquito, or something beyond it. The reading preferred is that it means greater than the mosquito, since the mosquito is the extreme of lowness and what lies beyond the weakest of things can only be stronger.

phrases.translation: As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?”
phrases.explanation:
The believers named are those who held Allah and His Messenger to be true, and their knowing that it is the truth from their Lord means that they acknowledge the parable Allah set forth, and that it answers what He set it forth for.

Those who disbelieve are explained as the people who denied the signs of Allah, rejected what they knew and hid what they knew to be true, which is the description of the hypocrites. The verse is finally used as the evidence for the occasion preferred at the start. The people for whom the two preceding parables were set forth are the same people who rejected the parable and asked what Allah meant by it, and this verse answers them, which is why the two groups are set against each other here.

phrases.translation: Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many.
phrases.explanation:
The pronoun in through it refers back to the parable, and this clause begins a fresh announcement rather than continuing the speech of the two groups. Allah leaves many of His creatures astray by the parable He sets forth.

The manner of it is explained on both sides. He adds error upon their error because they denied what they knew with certainty to be true of the parable, and that it agreed with what it was set forth for. He guides by the same parable many of the people of faith, adding guidance to their guidance and faith to their faith, because they affirmed what they knew with certainty and acknowledged it. One instrument therefore produces two opposite outcomes, and the difference lies in what each group did with what it already knew.

phrases.translation: And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—
phrases.explanation: The word translated as rebellious is explained from its root. Its origin in Arabic is going forth out of something, so a date is said to have gone forth when it comes out of its skin, and the mouse is called by a diminutive of the same root because it goes forth out of its hole. The hypocrite and the disbeliever are called by it for going forth out of obedience to their Lord, and the verse describing Iblis is quoted as witness, where he is said to have transgressed the command of his Lord, meaning that he left off obeying Him. The people whom the parable leaves astray are therefore those who had already stepped outside obedience, and the parable adds to a state they were in.

phrases.translation: those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed,
phrases.explanation:
This is the description Allah gives of the corrupt, the people whom the parable mentioned in the verse before leaves astray. The covenant they break was explained in more than one way, the explanation given being Allah's charge to His creatures, His command of obedience and His prohibition of disobedience.

The verdict is that these verses came down about the disbelieving rabbis of the Jews at the time of the Prophet's emigration, together with whoever among the hypocrites persisted in associating partners with Allah. Those who break the covenant are therefore the people who hold back from acknowledging Muhammad and what he brought, and who hide the plain statement of it after knowing it.

After its confirmation is then explained as after Allah had fixed the covenant firmly by taking His pledges for fulfilling it.

phrases.translation: break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained,
phrases.explanation:
What Allah urged to be joined, and whose severing He blames here, is the bond of kinship, and another verse is quoted in which corruption in the land and severing the bonds of kinship are named together. Kinship means the relatives whom the womb of a single mother joins to a person, severing it means withholding the rights Allah made obligatory toward it, and joining it means fulfilling them.

The grammar is settled so that the sense is they sever what Allah commanded to be joined. A wider explanation is also recorded, that they are blamed for cutting off the Messenger and the believers along with their kin.

phrases.translation: and spread corruption in the land.
phrases.explanation:
Spreading corruption in the land is identified with what was described earlier in the surah, where the same expression was used of those the parable leaves astray. It is their disobedience to their Lord, their disbelief in Him, their repudiation of His Messenger, their denial of his prophethood, and their giving the lie to what he brought them from Allah as truth from Him.

The phrase therefore names a state of rejection rather than a set of crimes on the ground. What is corrupted is their standing with Allah and with the truth He sent down, and the one word gathers the whole of that up. It is a description of what they are rather than a list of what they have done to the land.

phrases.translation: It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers
phrases.explanation:
Being in loss is explained as that which diminishes their share of nobility and generosity. It was also said that the meaning is that they perish, and whoever said that intended the perishing of the person whose trait Allah has described here, in that Allah withholds His mercy from him because of his disobedience and disbelief. That reading is then noted as resting on the sense of the statement rather than on the literal nature of the word itself, which is something the people of explanation do at times for reasons that prompt them.

So the word carries the sense of a shortfall rather than of a visible ruin. What is lost is not a possession that can be counted but the share of what is good that these people have given up.

phrases.translation: How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned
phrases.explanation:
The verse is read as a rebuke to those who say we believe in Allah and in the Last Day while not believing it, saying it only to deceive Allah and the believers. The question is therefore not a request for information but their denial put back to them in the face of what they already admit.

The exegetes differed about you were lifeless. Some took it as you were nothing, that is, forgotten with no mention of you. Others took the dying as the departure of the soul from the body, which would make the words an address to the people of the graves, and this is called far fetched, since the rebuke concerns what went before. Another account makes the first dying the return of the servants into the loins of their forefathers after they were taken from the back of Adam.

The sense of the whole is then given. How can you reject Allah when you were drops in the loins of your forefathers and He made you living human beings, then causes you to die, then brings you to life again and raises you on the Day of Gathering for reward and punishment.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens.
phrases.explanation:
The first clause is taken as a statement of favor. Everything on the earth was created for human beings and made subservient to them out of graciousness, so that it is sustenance in this life and a proof of the oneness of their Lord. Creating is explained as bringing the thing out of non being into existence.

Then He turned towards the heaven was explained in different ways. Some said it means He betook Himself purposefully toward it. Others said the word means loftiness and rising up, and they then differed about who rose, some saying it was the Creator of the heaven and others saying it was the smoke which Allah made into a heaven for the earth.

A difficulty is then pressed. Whoever rejects the meaning Arabic itself gives, for fear that rising would imply having been beneath the heaven, does not escape what he ran from. If the word means He turned, was He turned away from the heaven so that He turned toward it? And if this is a turning in governance rather than in action, let him say likewise that He rose above it with the loftiness of dominion rather than of movement.

A question of order follows, whether the turning to the heaven came before its creation or after. The answer is that it came after, and before He fashioned it into seven heavens, and another verse is quoted in which He turns to the heaven while it is still smoke and tells it and the earth to come, willingly or unwillingly.

Forming it is explained as arranging, governing and putting into good order. The summary is that He rose to the seven heavens while they were smoke, fashioned them and joined them firmly, and set in some of them the sun, the moon and the stars.

phrases.translation: And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things
phrases.explanation:
The pronoun here means Allah Himself, and knowing all things is then turned back on the people addressed. The one who created you and fashioned the seven heavens is not unaware of what you show and what you hide in yourselves. The address is to the hypocrites and to those among the People of the Book who deny Allah, who say with their tongues that they believe while working to deny it, and whose scribes rejected what the Messenger brought though they knew it was sound.

The word for knowing is given as an intensive form of the ordinary word for one who knows, and it is reported that He is the one perfect in His knowledge.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels,
phrases.explanation:
The opening particle raises a question of its own, since it means when and there is nothing before it in the sentence for it to attach to. The answer is that the verses before it were already a rebuke, condemning the hearers' deeds and their persistence in misguidance despite the favors given to them and to their forefathers. This clause joins that implied sense, so the meaning runs remember My dealing with your father Adam when I said to the angels that I was going to place a successor on the earth.

The name for angels is tied to the message, since the angels are Allah's messengers between Him and His prophets. One report holds that the address was not to all the angels but to a specific group, the tribe of Iblis, who fought the jinn of the earth with him before Adam was created. They were singled out as a trial, to show them how limited their knowledge was and how many weaker creatures were given excellence over them.

phrases.translation: “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.”
phrases.explanation:
The people of interpretation differed about the verb translated as I am going to place, some reading it as I am going to make and others as I am going to create. The view held correct is that the meaning is I am placing a successor on the earth and bringing him into being there. It was also said that the earth named here is Mecca.

The word for successor is explained from its root. It is built on a pattern meaning one who takes another's place after him in a matter.

A second explanation is recorded, that the word means successors who follow one another, the descendants of Adam, each generation taking the place of the one before. A reading offered by one of the early authorities is set aside as not being the interpretation of the word, even though Allah did inform the angels that He would place a successor on the earth.

phrases.translation: They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?” Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”
phrases.explanation:
A question is raised about the angels' reply. How could they say this when Adam and his descendants had not yet been created? Did they know the unseen, or did they speak from conjecture? The scholars differed in their answers.

One report has the angels first asking what that successor would be, and being told that he would have descendants who would work corruption and kill one another, and only then putting the question recorded here. It is criticized because its beginning undermines its end.

Another report is read as holding that the angels spoke without certain knowledge beforehand, on a supposition of their own, and that Allah answered it with I know what you do not know, meaning that from this successor's descendants would come prophets, messengers and the obedient.

phrases.translation: He taught Adam the names of all things,
phrases.explanation:
The scholars differed about which names were taught. Some said He taught Adam the names of the angels, and others said only the names of all his descendants.

A report from the Messenger is brought in confirmation of what was said about the name Adam itself. On the explanation that he was created from the surface of the earth, the name must have its origin in a verb, in the way that other Arabic names are built from the verbs meaning to praise and to make happy.

The difference about the next clause, that He presented them to the angels, is noted as corresponding exactly to the difference about the names, so the two questions stand or fall together.

phrases.translation: then He presented them to the angels
phrases.explanation:
The statement held most correct, and most in accord with the outward wording of the recitation, is that He taught Adam the names of his descendants and of the angels, and not the names of the remaining species of creation. Allah said that He presented them to the angels, meaning those named with the names He taught Adam.

The wide explanation reported from one of the leading exegetes, that He taught him the name of everything, is accounted for as resting on another codex, since he used to recite according to it. The explanation most fitting to the verse, in line with this reading and the script of the copies in use, is that He presented the bearers of the names, the sons of Adam and the angels, to the angels.

phrases.translation: and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?”
phrases.explanation:
Inform Me is explained as give Me tidings of, and to inform someone of a thing is to give him tidings of it and make it known to him. The explanation held most fitting is that the address runs as follows. Tell Me the names of those I have presented to you, O angels, you who said will You place in it someone who will spread corruption and shed blood while we glorify You with praise and proclaim Your holiness. That is, if you are truthful in your claim that were I to appoint My deputy from others than you his descendants would disobey Me, and that were I to appoint you, you would obey Me. If you do not know the names of these creatures who are created and present before you, then you are more ignorant still of what is not before you.

This way of addressing the angels by way of rebuke is set beside the words said to Noah when he pleaded that his son was of his family, and was told not to ask about what he had no knowledge of, lest he be among the ignorant.

A rival statement is then criticized as one part of which nullifies another. Whoever advanced it claimed that if you are truthful works like a man saying tell me of this if you know it, while knowing that the other does not. The answer is that there is no doubt the meaning is if you are truthful in your statement or in your action, since truthfulness in Arab speech is truthfulness in a report and not in knowledge.

phrases.translation: They replied, “Glory be to You!
phrases.explanation:
This is a notification of the angels returning to their Lord, acknowledging that knowledge of what they did not know belongs to Him, and disavowing any claim that they, or anyone else, would know anything of themselves.

The verse is then read as a proof in favor of the Prophet against the Jews in his midst, since Allah initiated him into knowledge of the unseen into which He had initiated none of His creatures. Allah had already rejected the angels' claim to be the fitter deputies, and He here admonishes those People of the Book, reminding them of the blessings given to their fathers, to turn back to Him and to His obedience.

phrases.translation: We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”
phrases.explanation:
The two names are then explained. All Knowing means that Allah knows without having been taught everything that has been and everything that will be, and knows the unseen, in contrast to all His creation, whose members had just said that they have no knowledge except what He taught them. The words are therefore the angels' own conclusion drawn against themselves.

As for the Wise, some said it carries the sense of the one who judges and rules, in the same way that All Knowing carries the sense of the one who knows and the Well Informed that of the one who is informed. The pattern is that these intensive forms name the one who possesses the quality completely.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.”
phrases.explanation:
The command to Adam is explained by what it achieved. Allah caused His angels, who had asked to be made the deputies on the earth and described themselves as obedient in contrast to others who would spread corruption and shed blood, to recognize that they were ignorant, before He informed them, of the places on which His decree descends, as they were ignorant of the names set before them, since that belonged to what He had not taught them.

They and the rest of the servants know nothing except what their Lord has taught them, and He gives particular knowledge to whomever He wills and withholds it from whomever He wills.

phrases.translation: Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”
phrases.explanation:
Inform them means inform the angels, while of their names means the names of those Allah set before them. The interpreters then differed about what the revealing and concealing refer to.

The saying held most fitting is that I know what you reveal means I know, alongside My knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, what you make manifest with your tongues, and what you were concealing means what you hid within yourselves. What they made manifest was the question reported of them above, and what they concealed was the contradiction and pride Iblis carried against Allah's command.

A second possibility, that the angels concealed a claim to be more honored than any creature Allah might make, is judged to have no proof in the Book or in a binding tradition.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,”
phrases.explanation:
The opening is joined grammatically to the clause before it, so it continues the reminder of favors addressed to the Jews in the place of the Prophet's emigration. Singling Iblis out from among them is read as showing that he was one of them.

Whether he belonged to the angels was disputed. Some said the jinn are a branch of the angels, a tribe of them, and that his tribe was called the jinn, since the Arabs so name whoever hides himself.

The arguments on the other side are judged to show weakness in their authors. It is not strange that Allah created the kinds of His angels from different kinds of creation, some from light and some from fire, and His reporting what Iblis was made from does not put him outside them.

phrases.translation: so they all did—but not Iblîs,
phrases.explanation:
The name is explained as a word on a derived pattern meaning despair of good, regret and grief, and a poet's use of the same root is glossed as dejection and gloom.

A question of grammar follows. If the name is built on that pattern, why was it not fully declined and given the nunation a regular Arabic noun takes? The answer is that full declension was dropped because of its weight, since it is a name with no equal among the names of the Arabs, and they therefore treated it like borrowed names not declined. Another name is cited as parallel, one derived from an Arabic verb yet left without nunation because it was first a name among non Arabs and was then adopted, and a third name is given the same account.

phrases.translation: who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful
phrases.explanation:
He refused means that Iblis refused to prostrate before Adam, and he acted arrogantly means that he thought himself great and too proud to obey Allah in prostrating before him. Although this is a report about Iblis, it is read as a rebuke to his likes, to everyone too proud to submit to Allah's command.

Becoming unfaithful is then explained. Allah described Iblis in the same terms as those for whom He set him as an example in arrogance and envy, meaning that he denied Allah's favors by opposing Him in what He commanded. The same denial is charged against the Jews, who saw the Prophet and beheld Allah's proof in him, then denied his prophethood after knowing it.

phrases.translation: We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise
phrases.explanation:
The verse is read as carrying a clear indication of the order of events. Iblis was expelled from the Garden after he refused out of arrogance to prostrate before Adam, and Adam was placed in it before Iblis came down. It follows that Iblis made them slip from obedience only after he had been cursed and had shown his arrogance.

The exegetes then differed about the state in which Adam's wife was created and the time at which she was made his companion, one placing her creation after he entered the Garden and another before he dwelt there.

The word for wife is discussed on its own account. The wife of a man is named in Arabic by a form without a final letter and by a form with one, the latter more frequent.

phrases.translation: and eat as freely as you please,
phrases.explanation:
The permission is then summed up. The sense is dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat of it an ample and pleasant provision wherever you wish. The word translated freely carries the idea of provision that is wide and agreeable, and the leave given is open as to place, so nothing in the Garden is held back. That makes the single restriction in the next clause the only limit on a permission otherwise complete.

The phrase carries both the quantity of the food and the ease of it, so the reader is not left with the impression of a plain meal but of as much as they want, of the kind they like, taken wherever they please. The single tree that is then named is the one thing excluded from that freedom.

phrases.translation: but do not approach this tree,
phrases.explanation:
The word for tree is explained first. It covers in Arabic everything that stands on a trunk, and a verse is quoted in which the plants and the trees prostrate, the second of the two terms being what stands upon a trunk.

The exegetes then differed about which tree it was. Some said it was the ear of grain, others said the grapevine, and others said the fig tree, and reports are given for each.

The position taken is that Allah informed His servants that Adam and his wife ate of the tree their Lord had forbidden them, and so committed the sin He had forbidden, after He had pointed the tree out to them by saying do not approach this tree. He gave them the indication they needed to know which tree was meant at the time. But Allah placed no indication for His servants, to whom the Quran is addressed, as to which of the trees of the Garden it was, so the identifications offered are not something the text establishes, and the obligation carried by the verse does not depend on settling the question.

phrases.translation: or else you will be wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation:
Two grammatical accounts are given of the verb that follows the prohibition. On the other, the clause carries the sense of an answer to the prohibition, so the meaning is do not approach this tree, for if you approached it you would be among the wrongdoers.

The sense given is that they would then be among those who reach past what is permitted and allowed to them.

The word for wrongdoers is then traced to its origin, which is putting a thing in a place that is not its own. An earth is called wronged when a digger digs in it where digging does not belong, and valley beds are called wronged when rain comes outside its season and pours where it should not.

phrases.translation: But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in,
phrases.explanation:
Two readings of the first verb are noted, the one followed here and another meaning the removal of a thing from another.

What accords with the Book of Allah is judged most in accord with the truth. Allah reported that Iblis whispered to the two of them, that he said their Lord forbade them the tree only lest they become angels or become immortal, and that he swore he was a sincere adviser, while bringing them down by deceit. As for how he reached the Garden after being expelled from it, what is reported contains nothing a person of understanding may refute.

He caused them to depart from what they were in means from the abundant sustenance and wide bounty of the Garden. The expulsion is ascribed to Satan, though Allah expelled them, because their leaving rested on an occasion he brought about.

phrases.translation: and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other.
phrases.explanation:
Allah's statement that follows makes clear that the one who expelled Adam is Allah, and that the ascription to Iblis stands as described.

The interpreters differed about who is intended by the plural in descend, while agreeing that Adam and his wife are among them.

A question about the enmity named is then answered. The enmity of Iblis toward Adam and his offspring is his envy and his arrogance against obeying Allah in prostrating to him. The enmity of Adam's offspring toward Iblis is the enmity of the believers toward him because of his disbelief. The war between us is held to go back to Iblis being brought into the Garden after Allah expelled him, until he made Adam slip by eating of the forbidden tree.

phrases.translation: You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”
phrases.explanation:
The people of interpretation differed about the residence named here, and one explanation given was that it means an abode in the graves.

The word itself is settled from the language. It means the place of settling, so wherever anyone is on the earth at this moment, that place is his dwelling. What Allah intended is that they have on the earth a dwelling and an abode in their locations, in place of the Garden and the heaven.

The provision mentioned with it was likewise explained in two ways, some taking it as sustenance until death and others as lasting until the coming of the Hour. The word in Arabic covers everything from which enjoyment is taken, whether sustenance, household goods or adornment. Since Allah made the life of every living thing an enjoyment for it during the days of its life, and made the earth an enjoyment for human beings during the days of their life, the enjoyment runs to the term appointed for each life, which is what both explanations describe.

phrases.translation: Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord,
phrases.explanation:
The verb translated as inspired is explained as taking the words up and accepting them, and its root is traced to a pattern derived from meeting, as when one man goes out to meet another.

The exegetes then differed about what the words were. One report gives them as a supplication opening with the confession that there is no god but Allah. The statements transmitted are said to differ in wording while agreeing in meaning: that Allah extended words to Adam, that Adam received them from his Lord, accepted them and acted on them, and that through them his repentance was accepted.

What the Book of Allah itself points to is then preferred.
