The words Adam received are the words Allah reported him saying when he excused himself before his Lord and confessed his guilt, our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us we shall be among the losers.

phrases.translation: so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation:
He accepted his repentance is explained with the pronoun fixed as returning to Adam, and the sense given is that Allah granted him repentance for his sin, the word itself meaning a turning back.

The two names that follow are then explained. The Ever Relenting is the one who accepts the repentance of whichever of His sinful servants turns back to Him, and who holds off from requiting him once he has turned. The Merciful means that He bestows mercy along with the repentance, and His mercy toward the sinner is the wiping out of his offense and the forgiving of the punishment his transgression had earned.

phrases.translation: We said, “Descend all of you!
phrases.explanation:
The command to descend had already been explained earlier in the surah, and its meaning here is the same as its meaning there, so it is not gone over again.

One point is drawn out. The outward sense of the address reaches only those who were told to descend, all of them, and the people addressed are the ones named on the authority of the Companions, so the command is not read as extending beyond them on the strength of this verse alone. The word all of them gathers those who were in the Garden when the command was given, and the sentence about whoever then follows My guidance is a separate statement about those who come after them, not a reading of this one.

phrases.translation: Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.explanation:
The opening particle is worked through first. The sense is if there comes to you, and the particle joined to if strengthens the utterance, which is why the doubled letter was added.

Guidance here means clarification and right direction, and whoever follows it means whoever follows what Allah sent on the tongues of His messengers. No fear shall come upon them then means that they are safe amid the terrors of the Resurrection from Allah's punishment, because they obeyed Him and followed His path, and nor shall they grieve completes the same promise.

A further view is recorded and answered. It holds that the command to descend, though addressed to Adam and his wife, is to be understood as intended for them and their offspring. That reading is acknowledged as one the verse could bear, but is judged farther from the correct meaning than what stays closer to the outward sense.

phrases.translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”
phrases.explanation:
Those who disbelieve and deny the signs are explained as those who rejected Allah's signs and accused His messengers of lying. The signs are His proofs and His indications of His oneness and His sovereignty, together with what the messengers brought as marks and testimonies of that and as proof of their own truthfulness in what they reported from Him.

The outcome named for them is that they are the companions of the Fire and will remain in it, which is the counterpart of the safety from fear and grief promised in the verse before to those who follow the guidance. The word for the inhabitants of the Fire is used to exclude everyone else, and to say that they will abide there eternally, with no end to it.

phrases.translation: O children of Israel!
phrases.explanation:
The children of Israel are the children of Yaqub, the son of Ishaq, the son of Ibrahim. Yaqub was called Israel, which is explained as the servant of Allah and His chosen one among His creatures, the second element of the name being a name of Allah.

The address is then placed. It is directed to the scholars of the Jews from among the children of Israel who were present in the region to which the Messenger of Allah had emigrated, and their lineage is traced to Yaqub in the way that lineage is traced elsewhere in the Quran. The word children means the descendants, and the whole address gathers them under the one name their ancestor was given.

phrases.translation: Remember My favours upon you.
phrases.explanation:
The favor recalled is then listed. Allah chose the messengers from among them, sent down the books on them, and saved them from the trial and affliction they were under with Pharaoh and his people, along with the provision that followed their rescue.

The reminder given here through Muhammad is set beside the reminder Musa gave their forefathers in his own time, about which Allah reported that he spoke to them, so the command to remember is of a piece with the earlier one and repeats it to a later generation. The favor is therefore not a private memory but a debt passed down, and the children of Israel are being asked to answer for what their forefathers received.

phrases.translation: Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine,
phrases.explanation:
The meaning of the covenant was already set out earlier, with the disagreement over it and the judgment preferred, so it is not repeated. Here it is Allah's covenant with them, and the second half states His side of it.

His covenant with them is explained as the promise that if they did what was asked He would admit them to the Garden. Their side of it is to fulfil what was required of them, and His side is the reward He has promised. The verse in which Allah took the covenant of the children of Israel and raised up twelve leaders from among them is quoted as the parallel, since it sets out the same exchange in full, with the conditions named and the reward promised.

phrases.translation: and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺
phrases.explanation:
Fear Me alone is explained as a command to fear Allah by Himself and to guard against His punishment. The people addressed are named as those among the children of Israel who neglect His covenant and deny His messenger, the one Allah took their oath about in the books He sent down to His prophets, that they should believe in him and follow him. The fear commanded is therefore directed at a specific refusal they are already committed to.

The word alone carries its weight. They are told to fear the one God without setting anyone alongside Him, and to take care of His punishment, which is the point the verse makes after the favors it has recalled. The whole address is turned on them, and the command is to hold to that one loyalty.

phrases.translation: Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures.
phrases.explanation:
Believe is explained as affirming something to be true, and what is affirmed is the revelation sent down to Muhammad. The word confirming is then given its grammatical place. It describes the state of what was sent down, referring back to the pronoun understood inside the verb, so the new revelation confirms the scripture they already hold.

Two readings of the command that follows are set aside. One took be not the first to deny it as meaning denial of their own Book, on the ground that denying Muhammad is denying a Book that carries his description. Both are judged to lie far from the apparent sense to which the recitation points, because the verse begins by commanding belief in what Allah sent down, and the denial spoken of is denial of that.

phrases.translation: Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain.
phrases.explanation:
A question of grammar is raised and answered. How can the word for disbeliever be singular when the command is addressed to a multitude? The answer is that the singular follows the sense of the word for whoever, with an explicit noun built from the verb put in its place, and elsewhere the same idea is put in the plural.

The meaning is then given as an address to the scholars of the People of the Book. Acknowledge as true what I sent down to My messenger of the Quran, which confirms your Book, and do not be the first to reject it after knowing it.

Trading the signs for a small price is explained last. The reading given is do not sell the knowledge I gave you through My Book and My signs for a contemptible price and a paltry worldly gain. Their selling of it is holding back what they were required to make clear, in exchange for what they are paid.

phrases.translation: And be mindful of Me
phrases.explanation:
Fear Me in selling My signs for a contemptible price, in buying the paltry goods of this world with them, in disbelieving what I sent down to My messenger and in denying him. A note on the language of satiety follows, with the saying that the food of one suffices for two and the food of two for four, since the gain they took fills a person and leaves him base.

The command is therefore not a vague instruction to be pious. It names the things they are doing, and the fear is pointed at those. The phrase alone rules out any other object of awe, so the weight of the command falls on what Allah has just said they did to His revelations.

phrases.translation: Do not mix truth with falsehood
phrases.explanation:
Mixing is explained from its root. The verb means to intermingle, and one says I mixed this matter up for him when one obscures a thing by mingling it with something else. A second verb from the same letters is distinguished from it, the one meaning the wearing of clothes, so the two are not confused.

The mixing named in the verse is then described. Among those addressed were hypocrites who displayed affirmation of Muhammad outwardly while concealing disbelief in him inwardly, and the majority of them said that he was a prophet truly sent, but sent to the Arabs alone and not to them. That is the mixing of truth with falsehood, since they joined a true acknowledgment to a false restriction of it.

Two possibilities that the verse can bear are set out, one reported by an early authority and another by two others. A point of grammar accompanies them, concerning a verb put in the accusative because it follows the same construction as the one for concealing, the sense being a single connected prohibition rather than two separate ones.

phrases.translation: or hide the truth knowingly
phrases.explanation:
Two interpretations of concealing the truth are noted. On the first, Allah forbade them to hide the truth just as He forbade them to mix it with falsehood, so the two prohibitions stand side by side. On the second, they form one connected act, the hiding being how the mixing is carried out. What makes the hiding culpable is the closing phrase, since they did it knowing that what they suppressed was the truth.

The knowledge is what turns the concealment into guilt. A truth hidden by someone who did not know it was the truth could be excused, but these were the scholars of the People of the Book, and the truth they suppressed was the truth they had. That is what the phrase knowingly is doing, and why the verse ends on it.

phrases.translation: Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down
phrases.explanation:
The command is placed first. It is reported that the scribes of the Jews and their hypocrites used to tell people to establish the prayer and give the alms tax without doing either themselves, and this verse is read as a command to those same people to perform what they had ordered others to do.

Establishing the prayer is not gone over again, since its meaning was set out. The alms tax is then explained from its name. It is called by a word meaning growth and purity even though it is wealth separated from wealth, because Allah makes what is separated out bear fruit and increase, so the name belongs to it by what Allah does through it rather than by the amount.

The closing command to bow with those who bow is read as a command to join those who pray rather than stand apart. It is addressed to the scribes and hypocrites named at the start, and requires them to do with the believers what they had been telling other people to do.

phrases.translation: Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture?
phrases.explanation:
The exegetes differed about the righteousness these people were urging on others. The statements recorded are judged to be close together in meaning, so the difference in wording does not divide the sense.

The explanation whose correctness is shown by the outward wording of the recitation is then given. It runs, do you command people to obey Allah and leave yourselves disobedient, while you recite the Book. The rebuke lies in the joining of the two. The people addressed read a scripture that carries the description of the messenger and the command to follow him, and they told others to do what that scripture requires while not doing it themselves.

The form of the sentence is a question, but it is not asked in order to be answered. It is put to them as a reproach, so that the ugliness of what they were doing is stated in the shape of something they have to admit. The scribes are therefore charged with two faults at once, urging obedience they withheld and knowing the Book they were not following.

phrases.translation: Do you not understand
phrases.explanation:
The closing question is explained as do you not then understand and grasp the ugliness of what you are doing. It is not a doubt about whether they have minds but a way of saying that their conduct is one no one who understood it would keep up.

This closing is then used as confirmation of the reading given before it, namely that the scribes of the Jews among the children of Israel ordered others to follow what they themselves were not following, since a reproach about failing to understand fits a people who knew better and acted otherwise. The question is put to them as a challenge, and it is put last so that it lands on everything that has been said before it.

phrases.translation: And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—
phrases.explanation:
Patience is explained first as patience in fulfilling the covenant they had concluded with Allah and in keeping His obedience. It was also said that the word here means fasting, fasting being one of the senses the word carries in Arabic, so the two explanations are not opposed.

A question is then raised about the second half of the command. If seeking help through patience is understood as holding to the covenant and to obedience, what is the meaning of seeking help through prayer? The answer given is that prayer is the means by which the servant asks for what he cannot carry by himself, so the two are joined because one is endurance and the other is a request for the strength to endure.

The verse is then placed. Allah commanded those whose case He had described, the scholars of the children of Israel, to take their refuge in fulfilling His covenant through patience and through prayer, so the command is directed at people who already knew what the covenant required of them.

The closing clause is explained last. It is heavy means that prayer, or the covenant it serves, weighs on the person who carries it, and the weight is lifted only for the humble, who are the people described in the verse that follows. The exception is therefore not about strength of body but about a disposition, since what makes the burden light is the fear of standing before Allah that the next verse describes.

phrases.translation: those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return
phrases.explanation:
A difficulty is raised about the first word. How can Allah describe as humble in obedience people of whom He reports that they suppose, when supposing is commonly understood as less than knowing? The answer is that the word in Arabic is used for certainty as well as for doubt, and that this is a regular feature of the language rather than a loose usage. Words of the same kind are cited, one that means both darkness and light, and another that means both the one who gives help and the one who calls for it, so a single form carries two opposite senses.

Witnesses are then brought from Arabic speech and from the Quran. A speaker says be certain that two thousand armed men are coming to you, using the word for supposing where certainty is meant, and a poet is quoted to the same effect. From the Quran, the verse in which the criminals see the Fire and suppose that they are about to fall into it is cited, where what they have is not doubt but the certainty of someone looking at what is in front of him.

The word for supposing in this verse is therefore read as certainty. What the humble are certain of is stated in the two clauses that follow, and each is explained on its own. That they will meet their Lord means that they will stand before Him and be brought to account, which is the meeting the Quran speaks of for the day of judgment. That to Him they return means that their going back is to Him and to no other, so the return is not to a place but to a person who judges.

The two clauses together are what makes the burden of the previous verse light. A person who is certain that he will meet his Lord and that his return is to Him carries patience and prayer differently from someone who treats this life as the whole of things. The description of the humble is therefore completed by naming the knowledge they hold, and the whole passage from the command to seek help through patience ends by explaining who is able to do it.

phrases.translation: O Children of Israel! Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you
phrases.explanation:
The command to remember the favor is explained here as in the earlier verse where the same words occur, so it is not repeated. What is recalled is the favor Allah bestowed on them, and the address runs to the descendants of those on whom it was bestowed, so the favor is theirs to remember even though it was given to those who came before them.

That is the whole of the explanation here, since the earlier verse has already said it. The repetition serves a purpose of its own. Having heard what the favor was and what was done with it, the children of Israel are now told to remember it, and the words that follow are the list of what is to be remembered and the duties that go with it.

phrases.translation: and how I honoured you above the others
phrases.explanation:
The preference named is also part of what Allah brings to their remembrance of His blessings on them. It is then limited in scope. The explanation preferred is that they were preferred above the worlds of their own time, that is, above the peoples who lived alongside them, rather than above every people until the end of the world.

The proof offered for that limitation is a narration from the Prophet which makes clear that the children of Israel were not preferred above the community of Muhammad. Since a later community is held to be greater, the preference claimed in the verse cannot be an absolute one, and the reading that confines it to the people of that time is the one that fits both the verse and the narration.

phrases.translation: Guard yourselves against the Day
phrases.explanation:
The command to guard against a day is a warning from Allah to the people addressed, and the day is described by what will not happen in it rather than by what will. It is the Day of Resurrection, on which no soul can recompense anything for another soul, on which no father can recompense anything for his child, and no child for his father.

A point of grammar is settled along the way. Something referring back to the day is left unspoken in the clause that follows, and it is omitted because what comes after is a sufficient indication of it, so the listener supplies it without being told. Some grammarians held that the omitted element could be nothing other than that pronoun, while others allowed a wider range, and both are reported.

phrases.translation: on which no soul will be of help to another.
phrases.explanation:
The verb translated as be of help is traced to its root, which in Arabic means satisfaction and recompense. One says I satisfied him his loan and his debt, using the same verb. The scholars of the language then differed about two related forms, some holding that one means I satisfied on your behalf and the other I did sufficiently, and others that both carry a single meaning.

The question is put, what does it mean that no soul can satisfy for another soul or bring it any benefit, and the answer is that it cannot discharge what the other owes. A claim by some grammarians that the sense is that one soul cannot take the place of another is rejected, on the ground that if that had been the meaning the wording would differ.

phrases.translation: No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given
phrases.explanation:
Intercession is explained from its root, a verbal noun taken from saying that so and so interceded for me with so and so. The verse is then read as a whole. Guard yourselves against a day on which no soul can discharge for another soul a right owed to Allah or owed to another person, on which no intercession is accepted from it, on which no ransom is taken from it, and on which no help is given to it.

The reason those four things are named is given. Allah addressed the people this verse concerns in this way because they were Jews who held that their righteous forefathers would intercede for them with Allah and so save them from His punishment. The verse deprives them of that hope, since it states plainly that on the day in question no intercession from a soul is accepted and no ransom taken, however the person claiming it may be related to the righteous.

A distinction is then drawn so that the verse is not read as a denial of intercession altogether. It is made clear that Allah may remit for His believing servants through the intercession of the Prophet on their behalf. The denial here concerns the day as it faces those who die rejecting what Allah sent, and it removes the specific claim these people were relying on, not the intercession Allah Himself permits for believers.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh,
phrases.explanation:
The word for people is explained first. It is used properly with names that are well known, as in the house of the Prophet or the kin of a named man, so the people of Pharaoh are those attached to him and following him rather than his family in the narrow sense.

Pharaoh himself is then described. It is said that the name was a title given to the kings of the Amalekites in Egypt, in the same way that some Roman rulers were called by one title and some Persian rulers by another.

A question follows about the address. How is it right to say We delivered you when the people being spoken to never met Pharaoh and were not present at any of it? The answer is that the favor bestowed on the forefathers is spoken of as bestowed on the descendants, because what befell the ancestors is counted among the blessings and the trials of the people who came from them.

phrases.translation: who afflicted you with dreadful torment,
phrases.explanation:
The dreadful torment is explained as the punishment that did them evil, and some said it means the most severe punishment. The question is then asked what that punishment was, and the verse answers it in the two clauses that follow.

A point about the ascription is settled. Allah ascribes to the people of Pharaoh what was done to the children of Israel, the imposition of the dreadful torment and the slaughtering of the sons, even though the order came from Pharaoh himself. The deeds are named as theirs because they carried them out, and this is how Arabic speech attributes the acts of a people to the whole of them.

phrases.translation: slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord
phrases.explanation:
A dissenting explanation of keeping your women departs from the others, and those who hold it are criticized for leaving the explanation of the leading exegetes. The reading preferred takes the phrase in its plain sense of sparing the women while killing the sons.

The trial mentioned with it is explained in two steps. In that means in what We did for you, namely Our saving you from the state you were in, so what is named is the deliverance, not the suffering before it. The word translated as test is also explained as meaning a favor, because its origin in Arabic speech is testing and trial, and it came to be used of good and evil alike. That is why a deliverance can be called by the same name as the torment it ended.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea,
phrases.explanation:
The clause is joined grammatically to the one before it, so this is a second item in the same list of favors. We parted the sea for you is then explained as We divided the sea for you, and the manner of it is given. They were twelve tribes, so the sea was split into twelve paths, one for each tribe.

Before your very eyes is then explained. It means that they looked on at the parting of the sea and at the destruction of the people of Pharaoh, so nothing in the event was hidden from them. The purpose of recalling it is stated as well. Allah brings them to a halt at the place of His proofs against them and reminds them of His favors toward their forefathers.

phrases.translation: rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes
phrases.explanation:
A question is raised about how Allah drowned the people of Pharaoh and saved the children of Israel in one event, and the answer is given from the reports of what happened at the sea. The two acts are named together because they were one happening seen from two sides, the rescue of one group and the destruction of the other, and both took place while those addressed were watching.

So the verse puts the saving and the drowning in one clause. What the children of Israel saw was not one thing and then another but a single scene, in which they were carried through on dry ground while the water closed over the people of Pharaoh. That is why the phrase before your very eyes is attached to both halves.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence,
phrases.explanation:
The appointment is discussed first. Two readings of the verb are recorded, both transmitted by the community and recited by the reciters, and the judgment given is that both are sound, so the verse is read either as Allah appointing a term or as Allah making an appointment with Moses. An objection is answered along the way, namely the claim that an appointment of this kind can only be between people and that Allah stands alone in promising and threatening. That claim is judged to have no validity against a recitation the community carries.

The name Moses is then explained. It is reported to be two words in Coptic meaning water and tree, the first part being the word for water and the second the word for a tree, and he was named from them because of where he was found. His lineage is given after that, tracing him through Imran back to Levi, then to Jacob who is Israel, then to Isaac and Abraham.

With the man named and the term fixed at forty nights, the verse turns to what the people did during it. They took the calf after he had gone, and that is the favor recalled here, since the appointment itself was a gift to them.

phrases.translation: acting wrongfully
phrases.explanation:
Wrongdoing is explained from its root sense. It is putting a thing where it does not belong, and what they did was place worship in a position other than its proper one. Worship belongs to Allah alone, and they gave it to a calf, so the closing phrase names the act as a wrong done to the order of things and not merely as a lapse.

The charge therefore falls on what they chose to worship and not on any flaw in how they carried it out. The people addressed were not rebuked for a careless act but for setting up something in the place of what should have been there, and the word used is the same one that describes the wrong done to the order of things itself.

phrases.translation: Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you so perhaps you would be grateful
phrases.explanation:
Pardon is explained first as restraint. Allah refrained from striking them with punishment immediately after what they had done, and that holding back is what the word covers here, rather than a wiping out that leaves no trace of the matter.

The closing clause is then explained. So that perhaps you would be grateful means so that you would be grateful, and the word translated as perhaps is discussed in this context, since it does not carry doubt on the part of the one who speaks. The sense of the whole is then given. Allah pardoned them after they had taken the calf as a god, so that they would be grateful to Him for the pardon, pardon being the kind of favor that calls for gratitude from the person who receives it.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture—the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺ that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation:
The two things given to Moses are explained together. The Book is the Torah, and the Criterion is that which separates truth from falsehood. Two interpretations of how the two names relate are recorded, and the one judged most fitting is that of the leading exegetes.

A point of grammar supports that choice. The word for the Book stands in the place of the Torah as a description of it, which allows the name Torah to be left unspoken, and the Criterion is appended to it. The meaning of the word for Book was set out earlier as that which is written.

The reason this reading is preferred is given last. What comes before it in the verse is the mention of the Book, and a description attached to something already named is the natural construction, so the guidance asked for in the closing clause follows from a scripture that carries the means of telling things apart.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf,
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as a reminder. Remember when Moses said to his people from among the children of Israel that they had wronged themselves, their wronging of themselves being their taking the calf as a god. The wrong is described as falling on them rather than on anyone else, which is why the sentence that follows is a way out rather than a threat.

Moses then commanded them to turn back from their sin and to repent to Allah from their apostasy, by showing repentance to Him and submitting to obedience. The command is therefore explained as a route back, and the harshness of what follows belongs to that purpose.

phrases.translation: so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.” Then He accepted your repentance.
phrases.explanation:
Turning in repentance is explained as a return to obedience to their Creator and to what pleases Him. The command to kill themselves is then reported with its outcome, that their slain reached seventy thousand according to what is transmitted, after which Allah lifted the killing from them and accepted their repentance.

The closing clause of the command is explained as telling them that their repentance carried out through the killing of themselves is better for them in the sight of their Creator, so the act is presented as a gain and not only as a penalty. The verse then reports that Allah turned in forgiveness to them, which is the acceptance that ended the matter.

phrases.translation: Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation:
The two names are explained by returning to the meaning of repentance, already shown earlier to be a turn from what Allah detests to what pleases Him in obedience. The Ever Relenting is then described as the one who returns to His servant with what the servant loves, here the forgiving of sins and the covering of them with mercy, and the Merciful as the name that completes it. The verse ends on the acceptance rather than on the killing, so the last word is left with the two names.

The people are said to have responded to what Moses commanded them, which was to show repentance for what they had done against their Lord. The turning was not a word but an act, and the names describe what answered it.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,” so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on
phrases.explanation:
The verse is placed first. Allah made known to those He addressed, the Jews of the children of Israel among whom the Prophet was living, what their forefathers had done, so the reminder falls on people who claim those ancestors as their own.

The demand itself is then explained. They told Moses they would not believe him until they saw Allah openly, which is a request for a sight that removes the need for belief rather than for a sign that supports it. The condition is what makes the demand culpable, since it makes belief depend on something no created being is given in this life.

The people of interpretation differed about the nature of the thunderbolt that seized them. What they agree on is that it came while they were looking on, which the verse states in its closing clause, so the event was witnessed by those it struck and by those who saw them struck.

phrases.translation: Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful
phrases.explanation:
Raising is explained as bringing back to life, and the death named after it is the death by the thunderbolt that destroyed them. The two clauses therefore answer each other, the raising undoing exactly what the previous verse described.

The purpose clause is then explained. So that perhaps you would be grateful means that Allah did this with them so that they would be grateful to Him for the favor He bestowed on them, the favor being their return to life after they had been struck down. Gratitude is thus attached to a second gift, since the pardon mentioned earlier was the first.

A second explanation of the raising is recorded as well. Others said the meaning is that Allah sent them forth as prophets, and that view is reported alongside the first. The reading preferred is the one that fits the sequence, because the verse before it speaks of the thunderbolt striking them while they looked on, and a return to life after that is the plain sense of the words.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds
phrases.explanation:
The shading is joined grammatically to the raising mentioned in the previous verse, so this is another item in the same list of favors. The word for the cloud is then explained. It is a plural formed like the word for clouds from its singular, and it names what covers the sky and wraps it.

Since the word means that which covers the sky and veils its surface from whoever looks at it, what they were shaded by is described as something spread over them rather than a single passing cloud. Some have said that the cloud with which Allah shaded the children of Israel was not an ordinary cloud, and it has also been said that it is that part of the clouds which is white. The favor is therefore a covering that stood over them and kept the sun off them in the wilderness.

phrases.translation: and sent down to you manna and quails,
phrases.explanation:
The two foods sent down are explained one after the other. The exegetes differed about the first of them, and the explanations are several. Some said it was a resin, others a drink that came down like honey and was mixed with water, others that it was honey, others that it was a thin bread like millet and flour, others that it was ginger, and others that it was what falls upon the trees and the grass, which the people went out to and ate. The verse names the thing without describing it, which is why the explanations differ, and what they share is that it came without cultivation and without labor on their part.

A saying of the Prophet is added to that, that the truffle is part of the manna and its juice is a healing for the eye.

The second food is a bird. The name given in the verse is explained as that of a bird resembling the quail, and a note on its form follows, that the singular and the plural share one shape, as in the ordinary word for quail. It was also said that the singular of the word is a longer form ending in the feminine, that it was a bird larger than the quail, that it was a fat bird like the dove, and that the south wind used to drive them together on the people.

Both foods are described as sent down, which places them with the shading as provision given from above in the same period. The question is then put, why the cloud was used to shade them and why these foods were sent. The answer is that the people had asked for food in the wilderness, where there was neither shade nor cultivation, and the sending down of the manna and the quails answered that need, and the cloud the need for cover.

phrases.translation: ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.”
phrases.explanation:
The command to eat is explained with a point of grammar. This belongs to the kind of speech in which what is stated is enough to indicate what has been left out, and the sense here is that Allah shaded them and sent down their food while saying to them, eat of the good things with which We have provided you. The saying is understood without being spelled out.

Of the two views recorded about how this clause attaches to what precedes, the first is judged the more fitting, because the verse is describing a condition of pleasant living that Allah bestowed on them. The word for what is also noted, that it carries the sense of that which, as though it were said, eat of the good things of that which We provided you.

phrases.translation: The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves
phrases.explanation:
Wronging is explained in the same way as before. Allah did not receive harm from what they did, and their disobedience did not diminish anything belonging to Him, so the wrong is described as falling on themselves. A note on the grammar accompanies it, this clause too belonging to the kind of speech in which what is stated indicates what has been left out.

The point is then made general. The disobedience of a disobedient person does not harm Allah and the wrongdoing of a wrongdoer does not lessen His treasures, which is why the verse can deny the wrong against Him and affirm it against them in the same breath.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please;
phrases.explanation:
The command to enter the town is explained together with the permission that follows it. Eat of it wherever you wish means a provision that is pleasant and ample, given without reckoning and without accounting, and the sense of that word was already expounded earlier in the work, so it is not repeated here.

The favor in the command lies in its openness. They are told to enter a town and eat from it wherever they wish, which removes both the question of where they may settle and the question of how much they may take. The reminder is placed at the head of the verse because the commands that follow are conditions attached to a gift already given.

phrases.translation: enter the gate with humility,
phrases.explanation:
Prostrating is explained as being humble and submissive. The explanation given by one of the leading exegetes is then set out, that the word means bowing, since the one who bows is bent over even though his posture is not a full prostration, and the two words therefore cover one act of lowering oneself.

A consequence is drawn about the next clause. On the explanation reported from another, the word for remission that follows would have to be read in the accusative, and the reasoning behind that requirement is given. A parallel is also cited from ordinary speech, the way a person says hearing and obeying to mean that he hears and obeys, which is the same construction the verse uses when it joins an act to a word said while doing it.

phrases.translation: saying, ‘Absolve us.’
phrases.explanation:
The word translated as absolve us is explained from its root. It is a noun on a known pattern, derived from the saying that Allah has removed your sins from you, so the word they were told to say is itself a request for the taking away of sins.

The exegetes then differed about what exactly the word amounts to. Some said something along the lines of the explanation just given, that it is a request for remission. Others said its meaning is that they were told to say there is no god but Allah, as if they directed the explanation toward saying that which removes your sins from you, since the confession of oneness is what removes them. The reports naming who held each view are given with them.

Both readings agree on the purpose of the word, which is that the people were asked to speak a sentence that acknowledges their need of forgiveness at the moment they entered the town in humility.

phrases.translation: We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers.”
phrases.explanation:
Forgiving is explained as covering. Allah will cover their sins with mercy and conceal them, so that He does not disgrace them by punishing them for what they did. A witness from ordinary speech is given for the sense of covering, the way one says that a person covers another's ignorance by forbearing with him, which is concealment rather than approval.

The word for sins is then explained, with the sense that the people described by it have missed the truth and gone wrong. The closing promise is explained last. Allah will increase the doers of good, which is read as an addition beyond the forgiving already promised, so the verse moves from covering what was done badly to giving more for what is done well, and the two together are the reward attached to entering as they were told.

phrases.translation: But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say.
phrases.explanation:
Exchanging is explained as altering, and the people described as wrongdoers are those who did what they were not permitted to do. The change is in the saying they were given, so the verse names it as a saying other than the one said to them, which is the word for remission they had been commanded to speak on entering the gate. The word for remission is explained as meaning that their sins will be taken away, and the reports agree that they entered the gate in a manner other than the one commanded.

The wrongness and the change belong together. They were told to enter with humility and to say the word of remission as they went in, and the wrongdoers altered it. What they changed was the word, not the place.

phrases.translation: So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness
phrases.explanation:
The punishment sent down is explained next. Upon those who did wrong means upon those who did what was not permitted to them, and the word for punishment is one whose meaning was already demonstrated earlier, namely punishment itself. Allah's punishment is then noted to be of various kinds, so the word does not fix a single form of it.

The reports about what was sent are weighed, and one explanation is preferred. The view reported from Ibn Zayd is judged to be the one that settles in the mind as correct, on account of a report mentioned from the Messenger of Allah, and that reasoning is given in full. The clause closes with the reason attached to the punishment, which is that they were going out of obedience, so the sending down is traced to a settled habit rather than to a single act.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place.
phrases.explanation:
Asking for water is explained as asking Allah for water for his people, that is, asking Him to provide it for them, and the people of Moses are the children of Israel whose stories Allah recounts here.

Two clauses are then discussed as grammar. The saying strike the rock with your staff and the gushing of the springs belong to the kind of speech in which what is stated indicates what has been left out, and the same is said of each group knew its drinking place, whose sense is that each group knew its place.

The reason that clause is mentioned is then given. Allah informed them of it because of their state with respect to the water He brought forth, since twelve springs answered to twelve groups and each had its own source.

phrases.translation: ˹We then said,˺ “Eat and drink of Allah’s provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”
phrases.explanation:
The permission and the prohibition are joined in one address. Alongside allowing them what He allowed and bestowing on them the pleasant life He gave them, Allah addressed them with a command, so the prohibition comes attached to a favor and not on its own.

Spreading corruption is then explained as going beyond the limits and striving on the earth as corrupters. The root of the word is examined, and it is said to mean intensity of corruption, indeed the most intense form of it, with a witness quoted for the way the verb is used of someone who has gone to that extreme among people. What the verse forbids is therefore not a small fault but the worst kind of disorder, named as such right after the provision that made their life easy.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺.
phrases.explanation:
Patience is explained first, and its meaning was set out earlier as the restraining and withholding of the soul. The complaint is therefore that they could not hold themselves to a single kind of food. What they could not endure is named as one food, which is the provision that came to them in the wilderness in the same form day after day, without cultivation and without trade.

The verse is placed among the favors that are recalled, and this one is put among them because it is the one that led to the provision of the earth produce in the next verse. The people were not complaining of hunger in the ordinary sense, but of the sameness of what they were given, and the answer was to give them variety.

phrases.translation: So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces
phrases.explanation:
The request is put through Moses rather than to Allah directly. They ask him to call on his Lord for them so that He brings forth for them some of what the earth grows, and what they name is the ordinary produce of settled land, herbs and cucumbers and the rest of the list that follows. The asking itself is not forbidden here, and the verse reports it without comment at this point.

The word for the earth produce is settled from the language and means the growing things of the ground. What they ask for is not a miracle but an ordinary harvest, and the phrase some of it leaves open that they are asking for a portion and not for everything.

phrases.translation: of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.”
phrases.explanation:
The crops named are discussed, and the disagreement falls on one word. The exegetes differed about it, some saying that it means wheat and bread and others saying that it means garlic. The naming of both wheat and bread by that word belongs to the old language, and it is transmitted from speakers of that language in the form of an order, bake for us, meaning bake bread for us.

A variant reading is recorded beside it. It is mentioned that one of the companions read the word with a different first letter, giving the word for garlic directly. If that is correct, it belongs to the cases in which letters are interchanged between two forms of one word, and an example of such an interchange in another word is given with it.

phrases.translation: Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for.”
phrases.explanation:
The rebuke is explained word by word. The word translated as worse is taken by some in the sense of nearer, as the comparative form of nearness, but the point is settled by the thing itself. There is no doubt that whoever exchanges the manna and the quails for herbs, cucumbers, lentils, onions and garlic has exchanged low sustenance for the high sustenance it replaced. A note on the language accompanies this, concerning a glottal stop in the word for what is near or low, reported as a dialectal variant whose omission is another variant.

Moses then asks, and the answer comes. It is explained that he called upon his Lord, that Allah answered him, and that He said to them, go down to a city. This belongs to the kind of speech in which something is left out and what is visible is enough to indicate it, since the asking and the answering are understood without being spelled out.

The city named is the largest question in the verse, and it begins with the recitation. The reciters differed about the word. Most of them read it with the full ending, which makes it a city among cities and not a particular place. Some read it without that ending and without the final letter, which makes it the Egypt of Pharaoh specifically.

The argument of those who took it as a city among cities is given. It rests on what Allah did with the land of Syria, and on His forbidding those people from entering it until they perished in the wandering of the wilderness, testing them with roaming in the land, so a command to go down to Egypt does not fit that history.

The verdict is stated plainly. In the Book of Allah there is no proof for the correctness of either explanation, and there is no report about it from the Messenger, so neither can be established on evidence. As for the recitation, however, the reading with the final letter and the full ending is the one beyond which nothing else is permissible, because the copies of the Quran held by the Muslims agree on it. The clause closes with the promise that they have what they asked for, which is the ordinary food of any settled place.

phrases.translation: They were stricken with disgrace and misery,
phrases.explanation:
Being stricken is explained as an imposing. The word means that the humiliation and the misery were made obligatory on them, so what is described is a settled state rather than a single blow.

The humiliation is then defined. It is the lowliness which Allah commanded His believing servants to see upon those who reject Him, and the verse about fighting those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden is quoted, since it ends with their paying the tax by hand while they are humbled. That is the same word, and it fixes the humiliation as a condition imposed on a people rather than a feeling they happen to have.

The misery is explained from its root as well. It is the verbal noun of the word for the destitute, and the ordinary saying is quoted, that there is none among them poorer than a given man, which is the sense carried here.

The two together are then read as an exchange. Allah reported to them that He would give them standing in place of humiliation and ease in place of misery, so the state described in the verse is what they were left with after refusing the exchange offered to them.

phrases.translation: and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations
phrases.explanation:
Returning with wrath is explained as turning back laden with it, and the ordinary use of the verb is given. The meaning of Allah's wrath toward His servant was dealt with earlier, so it is not repeated.

The reason for the state described before it is then explained. The word translated as this refers to the imposing of the humiliation and the poverty on them, and it is imposed because they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right.

The closing clause repeats the same word a second time, which refers back to the first. The sense is that humiliation and poverty were imposed on them because they disobeyed and transgressed. Transgression is then explained as overstepping the limit Allah set for His servants toward something else.

phrases.translation: Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—
phrases.explanation:
The four groups are named and explained one after the other. Those who believe are the people who hold the Messenger of Allah to be truthful in what he brought them of truth from Allah, and their faith is their affirmation of it. Those referred to by the second name are the Jews, and the verb used of them is explained as meaning that they repented.

The Christians are explained from the same kind of root. Verses are cited to show that they were given this name because they helped one another and gave one another mutual support, and it was also said that the name comes from the question asked by Jesus, who are my helpers on the way to Allah.

The fourth group is explained last. The word is the plural of a term meaning one who takes up a new religion alongside the religion he has, so the name covers people who have moved out of one faith without being counted in another.

A question is then raised about the sentence itself, whether it is complete with the four groups named and nothing said about them. Two answers are given. On the first, the completion of the sentence is the whole of the clause that follows, whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, and its meaning is whoever of them believes. On the second, the meaning is that those who believe, and the Jews, and the Christians, and the fourth group, whoever of them believes in Allah and the Last Day has his reward with his Lord.

A longer answer rejects a reading of the first group that would make belief here mean nothing more than passing from one religion to another. The story of Salman is brought in at this point, his panic and his search for the monk, since his question about people he had lived among is what the verse answers.

What each group was required to hold is then set out. The faith of the Jews was that whoever held fast to the Torah and to the practice of Moses, until Jesus came, and did not let it go, and the same is said of the Christians in relation to what was given to them.

The verdict is given at the end. The first of these explanations most resembles the outward meaning of the revelation, because Allah did not restrict the reward for righteous deed joined to faith to one group and withhold it from another.

phrases.translation: whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.explanation:
Belief in Allah and the Last Day is explained as holding the resurrection after death on the Day of Resurrection to be true and acknowledging it, joined to righteous deeds. A point of grammar follows about a verb put in the dual form because of the meaning of the word for whoever, the verb agreeing with the sense of the word rather than its shape, and the same is said of the parallel clause.

The two promises are then explained. No fear upon them means that no fear will come on them concerning what they will face of the terrors of the Resurrection, and they will not grieve means that they will not grieve over what they left behind of this world, so one clause removes what is ahead and the other what is behind.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you
phrases.explanation:
The covenant is explained from its form. The word is on the pattern of an instrument noun and is derived from the word for a surety, so it names a bond that makes a thing secure. What is meant by it here is the covenant Allah told them He had taken from them, the same bond described in the verses around.

The taking of it is then set out. It was the covenant taken from the children of Israel and from their fathers before them, and it bound them to believing what was sent down to the Prophet and to the obligations of the Torah and the Gospel. The mountain raised over them in the next clause is the visible sign of that bond, and the passage reminds them of what they accepted and broke.

phrases.translation: and raised the mountain above you
phrases.explanation:
The mountain is explained first as a common noun. The word means the mountain in the language of the Arabs. It was then said that it is the name of a particular mountain, and it is mentioned that this is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Moses. Others said that the word names, among mountains, specifically those that bring forth vegetation, and both accounts are recorded.

The word is therefore used in the verse for the mountain as a general word, and the raising of it above them is what the verse describes. Whatever the particular mountain may be, the image is the same, and it is the height of it that the word points to.

phrases.translation: ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you
phrases.explanation:
The command to hold firmly is discussed by the linguists, who differed about it. Some of the grammarians of Basra took the construction in a particular way, and the correct view is then stated, that every saying which is uttered and by which the intended meaning is understood is enough, so the words that follow are read as the speech the people were given.

The two parts of the command are then explained. Take what We have given you means what We enjoined upon you in the Torah, and with strength means with exertion in fulfilling what He enjoined there and made obligatory. The explanation of the verse as a whole is therefore that they were told to take what Allah imposed on them as obligations in His Book, to accept it and to act accordingly.

phrases.translation: and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”
phrases.explanation:
Remembering what is in it is explained as remembering what the Book given to them contains, that is, its promise and its stern threat, its encouragement and its warning. The purpose clause follows from that, since a person who keeps those two in mind is the one who guards himself, and the guarding asked for is the fruit of the remembering rather than a separate act.

The Book meant is the Torah, and what it contains is its covenants and its rulings. The word for mindfulness is the same one used for the fear of Allah elsewhere in the surah, and the verse makes the guarding depend on the remembering. Remembering the law is what produces the restraint, and the restraint is what the verse is asking for.

phrases.translation: Yet you turned away afterwards.
phrases.explanation:
Turning away is explained as turning aside thereafter, and the form of the verb is discussed as being in substance a form built from turning. Examples of this way of speaking in Arabic are said to be more numerous than can be counted, and by it Allah means that they abandoned what they had accepted.

A witness is quoted to show how the same idiom works elsewhere. A speaker says that chains have encompassed the necks, and what is meant by it is a restraint that keeps people from what they used to do in the time of ignorance, which is the same use of a physical image for a change of conduct that the verse makes when it says they turned away after the covenant was taken and the mountain was raised over them.

phrases.translation: Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you,
phrases.explanation:
The bounty named is explained as the bounty of repentance. Allah granted it to them after their turning away, so the sentence states that the punishment was withheld for a reason that came from Him and not from them.

The address itself is then discussed. It is directed to the People of the Book who were living in the place to which the Messenger of Allah had emigrated, in his days, even though the deed spoken of was done by their forefathers. Some have claimed that the address is delivered this way only by ascribing the deed to those being addressed while the deed belonged in reality to others, because the people addressed are the descendants of those who did it.

phrases.translation: you would have certainly been of the losers
phrases.explanation:
The consequence is stated in the same terms as the bounty before it. Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon them and His mercy toward them, by saving them through the acceptance of their repentance for their sin and their crime, they would have been among the losers. The saving is therefore located in the acceptance of repentance, and the loss they escaped is the loss of people whose sin stands against them with no way back.

The phrase among the losers is the one already explained earlier in the surah, and the pointing is back to it. What the verse adds is the cause, and the cause is mercy. The whole condition of the verse is what makes the acceptance possible, and once it is granted the loss is removed.

phrases.translation: You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath.
phrases.explanation:
Knowing is explained first as coming to know, and the ordinary saying is quoted as a parallel, so the verse addresses people who have this knowledge and not people who must be told it for the first time.

The verse is then placed. It and the verses after it enumerate for the children of Israel who were dwelling among the people of the Prophet what their forefathers did, which is why a story from the past is told as a matter the listeners already know.

The Sabbath is explained from its root. Its origin is rest and stillness in repose and ease. What was transgressed was therefore a day defined by leaving work alone, and the transgression lay in doing on it what the day required them not to do.

phrases.translation: We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained as addressed to those who transgressed concerning the Sabbath, and the two words joined in it are taken together. Being made apes is the change of form, and the word translated as disgraced is explained as being removed from the good and made humbled and lowly.

A dissenting statement is then rejected. What one of the early authorities said is judged to contradict the plain meaning to which the Book of Allah points, because Allah reported in His Book what He did to them, and it is noted in addition that this statement contradicts the totality of the authoritative tradition, in which error and falsehood are impossible.

phrases.translation: So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing
phrases.explanation:
The verse turns on a pronoun, and the scholars of exegesis differ over what it refers back to in the words We made it. Two sayings are recorded first, and then two more.

On the first saying the pronoun refers to the transformation of form, which is a verbal noun on a known pattern. The meaning on this interpretation is then spelled out. We said to them, be despised apes, and they became apes, and We made Our punishment of them into what the verse goes on to describe.

On the second saying the pronoun refers to the fish, even though no prior mention of them had been made, because there was in the report an indication of them. On the third it refers to the town whose inhabitants transgressed the Sabbath, so the sense is that We made it a deterring example. On the fourth it refers to the apes who had been transformed, and the sense is that We made them a deterring example for those who came before and after.

The sayings are then weighed. The interpretation that takes the pronoun as the fish is judged the furthest, since deriving that sense is more remote, and a note is added on the reading that takes what precedes and what follows as towns rather than as times.

The interpretation given is the one that follows from what was set out before. We said to them, be despised apes, and We made Our punishment of them a punishment for the sins before and after it, and We made it a deterring example for those who came after and a reminder for the God-fearing. Allah therefore made the punishment He sent down on those who transgressed the Sabbath into an admonition for the God-fearing and a warning for the believers, which is why the verse ends on them rather than on the punished.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”
phrases.explanation:
The command to slaughter a cow is explained together with the answer it drew. When they said to Moses what they said, he told them that whoever reports on behalf of Allah, command or prohibition, does not jest about it, and it is not fitting for the prophets of Allah to mock in what they carry from Him. His seeking refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant is therefore read as a denial that he was joking, since joking about what Allah commands is ignorance.

The occasion of the command is given. It concerns a killing among them and their dispute about who was responsible. The people addressed are identified with that occasion, which is why a command unconnected to what came before is the way out of a quarrel they could not settle.

phrases.translation: They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!”
phrases.explanation:
The question they asked is reported first, that he call on his Lord for them so that He makes clear to them what she is, and the answer describes the cow by her age.

The three terms used are explained in order. The word for old is taken in that sense, and in accordance with this explanation the commentators spoke, with the reports naming who said it recorded. The word for young is explained as the female of livestock, and among the children of Adam the one that the male has not yet come to, so it names an animal that has not been bred from. The third word means of middle age, and it is placed between the two, which is what the answer says in words, neither old nor young but in between.

The larger question raised by these verses is then discussed at length, namely whether their repeated asking was itself a fault. The statements reported from the Companions and the Successors and those who followed them are set out, and all whose statements are mentioned held the questioning of their prophet about the attributes of the cow to be blameworthy. They were of the view that when the people asked about her age and he told them, restricting them to one age rather than another and one kind rather than another, it became obligatory on them to slaughter any cow answering that description.

The same reasoning is applied to the second situation, where they were of the view that it was obligatory on them to apply the outward import of the command and slaughter any animal they wished to which the description applied, and likewise to the third matter, in which they were in the same condition as in the first and the second. On this reading each answer narrowed what they had to find, and each further question narrowed it again against their own interest.

A contrary claim is recorded and rejected. Some whose ignorance was great and whose confusion was severe claimed that the people asked Moses what they asked only after Allah had commanded them to slaughter a cow among particular cows. It is answered that had such a person reflected on his own statement, what appeared difficult to him would have become easy, since he found it astonishing that the people should ask about a matter they had already been given in full.

phrases.translation: He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”
phrases.explanation:
The closing command is explained as an instruction to stop asking and to act. Allah says to them, do what I command you, and then you will attain your needs and your requests with Me. Obedience is placed before the satisfaction of what they were asking for and not after it, and the answer to the whole exchange comes with the slaughter of the cow. By submitting to the command and killing the animal they will come to the knowledge of the slayer of their slain one, which is the thing they came to Moses to settle.

So the way out of the quarrel is not more information but the doing of what was commanded, and the verse says so plainly at the end.

phrases.translation: They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.”
phrases.explanation:
The second question is reported in the same words as the first, that he call on his Lord so that He makes clear to them what her color is. The meaning of the request is then explained, that they were asking what thing her color is, and a point of grammar follows from that reading, since the word for color stands in the nominative because the question is framed as what is her color rather than as a description to be supplied.

The reply therefore takes the form of a description, and the color is given as a bright yellow. This is the second thing they asked about, and the second thing they are told. The exchanges are all reported in the same words, that they called upon their Lord to make things clear.

phrases.translation: He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”
phrases.explanation:
The answer is explained word by word. The color named is discussed by the exegetes, who differed, some taking it in one sense and others saying it means yellow of horn and hoof. A witness from the language is examined, in which camels described by the word for yellow are in fact black, and it is answered that this does not belong to the way cows are described.

The word that intensifies the color is then explained as meaning pure of color, and it is noted that this form with yellow is the counterpart of the form used with white, so each color has its own word for being unmixed. The closing phrase is explained as meaning that this cow gladdens those who look at her, in the beauty of her form and appearance.

phrases.translation: Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow,
phrases.explanation:
The third question is reported, and the people who asked it are identified as the people of Moses, those commanded to slaughter the cow. His name is left out of the sentence while the pronoun refers back to him, which is noted as a feature of the wording.

The question is then read as a statement about them rather than a simple request. It is an announcement from Allah about the people concerning a third instance of their ignorance, for if they had been given what they needed at the first command they would not have come back twice more. The pattern is drawn out, that when the people went on causing their prophet more vexation, Allah increased for them the narrowing of what they had to find, so each question made the matter harder.

phrases.translation: for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”
phrases.explanation:
The complaint that the cows are confused to them is discussed in the recitation first. Some recited it with a form that announces about the masculine, for the reason given earlier in a parallel reading, and the correct view about the reading is stated, that it is recited with the lightening of one letter and a particular vowel on another, so the word is read as a plain statement that the cows have become alike to them.

Their closing words are then explained. If Allah wills, we will be guided means that they will come to perceive what they had been unable to distinguish, so the guidance asked for is guidance to the right animal, and it is tied to the will of Allah rather than to another round of questions.

phrases.translation: He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’”
phrases.explanation:
The answer is explained term by term. Moses says that Allah describes the cow they are commanded to slaughter, and the first description is that labor has not made it submissive, so it is an animal not worn out by work. The clause about ploughing is then explained as turning the earth over for cultivation, with the ordinary use of the verb in Arabic given, and the clause about watering the tilth as drawing water for the crops.

The word translated as wholesome is explained from its form. It is a passive derivation from the word for soundness, and the ordinary saying built on the same root is quoted. Others took it to mean made free of defects.

The last description is treated at length. No marking upon it means that there is no color on the animal differing from the color of its hide. The word is traced to its origin, which is the adorning of a garment, that is, embellishing its unevenness with various colors in its warp and its weft. From the same root comes the word for an informer, so called because he lies about a man to a ruler and embellishes his lie with falsehoods.

Two explanations of these terms are then weighed. What one of the early authorities said, and those who said the same as him, is judged more fitting for the verse than what another said. The reason is that if soundness had concerned the kinds of color other than the color of the hide, the word for wholesome would already have been sufficient and would have made the words no marking upon it superfluous. Since those words are there, they make clear that wholesome means something other than what they mean, so the two descriptions are read as covering soundness from defects on the one hand and evenness of color on the other.

phrases.translation: They said, “Now you have come with the truth.”
phrases.explanation:
The words they answered with are reported, and a claim made about them is recorded. Some of the predecessors held that the people apostatized from their religion and became unbelievers by saying now you have come with the truth, as though what had been given to them before was not the truth. The saying is read on its face as an admission that the description is now complete, so that nothing is left for them to ask about, and the verse moves at once to what they did with it.

The claim is set aside in favour of the plain sense. Their words are an acknowledgment that the matter has now been made clear, and what they say next is what they did with it, which is the opposite of apostasy.

phrases.translation: Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly
phrases.explanation:
The slaughter is explained first as a plain fact. The people of Moses slaughtered the cow that Allah had commanded them to slaughter, so after all the questioning the command was carried out.

The clause saying that they almost did not is then discussed. The exegetes differed about the reason why they came close to leaving the duty Allah had imposed on them, and the reports naming who gave each reason are recorded. One reason given is that they were almost brought to not doing it out of fear of disgrace, should Allah reveal through it the murderer of the slain man. The explanation preferred is that both reasons hold together, the high price of the cow and the fear of disgrace, since slaughtering it would make the murderer known and bring him to account.

phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was,
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as a reminder. By the words and when you killed a soul, Allah means, remember when you killed a soul, and the address runs to the children of Israel for what their forefathers did.

The dispute named after it is explained from the verb. Its sense is given as going against one another, and the ordinary saying is quoted in which a person does not dispute with his companion and business partner. It was also said that the meaning here is that they repelled one another about it, each pushing the charge onto another, which is the shape a murder takes when no one admits to it.

Their mutual difference, dispute and quarrel is then described as concerning the affair of the slain man whose matter has been mentioned, so the verse returns to the killing that the whole passage about the cow was sent down for.

phrases.translation: but Allah revealed what you concealed
phrases.explanation:
Bringing out is explained from its sense in this place. It means making visible and manifest to the one from whom a thing was hidden, so what Allah does here is not a new act of knowledge but an act of disclosure.

What was concealed and then brought out is named. It is the killing done by the killer of the slain man, and that killer had concealed his deed from the people among whom the dispute ran. Those who knew of it and supported the killer kept it secret with him, until Allah made it visible and brought it out. The disclosure is therefore the answer to the quarrel described in the first part of the verse, and it is what the command about the cow was for.

phrases.translation: So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.”
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained first. By the words then We said, strike him with part of her, Allah means that He said to the people of Moses, those who had disputed over the slain man, that they should strike him with a part of the cow they had been made to describe in such detail.

The scholars then differed about which part of the cow the slain man was struck with, and which bodily part of it that was. Several answers are recorded, one after another, with the reports naming who said each of them, and one of the answers given is that he was struck with the piece of flesh between the two shoulder blades.

A question is raised about the command itself. Where is the report showing that Allah commanded them this for that purpose, since the verse does not state the purpose in words? The answer is given at length, and it turns on the fact that the command and the killing it answers are joined in the passage itself, so the purpose is known from the sequence of the verses rather than from a separate report.

phrases.translation: This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life,
phrases.explanation:
The clause that follows is explained as an address from Allah to those who saw what happened, and its sense is that this is how Allah brings the dead to life. One dead man restored in front of witnesses is put forward as a sample of what He does on a larger scale.

Just as the one man was brought back to life in this world, so are the dead brought back to life after their death and raised up on the Day of Resurrection.

It is also noted that Allah adduced this as a proof against the polytheists among the Arabs, even though the event belonged to another people, since a proof of this kind does not depend on who watched it happen first.

phrases.translation: showing you His signs so that you may understand
