phrases.explanation:
The closing clause is explained as an address to those who deny the Resurrection. Allah shows them His signs so that they may understand, and His signs are His evidentiary tokens and His proofs which point to the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger, so that the hearers may perceive that he is truthful and sincere, and may believe in him and follow him. The address is to the people themselves, the ones to whom the sign was shown.

The signs named in the verse are the ones just described, the dead man brought back and the cow whose description was given in such detail that no one could mistake which animal was meant, and the object of the instruction is that they should reason from them and accept what is said to them.

phrases.translation: Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder,
phrases.explanation:
The hardening is placed in time first. After all that means after Allah brought to life for them the murdered man about whose death they had disputed, so what follows a sign they saw with their own eyes is described as a hardening of the heart rather than a lack of evidence.

The comparison is then explained. The word translated as they refers to their hearts, and the sense given is that their hearts hardened after they had seen what they saw, until they became like stones or harder still. The two degrees are named in one breath, which raises a question.

A questioner asks what the explanation of like stones or even harder is, since the wording appears to leave it open which of the two their hearts resemble. The answer is that it is not as the questioner imagined, and that the wording is not a doubt on Allah's part about which of the two is the case. The comparison is put to the one who hears it, so the listener is told that those hearts reached at least the hardness of stone, and that they may have gone past it, without the sentence having to settle which.

Two other readings are recorded, and each is given a valid basis within the speech of the Arabs. One takes the or as a contrast, so that the hearts are like stones and at the same time harder. Another reads the phrase as saying that in your eyes they are like stones, or harder in hardness.

phrases.translation: for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water;
phrases.explanation:
The three kinds of stone are then explained, since they are what the comparison rests on. The first is the stone from which rivers gush forth, and the verb used is traced to its form, which is built from the saying that the water gushed forth, meaning that it comes out in quantity and with force.

The second is the stone that splits open so that water comes out of it, and it is explained as a stone that cracks and releases what is in it, which is less than the gushing of the first kind but is still water leaving a stone.

The point of naming them is that stones are not all alike in what they give. Some pour out rivers, some release water when they split, so a heart that is harder than these is being compared to things that do yield something, and the comparison is meant to make the hardness look worse rather than merely great.

The third kind is then taken up, the stones that fall down out of fear of Allah, and the people of interpretation disagreed about what that means. Some said it is the bending of their shadows. Others said it is the mountain that was turned to rubble when its Lord manifested Himself to it. Some said it occurred because Allah gave some stones knowledge and understanding, so that they humbled themselves before Him. The word for fear has already been explained as the trembling and the dread that comes over a thing, and the awe in the verse is of that kind.

phrases.translation: while others are humbled in awe of Allah.
phrases.explanation:
The third kind is discussed by the people of interpretation, who disagreed about the falling of those stones. The explanation given is that among stones are some that fall down out of fear of Allah, and the falling is read in the light of that fear rather than as ordinary collapsing.

A note on the wording accompanies it. The letters attached to the word for what are placed there for emphasis of the report, so the sentence asserts the thing rather than leaving it open.

It is then observed that Allah described the stones only with what He describes them with here, namely that among them are kinds that gush, that split and that fall, and that in agreement with this the people of interpretation spoke, so the description is not extended beyond it.

phrases.translation: And Allah is never unaware of what you do
phrases.explanation:
The closing clause is explained as an address to the community. Allah is not unmindful of what they do, and the sense given is that nothing of their conduct is hidden from Him. It is placed after the description of their hearts because a hardening no one else can see is still known, and the verse ends by saying so.

The word for unmindfulness is then explained from its root, and its meaning toward a thing is the neglecting of it in the manner of inattention. So the statement is not merely that Allah will punish them but that He has never lost sight of a thing they did. The verse gives them the report that He is not unmindful of their evil deeds, nor does He forget them.

phrases.translation: Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you,
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained as addressed to the Companions of the Prophet. By do you then desire, Allah is speaking to them about their hope concerning these people, and the thing hoped for is explained next.

That they should believe you means that they should affirm the believers as truthful in what their Prophet brought them, so the belief spoken of is belief directed at people and not only at a message. The question therefore asks whether a group described in the rest of the verse can be expected to give that kind of belief. The word for the group is also settled, and it means the children of Israel.

phrases.translation: though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it
phrases.explanation:
The group named within them is then identified, and two interpretations of the clause are recorded. The correct one, and the one that most accords with what the outward wording of the recitation indicates, is the reading held by the leading exegetes.

On that reading Allah meant by it only those of the children of Israel who heard His word, just as Moses heard it from Him, and then distorted and altered it after they had heard it, understood it and comprehended it. The reason given for this reading is that Allah reported the distortion as coming from a party of them who heard the word itself and not one that received it second hand. Their alteration is therefore stated to happen after understanding, which is what makes it knowing.

phrases.translation: When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.”
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as an announcement from Allah about the people it describes, reporting what they say when they meet those who believe. A further saying is transmitted about its explanation, and other accounts are recorded beside it, so the words are read both as a report of a habit and as a description of a particular group among them.

The words of the verse are the same as those used earlier of the hypocrites, and the parallel is deliberate. There as here a group says we believe when they meet the believers and says the opposite when they are alone with their own. The saying reported is taken to be about the whole of that kind of people, and the other account is about a named set of them.

phrases.translation: But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you,
phrases.explanation:
Being alone with one another is explained as what happens when some of these Jews, whose character the verse describes, withdraw together and speak among themselves. The thing they speak about is then discussed, and the exegetes differed concerning the explanation of the words what Allah has revealed to you, with several answers recorded one after the other.

Since the meaning of the word translated as disclose is as described earlier, the sense of their saying becomes clear, and the reproach is understood as being about handing something over to the believers. The words are said to one another in private, and the question they ask is whether the knowledge will be passed on.

phrases.translation: so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”
phrases.explanation:
The explanation preferred for the verse is then given, and it is the saying of those who read the reproach as being about disclosing to the believers what their own books contain, since that is what the believers would use to argue against them before their Lord. Because that is so, it is necessary that their mutual reproaches, which took place among them, pertained to that matter and not to something else.

The closing question is discussed last. Do you not understand is explained as an announcement from Allah concerning the people who were reproaching one another, so the words stand as His description of what they said to each other when they were alone.

phrases.translation: Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained by naming the people it concerns. It is addressed to those among the Jews who reproach their brethren for saying we believe when they meet the believers, and for telling the believers what is in their books concerning the Messenger and his mission. What they conceal is what they keep hidden from the believers, and what they make public is what they say in front of them, and both are known to Allah.

The question is asked in a form that assumes they do know. It is a rebuke of people who behave as though the hidden things were safe, and the answer is that nothing is out of Allah's sight, neither the saying in private nor in public. The two are named together so neither is left out.

phrases.translation: And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies,
phrases.explanation:
The group described is identified first. Among them are unlettered ones, and the word is explained as naming those who neither write nor read. Another explanation of it is recorded and then set aside, on the ground that it goes against what is known from the widespread language of the Arabs, so the plain sense of the word is kept.

What they do not know is then explained. They do not know the Book means that they do not know what is in the Book that Allah sent down, which is a stronger statement than not being able to read it, since it concerns its contents.

The exception that follows is treated as a matter of grammar. With the word for except, what comes after it is excepted from the meaning of what comes before it and from its description, even where each of the two is of a different nature and kind from the other. Some grammarians call this a disjoined exception, on account of the expression after the word being disjoined from the meaning that stands before it.

What indicates the correctness of this explanation, and shows that it is more fitting than the other sayings, is the clause that closes the verse. Allah informs about them that they wish what they wish of lies out of conjecture on their part and not out of certainty. If the meaning were that they recite the Book, they would not be conjecturers, and the same follows if the meaning were that they desire it, because a person who recites a thing knows it when he reflects on it.

phrases.translation: and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate
phrases.explanation:
The last clause is explained as a statement about their state of mind. They do nothing but conjecture, and the meaning given for the exception is that they doubt and do not know, so what is denied to them is knowledge and what is left with them is guesswork.

The verse is then summed up as a whole. Among them is one who does not write, does not trace letters, does not know the Book, and has nothing but wishes of lies and conjecture. The description divides the people spoken of, since the group named here has no hold on the text at all, and the verses before it concerned people who heard the word of Allah and altered it after understanding.

The exception is then weighed against the readings that have been offered for it. The word for except takes what follows it out of what precedes it, and the reading preferred is the one that agrees with the closing clause of the verse. Where the exception is set aside and the words are read as a description of what they do, the sense is that they do nothing but conjecture. The distinction matters for the account given of them, because one group had no knowledge of the Book to distort at all.

phrases.translation: So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain!
phrases.explanation:
A question is raised about the mention of the hands. Writing among human beings happens with the hand in any case, so what does adding it here mean? The answer given is that the phrase points to the people doing it themselves, so the writing is theirs and not something they inherited or copied.

Those meant by it are then identified as the people who distorted the Book of Allah among the Jews of the children of Israel, who wrote something with their own hands and then said this is from Allah, in order to sell it for a small price. The hands are named to rule out any other account, since the deceit is in the writing as well as in the claim.

phrases.translation: So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned
phrases.explanation:
Two woes are then named, one for what their hands wrote and one for what they earn. The first is explained as concerning that which their hands wrote of what is not in the Book of Allah, so the wrong lies in the writing itself and not only in the claim made about it.

The second is explained as concerning what they gain by it, which is the price they take from people who accept the writing as revelation. The doubling of the woe is therefore not a repetition but a division, one for the act of putting words into the Book and one for living on what those words bring in.

phrases.translation: ˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”
phrases.explanation:
What the Jews said is explained first. By their words they meant that the Fire will not touch their bodies and that they will not enter it, except for a number of days. The days are called counted even though their number is not given, and the reason for that wording is discussed, since Allah reported their saying in the form they used it.

The answer they are given is then explained. When they said this, Allah told His Prophet to say to the community of the Jews, have you taken a covenant with Allah, that is, have you received from Him a firm promise that He will not put you in the Fire beyond those days, or are you saying about Allah what you do not know.

phrases.translation: But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin
phrases.explanation:
The opening word is treated first as a matter of language. The particle translated as but no is an affirmation that follows a statement beginning with a negation, so it turns back what was just denied and asserts the opposite of it. Here it answers the claim that the Fire will touch them only for a number of days.

The sentence that follows is then explained as a refutation by Allah of those who made that claim, and its shape is general rather than aimed at one group. Whoever earns an evil deed and is encompassed by his sin is named without restricting the description to the Jews, which is what makes it an answer to them.

The evil deed mentioned in this place is then identified. It is ascribing partners to Allah, and the reasoning for taking it that way is set out at length, since the verse goes on to promise its people an unending stay in the Fire and that promise does not fit a sin short of disbelief. The explanation is therefore fixed by the consequence attached to it.

A supposition is examined along the way. If someone holds that those among the believers to whom eternal abiding in the Garden is due are only some of them, the discussion that follows bears on who abides forever and who does not, and on the difference between a sin that surrounds a person and a sin that does not. The point of raising it is that the eternity named in the verse is tied to the kind of deed described, not to every wrongdoing a believer commits.

phrases.translation: will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever
phrases.explanation:
The people named are then explained. The inhabitants of the Fire means the people of the Fire, and the words they therein are explained as their abiding forever in it. The last word is given its sense of remaining without an end, so the verse states both belonging and duration.

It is this duration that answers the claim in the verse before it, since a number of days and an unending stay cannot both be true of the same people. The two readings of the claim are therefore settled by what follows, and the question of how long the Fire would touch them is answered by saying it does not stop.

phrases.translation: And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever
phrases.explanation:
Those who believe are explained as those who held to be true what the Messenger of Allah brought them, and their righteous deeds are joined to that belief as the second condition of the promise.

This verse and the one before it are then read together as an announcement from Allah to His servants concerning the lasting nature of the two states, so the pair is not a description of two groups only but a statement that what each group enters does not end. The two conditions are the same as those named in the earlier verses of this passage, belief and righteous deeds, and the promise attached to them is the one given there.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel
phrases.explanation:
The covenant is named first, and the word for it was already demonstrated earlier in the work, being derived from the word for a surety. What is meant here is the covenant Allah took from the children of Israel, and the verses that follow list what it required of them.

The covenant is the one He took from them at the mountain, and its terms are given in order. They were to worship none but Allah, and to establish prayer, and to pay the alms tax, and to give the pledge of the covenant. The whole passage is a reminder of what they agreed to and of how they answered it, and the verse after this one says what became of them.

phrases.translation: ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah;
phrases.explanation:
The first requirement is the worship of Allah alone, and the recitation of the verb that carries it is discussed at length. The reciters differ over it, some reciting it with the letter that addresses the people directly and some with the letter that reports about them, and the two readings give the clause two shapes, one a command spoken to them and one a statement of what they were bound to.

A point of grammar accompanies the difference. The particle that would ordinarily introduce the clause is omitted, and the omission is explained, since the sense is complete without it and the verb stands in a form that shows what was left out. A parallel is quoted in which a verb is placed in the nominative even though it would have suited the construction to introduce it with that particle.

The meaning of the covenant as a whole is then given in one sentence. Allah made the covenant with the children of Israel that they would worship none but Him, and be good to their parents, and the rest of the list that the verse goes on to name.

phrases.translation: be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy;
phrases.explanation:
Kindness to parents is followed by three further groups, and each word is explained. The near kinsman is described as the one whose ties they were required to maintain, and the word for kinship is traced to its form, a verbal noun on a known pattern derived from the saying that a person's womb drew near to mine, so the word itself carries the idea of nearness of birth.

The needy is then explained as the one who shows himself submissive and abased on account of poverty and want, and the form of the word is given with it. A point of grammar covers the construction, since the word for goodness stands in the accusative on account of a verb understood but not spoken, whose meaning is conveyed by the words before it.

phrases.translation: speak kindly to people;
phrases.explanation:
Speaking well to people is discussed first in its recitation. The word for good is read in more than one way, and most of the reciters of Kufa, with one exception, read it in a particular form. A claim about the meaning of one of those forms is examined and rejected, and the recitation that takes a different shape altogether is judged to contradict the recitation transmitted by the others, so the reading preferred is the one the copies agree on.

The good speech commanded is then explained. It concerns the speech those of the children of Israel whose case is described here were required to use toward people, and the explanation given is the one that fits the command as it stands in the covenant.

phrases.translation: establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.”
phrases.explanation:
Establishing the prayer is explained as performing it with the rights that the person praying is obliged to give it, so the word concerns more than going through the movements.

The alms tax follows, and its meaning and origin were set out earlier in the work, so they are not repeated here. The two requirements are named together, as they are in the other places where this covenant is listed. The point of the listing is that these are what the covenant bound the children of Israel to, and the prayer and the alms tax are the two things that appear together wherever the covenant is spoken of.

phrases.translation: But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent
phrases.explanation:
The turning away is then explained as a report from Allah about the Jews of the children of Israel, that they turned back from what the covenant required, with the exception of a few of them.

The closing words are discussed next. Some said that Allah meant by them the Jews who lived in the time of the Prophet, so the aversion named is that of people who were still alive when the verse came down. Others said that the sentence is an address directed to those present about what their predecessors did, and both readings are recorded. The indifference is the turning away from the covenant, and it is named after the turning.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes,
phrases.explanation:
The covenant taken here is a second one, and its content is explained. The shedding of blood means the pouring out of blood and causing it to flow, and the prohibition concerns the blood of one another, so it binds each of them toward the rest of his own people.

It is also noted as permissible that the meaning of the prohibition is wider than the act itself, namely that a man assists in the shedding of another's blood, since helping to bring it about falls under the same prohibition. In accordance with this explanation the people of interpretation spoke, and the reports naming them are given.

The second half of the covenant is the prohibition on expelling one another from their homes, which is joined to the first because both concern the safety of a person among his own people.

phrases.translation: you gave your pledge and bore witness
phrases.explanation:
Affirming is then explained. By the words then you affirmed, Allah means the covenant that He took from them, namely that they would not shed one another's blood nor expel one another from their homes, so what they affirmed is the same thing the verse has just described.

The words while you bear witness are discussed next. The people of interpretation differed concerning who is addressed by them. Some took the address as running to those present, and others said that the verse is an announcement by Allah about their predecessors, with the address turned toward the descendants because they hold to what those predecessors accepted. Both readings are recorded, and each is explained.

phrases.translation: But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression;
phrases.explanation:
The opening words are explained, and two interpretations are possible. On the first, the phrase points at the people addressed as they now stand, so the sense is here you are, doing this after that covenant. On the other, the meaning is that they are a people who kill one another.

The words for their mutual aid are explained. Mutual assistance is the same as supporting one another, and it is called by that name because one person's back is put behind another's. The enmity named with it is explained from its form, a pattern built from the word for transgression.

The conduct is then placed. An account was related of this behavior of theirs with the two tribes among whom they lived, so the verse describes something still happening when it came down, not only something their ancestors had done.

phrases.translation: and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?
phrases.explanation:
The reproach that follows is explained at length. If those expelled come to them as captives they ransom them, while the expelling of them was forbidden to them by the same covenant, so the verse holds two parts of one agreement side by side and shows them keeping one and breaking the other.

The word for captives is discussed in the recitation. The reciters differed concerning how it is read, and the explanation of each reading is given. Whoever recited it in one of the two forms meant the plural of the word for a captive, since it is built on a pattern that carries that plural, and some claimed that the two forms differ in meaning, with one naming captives in a particular state and the other naming them generally. The reports of who held each view are given with them.

The question that closes the verse is then explained. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part is put to people who acted on the clause about ransoming captives while ignoring the clause about expelling them, so belief in part of the Book is shown by what they did and rejection of the rest by what they left undone. The question is asked in the same tone as the rest of the verse, as one put to people who are already known by what they have done, and the answer is left to their own conduct.

phrases.translation: Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life
phrases.explanation:
The recompense is then stated and explained. What is the recompense of whoever does that among them except disgrace in the life of this world, and the explanation of the word for recompense is given with it.

The disgrace itself is discussed, and the reports differ about what it was. Some said it is the levying of the tax from them for as long as they remain under the rule of the believers, and others said that the disgrace with which they were recompensed in the worldly life was the driving out of them by the Messenger of Allah. Both accounts are recorded, and each is explained as a fulfillment of the verse in this world before the next.

phrases.translation: and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment?
phrases.explanation:
The punishment of the next world is then explained. On the Day of Resurrection they are returned to the severest punishment, and the recitation of the verb is discussed, the reading preferred of the two being the one in conformity with what precedes it. The point of the reading that is preferred is that it agrees with the wording just before it, which speaks of the punishment of the Hereafter.

A claim about the meaning is examined and set aside. Some said that they are returned to something severer than what they were in, but the statement of whoever says that is judged to have no valid meaning, because Allah informs in this verse of what awaits them on that day rather than comparing two punishments with each other.

phrases.translation: For Allah is never unaware of what you do
phrases.explanation:
The verse closes by stating that Allah is not unaware of what they do. The clause is attached to the two punishments named before it, one in this world and one on the Day of Resurrection, and it is the reason both can be promised with certainty, since nothing of their conduct is hidden from the One who repays it.

The recitation of the clause is then discussed, the reciters having differed over the form of the word for what they do, and the preferred reading is the one the general usage of the Arabs supports. The sense does not change with the reading, since in either case it is the same statement that Allah is not unaware. It is a closing word after the threat, saying the threat is not empty.

phrases.translation: These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped
phrases.explanation:
The people named are identified as those of whom Allah informed that they believe in part of the Book and reject part of it, so this verse continues the description of the same group rather than introducing a new one.

The buying described is then explained. Since they sold their share in the felicity of the hereafter for the life of this world, Allah informed that the punishment will not be lightened for them. The last clause is explained as a statement that no one will help them in the hereafter, so neither is the punishment reduced nor is anyone found to prevent it, and the two denials cover the only two ways a punishment ends.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers.
phrases.explanation:
Giving the Book is explained first as sending it down to Moses, since that is what the verb means here, and the Book he was given is the Torah.

The word translated as sent after him in succession is then explained. It means that Allah caused them to follow one another and to come after one another, and the same verb is used in ordinary speech of people or things following in a line, so the image is one of a queue rather than of a single replacement.

The messengers named are identified as the prophets, and the word is given as the plural of the word for one sent. What is meant by the clause is then stated in full, that Allah caused the messengers to come one after another to them after Moses, which is why the verse can speak of a long history of revelation rather than of one book and one prophet.

phrases.translation: And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit.
phrases.explanation:
The clear proofs given to Jesus are explained as the proofs and indications of his prophethood. Strengthening him is then explained as giving him strength and helping him.

The spirit of holiness is discussed, and the explanations recorded include that it is the Gospel and that it is the name by which Jesus raised the dead to life. The correct explanation is the saying of those who took it to be Jibril, since Allah reported that He strengthened Jesus with it. Jibril is called a spirit and attached to holiness because he was made by Allah's creating into a spirit from Him without birth from a father.

phrases.translation: Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others
phrases.explanation:
The verse is then summed up as a single address. Allah says to them, O community of the Jews of the children of Israel, We gave Moses the Torah, We caused the messengers to follow one after another after him, We gave Jesus the son of Mary the clear proofs and strengthened him with the spirit of holiness, and then whenever a messenger came to you with something your souls did not like, you acted arrogantly, denying a party and killing a party.

The shape of the sentence is what carries the rebuke. The gifts are listed first, so the people addressed are reminded that revelation reached them repeatedly and in more than one form, through a book, through a succession of messengers, and through signs given to one messenger in particular. What follows that list is therefore not a single failure but a habit, described as happening every time a messenger came.

Two outcomes are named rather than one. A party of the messengers they denied and a party they killed, so the response described runs from refusal to violence. The clause about what their souls disliked gives the reason attached to both, and it locates the objection not in the standing of the messenger but in what he brought, which is why the answer to it is described as arrogance.

A point of explanation is added about the holy spirit, and the views are given. Some said it is the angel who brings revelation, others that it is the Gospel, and others that it is the name by which Jesus raised the dead to life. The explanation preferred is the first, since if it were the Gospel the verse would be saying the same thing twice.

phrases.translation: They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”
phrases.explanation:
What they say about their hearts is discussed in the recitation first. The reciters differ over the reading of the word, some reading it in a form that means the hearts are within coverings, and others reading it with a different vocalization that they explained in another way. The reports naming who read each are given.

The reading that is alone permissible is then stated, and it is the one with a particular vowel pattern, on the ground that what the proof is unanimous about constitutes a binding proof for whoever it reaches, a principle demonstrated earlier. The sense of the saying is that they claimed their hearts were wrapped so that nothing said to them could get in.

phrases.translation: In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief.
phrases.explanation:
The answer to that claim is explained. By the words but Allah cursed them, Allah means that He rejected and banished them on account of their disbelief, so the covering they claimed is turned into the thing done to them.

The word for curse is then traced to its origin, which is driving away, removal and rejection, and the ordinary saying built on it is quoted, that Allah cursed such a one, meaning He removed and drove him away. In this sentence lies a refutation of their claim, since a heart rejected by Allah is not one that cannot receive anything but one that has been shut by its own disbelief.

phrases.translation: They have but little faith
phrases.explanation:
The closing words are explained, and the exegetes differ over them. Some took them one way, others said the meaning is that they believe only in a small portion of what they hold in their hands, so what is described as little is their belief, not their number.

A point of language accompanies. The particle attached to the word for little is examined, and a witness is quoted from poetry in which the same particle is treated as redundant, with the meaning of the line given alongside. Adding that which gives the word no meaning is judged not permissible to attribute to a word of the Book, so the statement is read in the sense that holds.

A further question is then raised and answered. Whether these people believed a little or not at all, the meaning of belief is affirmation, and they affirmed some part of what was sent down to them while denying the rest. So the little is not the absence of belief but the measure of it.

phrases.translation: Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists,
phrases.explanation:
Praying for victory is explained as what they used to do before this. They asked to be given the upper hand over those who disbelieved, and the asking is described as something they were in the habit of, so the verse recalls a practice of theirs rather than a single request. The explanation of the clause is then given in full, together with what they were asking by, since their prayer for victory was tied to a prophet whose coming they expected.

A question is then raised about the sentence, where the answer to the clause when there came to them is to be found, and the answer given is that it lies in the particle that follows, so that what is said about their rejection of the Book completes the sentence.

phrases.translation: when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it.
phrases.explanation:
The coming of the Book is then explained. A Book from Allah came to them confirming what was already with them, and the sense given is that they recognized it, so the rejection described is not of something unfamiliar.

A question of grammar is raised about the sentence. Where is the main clause answering the words when there came to them? One answer is that the answer lies contained in the particle that follows, so the clause about their rejecting it completes the sentence.

The recognition is what makes the conduct so strange. They had asked for a prophet, and their prayer for victory was tied to his coming, and when the Book arrived they knew it. Rejecting it was therefore a refusal of what they had asked for and claimed to recognize.

phrases.translation: So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers
phrases.explanation:
The curse is explained by referring back to what was already demonstrated earlier about the meaning of the word, so it is not set out again here.

The meaning of the verse is then given. So the abasement and banishment of Allah is upon those who deny what they have been given, and the curse is attached to disbelief in particular, which is the same thing the verse has just described them as doing when they recognized the Book and rejected it. The curse is therefore the closing of the account, and it falls on the refusal that has just been described rather than on any opinion about their persons.

phrases.translation: Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—
phrases.explanation:
The exclamation is explained from its root. The word translated as miserable comes from a verb meaning to be in misery and wretchedness, and the form is discussed, its first letter being made quiescent after a particular vowel, with the ordinary shape of the verb given. It is also possible that the word belongs to the usage of those who transfer a vowel from one letter to another, and that account is recorded beside the first.

The particle joined to it is then examined by the grammarians, who differed about it. Some of the grammarians of Basra took it in one way, and others said that the two words form a single whole which places what follows it in the nominative, as transmitted from one of the scholars of the language. The Arabs are then quoted using the construction, in a saying about a wretched marriage with no dowry, where the particle is made to carry the whole exclamation.

The reason named in the verse is explained last. The word translated as resenting means out of transgression and envy, so the disbelief described is given a motive rather than being left as bare rejection. The meaning of the verse as a whole is then stated. Wretched is the matter for which they sold their souls, namely their disbelief in what Allah sent down, carried out out of resentment that Allah should send it down at all.

phrases.translation: denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath.
phrases.explanation:
What is resented is then named. That Allah sends down of His grace on whom He wills of His servants is a clause whose explanation and meaning were already given earlier, and it is mentioned again here to complete the sense of the verse, since the grace resented is the revelation given to someone other than themselves.

The result of their choice is then explained. They returned with wrath upon wrath, and the sense of returning with a thing is that they came back carrying it. The doubling is explained at length, and the meaning of the wrath of Allah toward those of His creatures on whom He is wrathful was already set out earlier, so it is not repeated, but the two wraths are distinguished from one another.

phrases.translation: And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment
phrases.explanation:
The punishment named at the end is explained as one that humiliates. For the disbelievers there is a humiliating punishment, and the explanation given concerns both parts of the description, the punishment itself and the abasement attached to it, so what is promised is not only pain but a pain that puts the person beneath others.

The verse ends on this word because the arrogance described earlier in the passage is answered by it, and the humiliation named here is the counterpart of the disdain with which they met the messengers. A question is raised about what punishment there is that does not humiliate the one who undergoes it, and the answer is that the humiliating punishment is that which brings upon the one who undergoes it disgrace and abasement.

phrases.translation: When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,”
phrases.explanation:
The exchange is explained as a report of what they say. When it is said to them, believe in what Allah has sent down, they answer that they believe in what was sent down to them, so the command is general and the answer restricts it. The words are addressed to the Jews of the children of Israel, and what they claim is not disbelief but a belief limited to one book.

The answer is the whole of their trouble. They do not say they do not believe, they say they believe, and the belief they mean is belief in their own scripture and nothing beyond. The command is put to them in general terms and they narrow it to what they already hold, which is the shape of refusal the passage describes.

phrases.translation: they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,”
phrases.explanation:
Rejecting what comes after it is then explained, and the word for after is taken in this place as meaning other than or besides, as it is used in ordinary speech. The rejection is therefore not of a later time only but of anything other than the book they hold.

The saying is then taken up as it stands. By their words they believe in what was sent down to them, the answer to the command of the previous clause, and the sentence is left to answer the question that follows. A question is raised about how it could be said to them, why then did you formerly kill the prophets of Allah, and the answer is that the address is not to the killers themselves but to those who claim their forefathers as believers.

phrases.translation: and they deny what came afterwards,
phrases.explanation:
The Book they reject is described as the truth confirming what is with them. The explanation given is that what was sent down agrees with the scripture they hold rather than contradicting it, so the confirmation is offered as the reason the rejection makes no sense, since a book that supports what they already accept cannot be dismissed on the ground that it is not theirs.

The word after it is then explained, and its sense here is other than or besides. So what they reject is not a single later passage but everything that comes beyond the book they hold. The two halves of the verse therefore fit together, the claim to believe in what was sent down to them, and the refusal of what was sent down after that.

phrases.translation: though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before,
phrases.explanation:
The question put to them is then explained. Say, why do you kill the prophets of Allah formerly, is addressed to those among the Jews of the time, and the correct view about the address is given at length, since the killing was done by their forefathers and not by them.

The word formerly is explained as meaning before today, which fixes the question on a past they own rather than on something happening now. The clause before it is also explained, that the Book is the truth confirming what they already possess, and the question is put immediately after it so that the confirmation and the killing stand side by side.

phrases.translation: if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”
phrases.explanation:
The condition attached to the question is then explained. By the words if you are believers, Allah means if you believe in what He sent down to you as you claim, so the condition takes their own claim and turns it against them. A people who killed the prophets sent to them are asked how they can be believers in what those prophets brought, and the question is left for them to answer.

The address is to those among the Jews of the children of Israel who were in the country when the verse came down, and formerly is explained as meaning before this day. So the question is not about what they used to believe but about what they claim now, while the evidence against them is the history of their own forefathers.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully
phrases.explanation:
The coming of Moses is explained first. Verily Moses came to them with the clear proofs, and the meaning of the address is given, that there came to them, O company of the Jews and children of Israel.

The proofs are then explained as proofs. Allah called them clear proofs because for whoever looked at them they made clear that they were a sign from Allah, so the clarity lies in what the looking produces rather than in the number of signs.

What followed is then explained. After him they took the calf, and the pronoun in after him is discussed, since it can refer back to Moses or to the mention of his coming,  The wrongdoing named at the end of the verse is attached to that taking, so the sequence is a coming with clear proofs followed at once by worship given to something else.

phrases.translation: And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.”
phrases.explanation:
The covenant is explained as one Allah took from them, and the verse is read as a reminder, remember when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you. What the covenant required is then given, that they hold fast to what Allah gave them with strength and listen.

The two words for hearing and obeying are explained. By hearing is meant accepting what one hears, and by obedience, obedience to what is commanded, so the two describe a person who takes in a command and then acts on it.

Their answer is then explained. They said we hear and we disobey, which joins the first half of what was required to the refusal of the second, and the verse reports the answer as they gave it rather than correcting it at that point.

phrases.translation: The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”
phrases.explanation:
What was put into their hearts is explained first. They were made to drink the calf in their hearts by their disbelief, and the exegetes differed. Some said what is meant is that the love of the calf was made to enter their hearts, and others said they were given to drink the water in which the filings of the calf had been scattered, so one reading takes the drinking as an image and the other as an event.

The image is then explained from the language. A witness is quoted in which a speaker names a black poison and is content with the mention of black, because the word already carries it.

The verse closes with the rebuke. Say, how evil is what your belief prompts you to do, if you are believers, which turns their own claim back on them, since a belief that produces the killing of prophets and the worship of a calf is described as no belief.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained first as a proof. It belongs to the arguments by which Allah furnished His Prophet against the Jews, and it puts their claim to a test they cannot take.

The claim is that the home of the hereafter belongs to them alone with Allah, apart from the rest of people. The answer to it is a challenge rather than a counter argument. If that is so, they are told to wish for death, since a person certain that the next world is his alone and better than this one has no reason to hold on to this one.

A report is then given which fixes the outcome. It is reported that the Messenger of Allah said that if the Jews had wished for death they would have died, and that none of them would have been left on the earth. The point drawn from it is that on that day the affair of the Jews became clear even to whoever had been unsure, and their lying was exposed by their silence rather than a reply.

The exegetes then disagreed about why Allah commanded His Prophet to call the Jews to this.

phrases.translation: But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation:
That they will never wish for it is explained as an announcement from Allah concerning the Jews and their aversion to the thing they were challenged to, so the verse states in advance what their answer would be and then reports that they gave it.

The reason attached is then explained. Because of what their hands have sent ahead means because of what their hands have done, and the question is asked why the deed is ascribed to the hand when much of it is done otherwise. The answer given is that this way of speaking is used because most of the offenses people commit are committed with the hand, so the hand is named for the whole of the acting.

The closing clause is explained last. Allah is all knowing of the wrongdoers, and the sense given is that nothing of what they sent ahead is hidden from Him, so the knowledge named here makes their unwillingness to wish for death a confession rather than a hesitation.

phrases.translation: You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people,
phrases.explanation:
The description is explained as a report about them. Allah says that the Prophet will find them the most avid of all people for life, and the reason for that description is then given. Allah described the Jews as the people most avid for life only because of the knowledge they carry, since a people who know what awaits them have more reason to hold on to this life than people who do not.

Their aversion to death is said to be solely on account of their knowledge of the disgrace and the prolonged humiliation that awaits them. The comparison with those who associate partners with Allah is then taken up, and the point of it is that these have still less reason to cling to life, since they know less of what is coming.

phrases.translation: even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years.
phrases.explanation:
The comparison with those who associate partners is then explained. Even more than the polytheists, and the sense given is that the polytheists are described in a report from Allah as people who also long for life, since they have no expectation of anything beyond it, and the Jews are placed above them in avidity. The difference between the two groups is therefore not that one loves life and the other does not, but that the Jews love it more while knowing what they are going toward.

The wish named after that is explained as each of them wishing that he might be given a life of a thousand years, which is a way of stating the length of the longing rather than a limit set on it.

phrases.translation: But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment.
phrases.explanation:
The answer to that wish is then explained. It will not remove him from the punishment that he should be given a long life, and the construction of the sentence is discussed. Others said that this saying amounts to something else, and the most correct is judged to be that in which a pronoun is understood but unspoken.

Two points of grammar accompany the reading. The particle introducing the clause about living long is said to carry a particular sense, and it is placed in the nominative because it is governed by the word for removing him.

The verb translated as remove is then explained from its root. It means to get away to a distance, so what is denied is that a long life pushes the punishment away from the one who lives it.

phrases.translation: And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do
phrases.explanation:
The closing clause is explained as a statement that Allah sees what they do. The word for seeing is then examined from its form. Its root is a word meaning one who sees, built from the saying I saw so I am one who sees, but the form used here differs from it, and the discussion of that difference is given, so the name describes a seeing that is not limited to what the eye takes in.

The clause closes the passage, and it closes on the same note as the verse before it. Allah is not unaware of what they do and He is seeing of what they do, and both are said of the same people whose excuses have just been shown to be empty.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know
phrases.explanation:
The scholars of interpretation are all agreed that this verse was revealed as a response to something said to the Prophet, and the occasion is reported in more than one form. On one account it answers a statement made by some of the Jews about Jibril, and on another the occasion was a dispute that took place between Umar and some of them, and the reports naming who transmitted each account are given.

The occasion in each account is the same at heart. They claimed that Jibril was their enemy because in their view he comes only with harshness and bloodshed, while Mikail was their patron, and so they refused to follow the Prophet on that ground.

The explanation of the verse is then set out at length. Whoever is an enemy of Jibril is told that Jibril is the one who sent the Quran down upon the heart of the Prophet by the permission of Allah, so the enmity is aimed at the one who carried the message rather than at the message itself, and the verse answers it by naming what he carried and how.

The mention of the heart is part of that answer, since the sending down is described as reaching the heart of the Prophet, which is the place of understanding and of holding what is given, and the permission of Allah is named with it so that the act is placed under His authority and not under the angel's own choice.

phrases.translation: that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—
phrases.explanation:
Confirming what was before it is then explained. What is meant is that the Quran confirms the scriptures that came before it, and the form of the word is given with its grammatical place in the sentence.

The meaning of the clause as a whole is stated, that Jibril sent the Quran down upon the heart of Muhammad confirming what was before it, so the confirmation is offered as a reason why hostility toward the one who brought it makes no sense, since what he brought agrees with what the people hostile to him already hold.

So the revealing was by the will of Allah, and the one who brought it down was Jibril, and what was brought down was the Quran.

phrases.translation: a guide and good news for the believers.”
phrases.explanation:
Guidance is explained as an indication and a proof, so the word covers both the showing of the way and the evidence that supports it. The glad tiding is then explained as the glad announcement, and what Allah announces by it to the believers is set out.

The two are joined to the believers in particular, and the clause is read as the completion of the description of what Jibril brought down, so the verse ends by naming who benefits from it. The glad news is what Allah has in store for those who believe, and the guidance is the way they are shown. Both are for the believers in particular, and the verse closes on that.

phrases.translation: Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as an announcement from Allah. Whoever is an enemy of Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mikal, then Allah is an enemy of the disbelievers, and the announcement is general, so the enmity named in the answer covers more than the single angel the verse began with.

The occasion is then confirmed by a narration, which indicates that Allah revealed this verse as a rebuke to the Jews because of their disbelief, and the rebuke is answered by widening the sentence rather than by repeating it.

A question is raised about the wording. If the angels have already been named, what is the meaning of repeating the mention of the two by their own names? The meaning of mentioning the two separately is that when the Jews said that Jibril was their enemy, the two were named so that the hostility they had expressed toward one of them is shown to reach both, and so that the answer given to them covers the angel they named and the angel they did not.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained in two parts. What is meant by the clear revelations sent down to the Prophet is given, and the purport of the verse is then stated as a whole, that Allah sent down to him, in what He revealed to him of the Book, signs that are clear in themselves and do not need something else to make them plain.

The second half is explained as a description of the people who reject them. None rejects them except the perverse means that none denies them, and the word for the perverse is then explained, so the denial described is not the doubt of a person weighing evidence but the refusal of someone who has left the right course.

phrases.translation: Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe
phrases.explanation:
The question at the head of the verse is discussed first. It is noted that what was explained earlier still applies, namely that it is not permissible for a particle to occur in the Book of Allah without a meaning, so the word translated as every time is read as carrying its own sense and not as filler.

The covenant is then explained. It is the solemn pledge which the children of Israel gave to their Lord, and the verse describes what a party of them does with it whenever it is made. Casting it aside is explained from the verb, and the pronoun attached to it is identified as referring to the covenant, so the sense is that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them throws it away behind them.

The closing words are then explained. Nay, most of them do not believe, and the sense given is that the casting aside is not the fault of a few among them but of most, which is why the verse ends by naming the majority rather than the party that broke the pledge.

phrases.translation: Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as describing a particular group. By the words when there came to them, what is meant is the scribes of the Jews, so the people who received the messenger are named.

A messenger from Allah came to them confirming what was with them, and the explanation of that clause is given at length, since the confirming makes their response inexcusable.

The response is explained from the image used. Casting the Book of Allah behind their backs is a figurative expression, and its sense is that they put it behind them as a person puts away a thing he does not want to see.

The closing words are explained. As though they did not know means it was as if those who threw the Book away had no knowledge of it.

phrases.translation: They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon.
phrases.explanation:
The people described as following are identified, and the sense given is that they followed what the devils recited, that is, what the devils composed and spread during the reign of Solomon. Two views are then recorded about who is meant by the followers. Some said that Allah meant the Jews who lived in the region to which the Messenger of Allah had emigrated, so the verse speaks of people who were alive when it came down. Others said that He meant the Jews who lived in the time of Solomon, so the verse speaks of an earlier generation.

The occasion is described. The devils had recourse to a book, wrote in it the sorcery and the soothsaying, and buried it under the seat of Solomon. When Solomon departed from the world they brought it out and deceived the people with it, saying that this was knowledge Solomon had concealed and begrudged them, and so they spread the sorcery among the people and learned it and taught it.

The thing followed is then described as reciting, which is the word used of reading something aloud and repeating it, so what the devils did is presented as teaching and spreading rather than as a single act, and what they spread during that reign is the magic the rest of the verse describes.

The reign of Solomon is named as the period in which this spreading took place, and the verse goes on at once to clear him of what was attached to that period, since the next clause denies that he disbelieved. The naming of the reign is therefore not an accusation against the king but a way of fixing when the magic was circulated among them.

The correct judgment is then given. Those who followed what the devils recited in the time of Solomon and those who followed it after him are both included, and the explanation chosen is the one that gathers them together, since it is the reading that makes the sense of the following clauses complete.

phrases.translation: Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved.
phrases.explanation:
The denial concerning Solomon is explained first, and a question is raised about the construction of the sentence, with the manner of its precedence explained at length. Others said that the word translated as never carries the meaning of that which, and is a conjunction on what precedes it, and the reports naming who said so are given.

The clause about teaching people magic is then joined to the devils, so the teaching is described as theirs and not his. A further question is raised about whether the two angels named later are a closer specification of the people who were taught, and the answer is given at length, since the wording allows more than one way of attaching the names.

phrases.translation: They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew
phrases.explanation:
What was sent down to the two angels in Babylon is discussed in its wording. The people of knowledge differed concerning the particle used here, some taking it as a negative and others as relative. The two angels are then named, and what they did is described. They taught no one without first saying that they are a trial, so do not disbelieve.

What people learned from them is described as something that brings about separation between a man and his wife, and their magic harms no one except by Allah's permission.

The loss that follows is stated in two parts. They learned what harms them and does not benefit them, and they knew that whoever buys magic has no share in the hereafter. The verse ends by calling what they sold their souls for a wretched price.

phrases.translation: If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew
phrases.explanation:
The wish expressed at the start of the verse is explained first. By the words if only they had believed and been God fearing, Allah means that if those who learned from the two angels the thing by which they brought about separation between a man and his wife had believed, that is, had held Allah and His Messenger to be true together with what He brought, and had feared Him, then what follows would have been theirs instead. The people spoken of are therefore the same people described in the verse before it, and the belief asked of them is stated in full rather than left general.

The wish is then expanded, that the requital of Allah and His reward to them for their belief in Him and their fear of Him would have been better for them than the sorcery and what they acquired by it. And by the words if only they had known, He denied them knowledge, that is to say, they would have known the extent of Allah's reward and the measure of His requital for obeying Him.

The reward named is then explained from its root. The word used here is a verbal noun in Arabic from the saying of a person who says that he rewarded someone with a reward, and its origin is a verb meaning that a thing returned to you. One then says that he caused it to return to you, so the reward is named from returning, which is why the same root is used for what a person comes back to at the end of an action. The explanation of the verse is that a reward from Allah would have been better for them than what they took, and the word itself carries the sense of something given back in return.

The construction of the sentence is then discussed by the grammarians. Some of the grammarians of Basra claimed that this sentence belongs to the kind in which the indication lying in the wording is enough, so that the second clause, which answers the condition, can be left unspoken because the listener supplies it. On that reading the answer to if only is understood and not stated.

Others among the grammarians of Basra rejected that claim. They held that the response to the words if only they had believed and been God fearing is the word for reward itself, and that the particle for if was answered by it even though Allah reported the matter with the completed form of the verb, and the reason for that is given, since the completed form is used here of something certain enough to be spoken of as already done.

The two positions are recorded side by side, and the difference between them concerns the grammar of the answer rather than the sense of the verse, which on either reading is that belief and fear of Allah would have brought them something better than what they chose. The verse closes by saying that they would have known this had they known anything at all, which puts the loss back on their own knowledge.

phrases.translation: O believers!
phrases.explanation:
The verse opens by addressing the believers directly, and the explanation of the saying is given together with the command that follows it. What is forbidden is a single word, and the people forbidden it are those who believe, so the prohibition concerns the language they use with the Prophet.

The exegetes differed over the sense of the word forbidden. Some took it as meaning listen to us, and others as meaning direct your hearing toward us. They then differed again about the reason Allah forbade the believers to say it, and the explanations are recorded. One reason given is that it was a word the Jews used by way of mockery, and another that some of the Muslims had taken to saying it until Allah made hateful to them what the Jews said.

phrases.translation: Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment
phrases.explanation:
The exegetes differed over the meaning of the word they were forbidden to say. One view was that it means words of contradiction, and another that it means direct your hearing toward us, listen to us and we listen to you. The verb behind the second reading is explained as inclining the hearing toward someone and freeing it for him, so the word is not an insult but an ordinary request for attention. The point of language behind the prohibition is then set out, since Arabic has pairs of words with one and the same meaning, where one form carries a good sense and the other a sense people avoid, as with the grapevine and with my boy rather than my slave.

The reason for forbidding it is then discussed, and the exegetes differed about that as well. Some said that it was a word the Jews used by way of mockery and insult, and others that it was a saying of the helpers in Medina in the time of ignorance.

Other readings are then examined. One takes the forbidden word as meaning contradiction and holds that the expression is not intelligible in the language of the Arabs, since the verb behind it has only two senses, one of guarding and protecting and the other of turning away. Another takes it as naming a foolish saying.

The reason for the prohibition is then placed in a wider setting. Allah had commanded the believers to honor and revere His Prophet, forbidding them to raise their voices above his voice and making them fear that their works would be brought to nothing. That is what rules out a word that could be turned into an insult. The verse therefore closes by giving the believers another word to use, one that carries the same request without the risk attached to the first.

phrases.translation: The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists
phrases.explanation: The people named are the disbelievers among the People of the Book together with those who associate partners with Allah. The verb used of them is explained as meaning that they do not love, so the unwillingness described is a settled dislike of the heart rather than a passing preference. The verb is then illustrated from ordinary usage, where a person says that he wished for such and such, and its different forms are set out, so that the sense of not wishing is seen to be the sense of disliking what another has. The wish is also attributed to many of them and not to all of them, and the verse moves on to what they wish not to happen.

phrases.translation: would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord,
phrases.explanation:
The two groups are joined in the grammar, the word for those who associate partners standing in the genitive by conjunction on what precedes it.

The explanation of the statement is then given. Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not love that any good should be sent down to the believers from their Lord, and the same is said of those who associate partners.

It is then noted that this verse carries a clear indication that Allah has forbidden the believers to lean on such people, since a person who does not want any good to come to you is not one whose support can be relied on.

phrases.translation: but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty
phrases.explanation:
Their unwillingness is answered in the second half of the verse. Allah singles out with His mercy whom He wills, and the singling out is His own choice. He singles out whom He wills with His prophethood and His message, sends his prophet to whom He wills, favors with faith whom He loves, and guides him to it.

The closing name is then explained. Allah is the possessor of tremendous bounty, and the clause is read as a statement that every good that reaches His servants comes from Him as a favor, with no right of their own to it.

The verse also contains an allusion to the People of the Book, since the guidance given to the Prophet and the believers is a favor from Allah and not something owed to them.

phrases.translation: If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten,
phrases.explanation:
The phrase for abrogate is explained from its origin. It comes from the copying of a writing, the transferring of a text from one copy to another, so the root sense is not destruction but replacement by something else. What is meant by whatever verse We abrogate is then set out. It means the change to something else, so that one ruling replaces and changes another, and the permitted becomes forbidden and the forbidden permitted, which can occur only with regard to command and prohibition.

The consequence of that meaning is then drawn. When this is what the abrogating of a verse means, it makes no difference, once its ruling has been abrogated, whether the wording remains with the ruling removed or both are taken away, since in either case the thing that governed conduct is replaced. The point settles what change is meant. The commentators then differed concerning the words whatever We abrogate, and the reports naming who said each are recorded.

The second thing named in the verse is the causing of a verse to be forgotten, and it is placed beside abrogation as the other way a ruling ceases to be carried by the community. The recitations of this word are compared, and the reading of the reciters of Medina and Kufa, which has the sense of causing to forget, comes first. Two readings of it are possible, one taking the clause as meaning that the ruling is changed or left to be forgotten, the other as meaning leaving and abandoning. Others read it as deferring, from the expression of deferring a matter, and a group of the Companions and the Successors read it thus. Yet another reading makes the Prophet the abrogator, and is rejected as an error.

The judgment is then given on which reading is best. The most correct is the one that means that We leave it, since whenever He replaces or changes a ruling, or leaves it as it is, He brings something better than it or something like it. Read this way the word covers both leaving behind and postponing, since everything left is also in a sense deferred.

Two further points are noted. The choice was made for the sake of the words running together in an orderly sense, and not because it is denied that Allah can cause His Prophet to forget part of what is abrogated. And Allah did not say that He takes away nothing of what He revealed, only that He would take it away entirely if He willed. The sense of the verse is then settled. He meant only the ruling of a verse, and since its meaning was comprehensible to those addressed it was enough to mention the verse in place of the ruling.

phrases.translation: We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation: The replacement is then explained. We bring something better than it or something like it, and the commentators differed, one holding that He brings something better than what He has abrogated and another that He brings something better than what He has left standing. The sense of better is then set out, since the comparison is not between two texts but between what each of them requires of people, being better in this life because it is lighter for the one charged with it, or in the hereafter because of the greatness of its reward. The verse closes with a question that answers the objection behind it, do you not know that Allah is capable of everything, since the power to replace one ruling belongs to the same power that made the first.

phrases.translation: Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah,
phrases.explanation:
The kingdom named is explained first, and the sense of the clause is that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so nothing in them is outside His disposal. The word for dominion is distinguished from the word for ownership, since the Arabs use it of authority rather than of property.

A question is then raised about the form of the address. Did the Messenger of Allah not already know that Allah is capable of all this? The answer is that this is an announcement from Allah that Muhammad already knew it, put in the form of an affirmation as the Arabs do when one says to his companion, have I not honored you. The reading preferred is then given. Even though the sentence appears on its surface as an address directed to the Prophet, in reality it is aimed at his community, and this is widespread among the Arabs.

The announcement is also read as a refutation of the Jews, who denied that the ordinances of their scripture could be abrogated and rejected the prophethood of Isa.

phrases.translation: and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah
phrases.explanation:
The two things denied are explained from their forms. The word for helper is a noun on a known pattern, derived from the saying of a person who says, I helped you, so I am your helper, and the two forms built from it are given.

The words besides Allah are then explained as meaning other than Allah and after Allah, so the phrase excludes every other source of protection and support at once. Guardian and helper are named together because the first covers the one who takes charge of a person's affairs and the second the one who comes to his aid, and neither is to be found for them apart from Him.

phrases.translation: Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before?
phrases.explanation:
The verse is discussed first in its occasion. The people of interpretation differed concerning the reason it was revealed, and several accounts are recorded, each naming a different thing that some people asked of the Prophet. The reports are given with the names of those who transmitted them, so the question in the verse is read against a particular asking rather than as a general warning.
