The particle at the head of the verse is then examined. The grammarians differed concerning the meaning of the word translated as or, since it can introduce a second alternative or can turn the sentence back on what came before, and each reading gives the question a slightly different place in the argument. The explanation preferred is given with the reasoning for it.

The comparison drawn in the verse is then explained. Asking the Messenger as Moses was asked before means asking in the way that people asked of Moses, which the earlier verses in this chapter have already described, so the warning is that the same kind of asking produced the same kind of trouble for the people who made it.

phrases.translation: But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way
phrases.explanation:
Exchanging is then explained. By the words whoever exchanges unbelief for faith, Allah means whoever puts one in the place of the other, so the verb carries the sense of a trade in which a thing is handed over and something else taken in return.

A second explanation of the two words is recorded beside it. It has been said that the word for unbelief in this place is used in the sense of hardship and the word for faith in the sense of ease, and the reports naming who said that are given. On that reading the exchange described is of one condition for another rather than of belief for its opposite, and both readings are left standing.

The consequence is then explained. Such a person has strayed from the middle of the road, and the phrase is explained from its parts, the middle of the road being the part of it that leads where the traveler intends to go. What is said about the exchange is drawn out at length, since the verse connects the asking described before it with a loss that is described here as losing the way itself.

phrases.translation: Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy,
phrases.explanation:
The verse is placed first, and it settles who is spoken to. This saying of Allah makes clear that His address in the verses from here on, although the discourse is on its face directed to the Prophet, is in reality an address to the believers and his companions. Many of the People of the Book wish that they could turn the believers back into unbelief, and the motive named with it is envy.

The phrase from themselves is then explained. It means from within themselves, as a person says he has such-and-such on your side, and it notifies the believers that this was never commanded to them in their Book. The grammar of the sentence is discussed, since the construction carrying the wish and the motive is one Arabic uses in a particular way.

phrases.translation: after the truth has been made clear to them.
phrases.explanation:
The clause after the truth has been made clear to them is then explained, and its sense is that the truth had already become plain to the people described. The matter on which it became plain is named, namely the message of the Prophet and what he brought from his Lord, and the religion to which he called them, so the clarity is not of some remote knowledge but of the thing they were shown.

The word is then drawn out for what it indicates. The disbelief of those whose account Allah relates in this verse was obstinacy, and it happened while they had knowledge and awareness that they were fabricating lies about Allah. That is what makes the envy named in the verse a choice rather than a mistake.

phrases.translation: Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision.
phrases.explanation:
The command to the believers is then explained. Pardon means overlook what proceeded from them of evil and error in a view that they counseled you concerning your religion, with the intent of turning you away from it and bringing about your apostasy after your faith. It covers also what had already passed from them of their word to the Prophet, when they used to ask him to ignore what he said and to use the word forbidden them.

Turning away is joined to it, and the two together describe a conduct toward people who are wishing harm. The limit set on that conduct is then noted, since the command runs only until Allah brings His command, so what is asked is patience for a period and not permanent silence.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation:
The closing name is explained by referring back to what was demonstrated earlier, that the word for the all capable means the one who is able to do what He wills. The meaning of the verse here is then set out. Allah is capable of all that He wills with respect to those whose matter has been described, among the People of the Book and others. If He desires to take vengeance upon them for their obstinacy toward their Lord, He is able to do so, and no one can hold Him back.

The name closes the verse because the command before it asks the believers to wait, and it tells them that the one they are waiting on is able to bring the matter to an end.

phrases.translation: Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do
phrases.explanation:
The two commands are explained first. Establishing the prayer and giving the alms tax are the same two requirements named in the covenant described earlier in this chapter, and establishing the prayer means performing it completely with its obligations.

The promise attached to them is then explained. Whatever good you send forward for yourselves you will find it with Allah, and the good a person does is described as something sent ahead, so whatever good deed is performed in the days of life and sent forward before death as a treasure kept for the return arrives with Allah, and its reward is found there. The command is then read as part of what the city was told to do, so that the people might purify themselves of the fault they had committed.

phrases.translation: The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation:
What they said is explained first. The Jews and the Christians said that none will enter the Garden except whoever is a Jew or a Christian. The wording of the claim is then examined, since the word for Jew has two views and the clause has also been read as a condition.

The answer is then given in two parts. Those are their wishful fancies is described as a report from Allah about the standing of the claim, and the Prophet is commanded to call on those who made it to produce their proof, on a matter lying between all the factions, the Muslims, the Jews, and the Christians. Although the outward import of the command is a call for proof, it in reality carries the meaning of a refutation by Allah of their claim.

phrases.translation: But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good
phrases.explanation:
The opening word is explained by referring back to what was set forth earlier, that the word translated as but no is an affirmation answering a negation. The condition that replaces that claim is then explained. Whoever submits his face to Allah means whoever surrenders himself to obedience to Him, and the image is illustrated from ordinary speech, in which a person says that he has surrendered to the one to whose obedience the rain clouds surrender. The word for submission is traced to the word for surrender, so the sense is obedience to His command.

The report concerning the person Allah describes is then given, and the submission of the face is singled out to the exclusion of the rest of the limbs, since the face is the noblest of the organs.

phrases.translation: will have their reward with their Lord.
phrases.explanation:
The second half of the condition is explained as well. While he is a doer of good means in the state of doing good, so the explanation is that whoever performs his obedience to Allah and His worship sincerely is a doer of good in that deed of his. The surrender is the direction of the person and the doing of good is what he does while he faces that way.

The reward promised is then explained. His reward is with his Lord, and the sense given is that to the one who submits his face to Allah as a doer of good belongs his recompense and his reward for his submission and his obedience to his Lord, with Allah, and not with anyone else.

phrases.translation: And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.explanation:
The two assurances that close the verse are then explained. No fear upon them is explained as concerning the Muslims who submitted their faces to Allah while they are doers of good, so no fear shall come upon them in the hereafter for His punishment and the torment of His blazing fire, nor for what they sent forward of deeds.

They will not grieve removes what is behind them, and the sense given is that they will not grieve over what they have left behind in the world, nor that the bliss Allah has prepared for the people of His obedience should be withheld from them. The two together are the same pair of assurances given earlier in this chapter to those who believe and do righteous deeds.

phrases.translation: The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures.
phrases.explanation:
The verse is placed first, and it is transmitted that it was revealed concerning a group of the people of the two religions who disputed with one another in the presence of the Messenger of Allah.

The explanation of the verse is then given. The Jews said that the Christians are not upon the truth in their religion, and the Christians said the same of the Jews. The clause about reciting adds the point, since each group was reciting its own book while denying the other any standing.

A question is then raised. Did they have anything to stand on after Allah sent His Messenger? The answer refers back to a report transmitted earlier, and the denial in the verse is a denial of the prophethood of the Prophet.

phrases.translation: And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺.
phrases.explanation:
The third group named is discussed first in its identity. The exegetes differed concerning whom Allah meant by those who have no knowledge. Some gave one answer, and others said that what is meant are the polytheists of the Arabs, because they were not People of the Book and so had no scripture to appeal to in what they said.

The correct view is then stated. Allah intended by His saying that those who have no knowledge speak in the same manner to the believers and to one another, so the likeness named in the verse is a likeness of speech, and a group with no book says about others what the two groups with books said about each other. The explanation of that is given at length.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute
phrases.explanation:
The judgment promised is then explained. Allah will pass judgment and thus make a separation between those who differ, who say to one another that the other has nothing to stand upon, on the day when the creatures rise before their Lord. Then the truthful among them is distinguished from the one who is in the wrong.

The word for the Resurrection is explained from its form. It is a verbal noun from the saying of a person who says, I stood, standing and rising. By it here is meant only the rising of the creatures from their graves before their Lord, so the Day of Resurrection is the day of that rising, and the dispute named is what will be settled on it.

phrases.translation: Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them?
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained first by referring back to what was already demonstrated, that the meaning of wrongdoing in Arabic is putting a thing in a place other than the place it belongs to. The question who is more unjust is therefore not asking for a comparison among kinds of injustice but naming the worst placement of all.

The places named are then explained. The word used is the plural of the word for a place of worship, and it is explained as covering every place in which Allah is worshipped, so it is not limited to buildings of one kind or to one community. What was already shown about the word is referred to rather than repeated.

The clause about the mention of Allah's name is discussed next, and two manners of interpreting it are given. On one of them the preventing is described in terms of the places themselves, and on the other the meaning is, who is more unjust than he who prevents that the name of Allah be mentioned in them, so the thing prevented is the mention and the people prevented are those who would make it.

The second half of the description is explained last. Striving to ruin them means working toward their destruction, and the explanation given joins it to the preventing before it, since both are ways of ending the worship that those places exist for.

phrases.translation: Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear.
phrases.explanation:
The sentence that follows is explained as a report from Allah about the person who prevented the places of worship from having the name of Allah mentioned in them. He has forbidden him the entering of the mosques which he strove to ruin and in which he turned the servants of Allah away from remembering Him.

The form of the wording is then discussed. The words are used in this form because of what the exception carries with it, and the sentence is worded as a report about all of them while it is in fact a report about the one man. So the verse does not forbid them from entering at all, but says that it was not for them to enter except in fear.

phrases.translation: For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation:
The two punishments are then explained. For them means for those about whom Allah reported what He reported in this verse, namely the people who prevented the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them, so the description runs back to the same people.

Disgrace in this world is named first and the tremendous punishment in the hereafter second, and the two are joined in one sentence so that what they receive is described in both worlds. The word for disgrace is explained as the ignominy, the evil and the humiliation, and it is said to be either the death penalty and captivity or the humiliation set aside for them in the life to come.

phrases.translation: To Allah belong the east and the west,
phrases.explanation:
The ownership stated at the head of the verse is explained first. By the words to Allah belong the east and the west, Allah means that both directions are His in ownership and disposal, just as one says a house belongs to a person.

The word for the east is then explained. It is the place where the sun rises, and the same formation is used in ordinary speech for the place where a thing happens, so the word names a direction by what occurs in it.

A question is raised about the wording. Did Allah then have only one east and one west? The answer is that the two words are used in Arabic for directions in general and not for two single points, and if the objection is pressed, that everything else and all the creatures belong to Him.

The reason for singling out these two directions is then discussed. One is that the verse was revealed as a permission to the Prophet to perform the voluntary prayer wherever he turned, toward east or west, during travel and in battle. Another is that it was revealed concerning a group of people for whom the direction of prayer had become unclear. A third is that it was revealed on account of the Abyssinian king, because the companions had disputed his case.

The judgment is then given. The correct view is that Allah singled out the east and the west here by mentioning that they belong to Him in ownership, as an announcement to His servants that to Him belongs the ownership of everything between them. The meaning of the verse is that to Allah belongs the ownership of the creatures between the east and the west, that He causes them to worship what He wills and decrees concerning them what He desires, and imposes upon them His obedience, and then the command to turn the face toward His.

phrases.translation: so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah.
phrases.explanation:
The word for turning is explained first. The most fitting interpretation of it is that it means you turn toward a direction, so the verb describes the facing of a person rather than the movement of his body from one place to another.

The word translated as there is then explained as carrying the sense of in that place, which fixes the second half of the sentence to the direction a person has turned toward.

The phrase there is the face of Allah is discussed last, and there is disagreement about it. Some said one thing, and others said that the meaning is that there is the direction Allah has appointed for prayer, so the face is read as the qibla. Others again said that the meaning is that by turning toward it a person obtains what Allah has attached to that turning. The reports naming who said each are given with them.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation:
The two names that close the verse are then explained. The All Encompassing means that Allah encompasses all His creation, and the explanation given is that He holds all His creatures with sufficiency, munificence, generosity and governance, so nothing of them is outside what He holds.

The All Knowing is joined to it, and the sense given is that He knows all their deeds, that nothing of them remains hidden from Him and nothing escapes His knowledge. The two together are what makes the permission given in the verse safe, since a person turning in any direction is turned toward something encompassed by Allah and known to Him.

phrases.translation: They say, “Allah has offspring.”
phrases.explanation:
The saying reported is explained first, and the explanation of the verse is then given in connection with what precedes it, since the claim that Allah has taken a son is answered by what follows. The people meant are the Christians who claimed that Jesus is the son of Allah.

Allah then informs that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, in ownership and in creation. That is the answer to the claim, because what belongs to Him in that way is not the kind of thing a child can be. The sense of it is added that how could the Messiah be a child to Allah, since he must be in one of these two places, the heavens or the earth.

phrases.translation: Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will
phrases.explanation:
The obedience stated at the end of the verse is discussed by the people of interpretation, who differed concerning it. Some took it to mean obedience, and others said that the meaning is that all of them acknowledge before Him servitude, so what is described is a standing of everything in creation.

The word used is then examined in the language. It has in Arabic several meanings, the first obedience, the second standing, and the third refraining from speech concerning it.

The meaning most appropriate here is then chosen, which is obedience together with the acknowledgement before Allah of servitude, through the testimony of their bodies with the traces of being created. It is not permissible to restrict a verse whose outward meaning is general except on the basis of a proof.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth!
phrases.explanation:
The name is explained first as meaning the originator of the heavens and the earth, so it names a bringing into being without a model already there, and the form of the word is discussed, since in reality it is the active pattern turned into the shorter one. The meaning is given as the one who calls a thing into existence without anyone preceding him.

The meaning of the verse as a whole is then stated. Glory be to Allah, and how could He have a child while He is the possessor of all that is in the heavens and the earth, all of which bear witness for Him by their indication of His oneness and testify their obedience.

This is a notification from Allah to His servants, and it concerns those who bear witness to what the verse describes, since the origin of everything rules out the claim before it. Among those who bear witness for Him is also the Messiah, whose sonship they ascribed to Allah.

phrases.translation: When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is
phrases.explanation:
The decreeing named here is explained from its root. The basic meaning of every decreeing of a matter in Arabic is the determining of it and the completing of it, and the discussion of that meaning is given at length, since it fixes what kind of act the verse is describing.

The clause that follows is then explained in the same terms. When He determines a matter and completes it, He says to it, be, and it is, so the saying is attached to the determining rather than standing on its own.

A question is then raised about the wording. What is the meaning of saying that He speaks to a matter when a matter cannot hear speech? The answer begins by noting that the exegetes disputed concerning the meaning, and what they said is reported.

Some of them said that this is a notification from Allah concerning His irrevocable command, and that the description of it as speech is a way of stating that nothing stands between His willing a thing and its being, so no delay and no means come in between. The explanation of that reading is given in full.

The correct view concerning the saying is then stated at length. It settles how the words are to be taken, and the reasoning turns on the fact that the sentence describes the manner of Allah's acting rather than reporting a conversation, so the command named is the effect itself and not a sound addressed to something that listens.

phrases.translation: Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!”
phrases.explanation:
The demand is reported first, and then the people who made it are discussed. The exegetes differed concerning whom Allah meant by those who have no knowledge. Some named one group, with the reports of who said so given. Others said that what is meant are the Jews who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah. Others again said that what is meant are the polytheists among the Arabs.

The three answers differ about the identity of the people and not about the thing said, since all of them agree that the demand was for Allah to speak to them directly or for a sign to come to them, and that the demand was made by people described as not knowing.

The description of them as having no knowledge is what the verse turns on, since the demand is presented not as a request for evidence but as the speech of people who do not know what has already been given to them.

phrases.translation: The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike.
phrases.explanation:
The comparison drawn is discussed next. Thus also said those who were before them the like of their saying, and the exegetes differed concerning whom was meant. Some said they are the Jews and the Christians, on the ground that those who have no knowledge are the Arabs.

The reading preferred is then given, and it rests on what was demonstrated earlier, namely that those who asked why Allah does not speak to them are the Christians, and that those who said the like of their word are the Jews.

The likeness of their hearts is explained last. Another said that the hearts of the disbelieving Arabs and of the Jews and the Christians resemble one another, so what is compared is not the wording of the demand but the state of the people making it. The form of the word for likeness is also discussed, and the doubling of the letter is not read in it.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith
phrases.explanation:
The closing clause is explained as a statement that the signs have already been made clear, and that they were made clear for a people who have certainty.

The signs in question are then named. They are the indications why Allah became wrathful with the Jews, and made of them apes and swine, and prepared for them the humiliating punishment at their return, and the indications why Allah disgraced the Christians in this life and prepared for them a painful punishment in the hereafter.

The certainty named here is what allows the signs already given to be seen as signs, and the demand for another sign is answered by pointing to what has been made clear rather than by promising something further.

phrases.translation: We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation:
The sending described is explained first. The meaning of Allah's saying that He sent the Prophet with the truth is set out at length, and the truth he was sent with is described as the message itself, that is, Islam, which Allah accepts from no one else.

A question of recitation is then discussed. The reciters differ over one of the words in the verse, some reading it as a statement about the Prophet and others about what was sent. The correct view is the reading that makes it a statement, and the reasoning for preferring it is given.

Some of the grammarians of Basra are then reported on the second half of the verse, and their way of taking the clause that follows is explained.

phrases.translation: as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire
phrases.explanation:
The clause about not being asked is discussed in the recitation. Most of the reciters read it with a vowel that makes it a statement, so the sense is that the Prophet will not be asked about the people of the blazing fire, and upon him rests only the conveyance of the message.

Some of the people of Medina read it in the shortened form, which makes it a prohibition, so the sense is do not ask about them, and the meaning on that reading is that the Prophet was sent to convey the message, not to question about the people of the fire. The difference between the two readings is then explained, since one reports what will not happen and the other forbids something, and the accounts of each are given.

phrases.translation: Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah
phrases.explanation:
The statement about their displeasure is explained first. The Jews and the Christians will not be pleased with the Prophet until he follows their religion, and the command to the Prophet is to abandon seeking what pleases them.

The answer he is told to give is then explained. Allah said to His Prophet to say to these Christians and Jews that the guidance of Allah is the guidance. He commanded His Prophet only to call them to the guidance of Allah.

The warning that follows is then explained. If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, the verse states what would follow, that he would have no protector and no helper against Allah. The knowledge named makes the supposed following a choice rather than a confusion.

phrases.translation: Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed.
phrases.explanation:
The people described are discussed first. The exegetes differ over whom Allah meant by those to whom the book was given, and the answers are reported one after another. Some said the believers among the People of the Book, and others said that what is meant are the scholars of the Children of Israel who believed in Allah and held His messengers to be true, and thus acknowledged the ruling of the Torah and acted upon what Allah had sent down to them.

The reading preferred is then argued for. It is closer to the truth than the saying that others made, and the reason looks back at the verses before it, which dealt with the same people, so the description here continues what the surrounding passage is about rather than introducing a new group. It is also said that the name of the book is used with the definite article because it is definite, for the Prophet and his companions knew which book was meant.

The following named in the verse is then explained. The exegetes differ over the words as it ought to be recited. Some said the meaning is that they follow it as it ought to be followed, and others said they read it as it ought to be read. The correct view is that it means they follow it as it ought to be followed, and the reasoning for it is given. The form of the words is then noted as a form of emphasis in the description of their following and their acting upon the book, and the sense of the whole is stated: those to whom We have given the book, namely the people of the Torah who believed in the Prophet and in what he brought them of truth, follow it as it ought to be followed.

phrases.translation: It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers
phrases.explanation:
The pronoun is explained first. By the word them, Allah means these people of whom He reported that they recite the book as it should be recited, so the belief named here is attached to the group just described, not to readers in general. The connection between following and believing is then made explicit, since Allah reported that the believer in the Torah is the one who follows what is in it of permitted and forbidden matters and acts upon the obligations laid on him.

The second half is then explained. Whoever disbelieves in it, and the sense given is that the disbelieving is in the book just named, is one of the losers, and the explanation is given at length, since the loss belongs to the same act of following the first half.

phrases.translation: O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others
phrases.explanation:
The address is explained first, and the meaning of the call to the Children of Israel to remember the favour Allah bestowed on them and to remember that He preferred them above the worlds is set out at length, since the preference named is a particular one and the favour is what the remembering is called back to.

The favours themselves are not listed again here. They were mentioned previously, and the verse is referred back to that listing rather than repeating it, so what is being asked of them is remembrance of what has already been set before them, and the preference named is the same one described earlier. The point of the repetition is that the earlier passage told of what was done for them and this tells them to remember.

phrases.translation: And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given
phrases.explanation:
The warning is explained first. This verse is a warning and a deterrence from Allah directed to those who were addressed in what precedes it, and the explanation of that is given at length, since the verse names four things that will not be available on the day described.

The four are set out together. No soul will avail another soul anything, no ransom will be taken from it, no intercession will benefit it, and it will not be helped. Each rules out an escape that the people addressed relied on. The exposition of all the meanings of this verse is then noted as having been given earlier, in connection with the corresponding verse that came before it, so what is added here is the repetition rather than a new reading of the words.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled.
phrases.explanation:
The testing named in the verse is explained first. By the word for trying, Allah means that He put Abraham to the test, and the verb is then set out in its Arabic form, with the shape of the past and present given and another use of the same word in the Quran cited as a witness for it.

The nature of the test is then explained. Allah's putting Abraham to the test was a trial by means of obligations that He imposed on him, so what is described is not a trial of patience in suffering but a trial of carrying out what was required.

The words with which he was tried are then discussed. The exegetes differed concerning their nature. Some of them said that they are the legal prescriptions of Islam, and that these are thirty portions. Others said that they are ten qualities from the established customs of Islam. The reports naming who said each are given with them.

The completing named at the end of the clause is explained last. By his fulfilling them, Allah means that Abraham completed the words, and the explanation of what that completing amounts to is given.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?”
phrases.explanation:
The disagreement about the words continues, and the remaining answers are reported. Others said that what is meant is the statement I make you a leader for the people, so the words are read as the promise itself. Others said that they are exclusively the rites of the pilgrimage. Others said that they are matters of practice, among which is circumcision. Others again said that they are six things, and the six are listed as the star, the moon, the sun, the fire, the migration, and circumcision, each of them belonging to a part of Abraham's story told elsewhere in the Quran. The reports naming who held each answer are given one after another.

The correct view is then stated, and it is argued at length. It does not choose one of the lists as the exclusive answer but explains what the words named in the verse must be taken to cover, since the verse says only that Allah tried Abraham with words and that he completed them, without naming them. The reply that the correct position concerning the meaning of the words is what has just been set out is then given, and an objection is raised against that view. It is said that what the named authorities held is more in agreement with the wording, and the objection is answered in turn, with the answer explaining why the particular lists they gave cannot carry the whole of what the verse states.

The promise of leadership is then explained on its own. By the words I make you a leader for the people, Allah said to Abraham that he would be followed, and the sense given is that leadership here is a being followed in religion rather than a holding of authority. The word used is explained from the language of the Arabs, where one says of a man that he led the people and so he leads them, when he is their leader.

Abraham's question about his offspring is explained last. It is put in its place, after Allah raised his rank and honoured him and informed him of what He had made him, so the question is asked by someone who has just been given the promise and wants to know whether it passes on. The explanation of the question and of what it implies about his concern for those after him is given at length, and the answer is explained as promising that the promise will reach the upright among his offspring.

phrases.translation: Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation:
The answer to that question is explained first. This is an announcement from Allah that the wrongdoer will not be a leader followed by the people of good, so the answer does not refuse the promise outright but limits who it can reach.

The covenant named in it is then discussed. The exegetes differed concerning the covenant that Allah withheld from wrongdoers, and some of them said that it is prophethood, so that prophethood does not reach the people of wrongdoing and those who associate partners with Allah. A note is added about the reading of the sentence. In one reading the wrongdoers are made the ones who do not reach, so the sentence is turned around while carrying the same meaning, and the grammatical discussion of the two shapes is given.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people
phrases.explanation:
The verse is connected first to what precedes it. The statement that Allah made the House a place of resort for the people and a sanctuary is joined to the earlier verses by way of continuation, so the House is brought in as part of the same account rather than as a new subject, and the word when is what joins the two. The House meant is then named, and it is the Sacred House.

The word for a place of resort is then examined, and the linguists are said to differ over its meaning and over the reason why the word is in the feminine form. Some of the grammarians of Basra said that the extra letter at the end of the word was added on account of the great number of people who return to the place, so the form of the word carries the repeated character of the returning. The word is also given in its pattern, which is the pattern of a place noun, and it is derived from the saying of a person that the people returned to the place, when they return to it. And from this comes the expression that a person's reason returned to him, when it comes back to him after it had left him.

The meaning of the whole clause is then stated. By Allah's saying that He made the House a place of resort for the people, the sense is that He made it a place people come back to again and again, and a refuge to which they come every year, and the poetry of the Arabs is quoted in support of that sense.

The second description is then explained alongside the first. Security is a verbal noun, derived from the saying of one who says he was secure, he is secure, security. Allah called the House only a place of security because in the time of ignorance it was a refuge for whoever sought refuge in it, so that a man who met there the murderer of his father was not harmed there. It was called a place of resort because it was always the place people returned to, and the two descriptions together say something about what the House is for.

The grammar of the sentence is then discussed. Some of the grammarians of Basra said that the sense of the words is that the House is a place of resort for the people and a place of security, with both descriptions belonging to the House. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said that the security is joined to the making of the House itself, so that the meaning of the statement is that when We made the House a place of resort for the people, We made it a place of security as well.

phrases.translation: ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.”
phrases.explanation:
The command about the standing place is discussed in the recitation. The reciters differ over the word. Some of them read it with the vowel that makes it a command, so the sense is take the standing place of Abraham as a place of prayer, and the reading is addressed to those who hear the verse.

Others read it differently. Some of the reciters of Medina and Syria read it with the vowel that makes it a report, so the sense is that they took the standing place of Abraham as a place of prayer. The two readings therefore differ about whether the sentence commands something or tells of something already done, and the accounts of each are given.

phrases.translation: And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House
phrases.explanation:
The charge given to the two of them is explained first. By the word for charging, Allah means commanding, so what follows is an instruction and not a report of what they decided.

The purifying named in the instruction is then explained, and the House is described as belonging to Allah, since the wording used is My House. A question is raised about the sense of the charge, since it was said for the sake of those who perform the circumambulation, and the answer is that there are two ways of reading it. The first is that the charge is to build the House purified of shirk and of doubt. The second is that they were commanded to purify the site before the building and the House after the building.

phrases.translation: for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺
phrases.explanation:
The three groups named at the end of the charge are then explained one after another. The first is those who perform the circumambulation, and the people of interpretation differ over the meaning of the word in this verse. Some took it to mean the foreigners who come to the House, and others said that those who perform the circumambulation are the people who go around it, whether they are residents of the city or people who have come to it. The reports naming who said each are given.

The more correct of the two interpretations is then chosen, and the reason is drawn from the word itself, since the one described by it is a person who goes around something, and the one arriving from a far land does not deserve to be described in that way.

The second group is those who remain at the House, and here too the exegetes differ. Some of them said that what is meant is the person who sits in the Sacred House without circumambulating and without praying, so the word covers a sitting that is not itself an act of worship of either kind. Others said that those who remain are the people who take up residence beside the House, so the word covers the neighbours of the sanctuary rather than visitors to it, and others said that they are the inhabitants of the precinct. The name itself is explained as given only to the one who stays in the place where he holds himself for Allah.

The judgment is then given, which is that the one who remains is the one who dwells in the House, residing beside it, without circumambulating and without praying.

The third group is those who bow and prostrate, which names the prayer itself, since the sense given is that it refers to the people who bow before Him there, and it has also been said that it means those who perform the prayer. The three together cover what is done at the House, and the charge to purify it is therefore given for the sake of everyone who comes to it in any of these ways, x

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure
phrases.explanation:
The request is explained first. By his saying, my Lord, make this a secure city, Abraham asks that the city be made safe, and the security asked for is described as security from tyrants and from others gaining power over it, so what is asked is not merely an absence of fear but a standing that keeps others out.

A question is then raised about the request. If the sanctuary has always been secure, what was there for Abraham to ask for? The answer notes a difference of opinion on the point, and the correct judgment is then given at length, explaining that Allah made Mecca a sanctuary when He created it, so that the request asked for the protection already prepared.

The outcome is described last. Mecca became what it is after Allah had protected it by repelling harm from it, and had made it sacred, and for this reason its consecration is attributed to Abraham.

phrases.translation: and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while,
phrases.explanation:
The second half of the request is then explained. Abraham asks that the people of the city be provided with fruits, and the request is limited in the wording to whoever of them believes in Allah and the last day. The limiting of the provision to believers is what the rest of the verse turns on, since the answer that follows takes up those who disbelieve separately.

The sense of the request is then set out more fully, namely that his Lord should provide the believers among the inhabitants of Mecca with fruits and not the unbelievers, and the word for whoever is explained as a further specification of the inhabitants. The reason for the request is given too, since Abraham alighted in a valley without vegetation, without water and without inhabitants.

phrases.translation: then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire.
phrases.explanation:
The answer is discussed first in its wording. Others said that Abraham said this as a request of his to his Lord, so on that reading the words about letting the disbeliever enjoy himself are part of what Abraham asked for, not what Allah said.

The correct reading is then stated, and the reasoning is set out at length, since the two readings put the words in different mouths and give the verse a different shape. The letting enjoy is then explained. By him I will let enjoy for a short while, the meaning is that what Allah provides him will last only a little while, and it has also been said that it means continued existence here.

The compelling that follows is then explained. By then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, the word for compelling is set out from its use in Arabic, since a person says I compelled someone to this matter when he constrains him to it. The meaning is therefore that he will be driven toward the punishment.

phrases.translation: What an evil destination!”
phrases.explanation:
The closing description is explained. By evil is the destination, the word used is discussed first, and it has already been shown that it comes from the word for misery, with the account of how the second letter of the form was changed given rather than repeated here.

The meaning of the statement is then given. Evil is the destination, and the destination named is the punishment of the Fire, which comes after the enjoyment of this world in which those described were living. The sentence therefore closes the verse by naming where the short enjoyment ends, and the word for the destination is explained from the language of the Arabs as the place where the one who disbelieves will end.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael,
phrases.explanation:
The raising described is explained first. By Allah's words about Abraham raising the foundations of the House while Ishmael was with him, the sense given is that Abraham was in the act of raising them, and the verse places the two of them together at that work.

The word for the foundations is then explained. It is the plural of a singular form, and a single foundation of the House is called by that singular, so the plural names the parts on which the building stands.

A disagreement about those foundations follows. The exegetes differed concerning whether the two of them raised the foundations themselves or whether these already existed. A group said they were the foundations of a house that Adam had built on Allah's command, and others said they were the foundations of a house Allah sent down from heaven for Adam. The correct view is then given, that Abraham and Ishmael raised them.

phrases.translation: ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us.
phrases.explanation:
The supplication is explained first in its setting. By our Lord, accept from us, the sense is that Abraham said this while raising the foundations of the House, so the words come during the work rather than after it, and the explanation of that placement is given.

The question of who spoke them is then discussed. The verse according to one view has Abraham saying them. Others said that the one who said this was rather Ishmael, since on that reading the supplication belongs to the younger of the two.

A further disagreement is recorded about the work itself. The exegetes differed concerning who raised the foundations, after they had agreed that Abraham was among those who did. Some said that Abraham and Ishmael raised them together. Others said that Abraham raised them while Ishmael handed him the stones. Others again said that Abraham raised them alone and that Ishmael was a small child on that day.

The correct view is then given. The implicit speech is attributed to Abraham and Ishmael together, and the two of them raised the foundations of the House together, and this is said only because all the exegetes agree that Ishmael is meant in the report Allah gave concerning him and his father. The explanation of the text is therefore: and when Abraham was raising the foundations, and Ishmael, while the two of them said, our Lord, accept from us our work and our obedience to You.

phrases.translation: You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: The two names that close the supplication are then explained. By You are the All Hearing, the All Knowing, the sense given is that Allah hears the supplication the two of them have just made and knows what stands behind it, so the closing words answer the request for acceptance by naming the two attributes that acceptance depends on. The explanation of the words is given at length. It is set out that the hearing is of their supplication and of their request for acceptance, and that the knowing is of the work they ask to be accepted and of the state they are in when they make the request, so that nothing about the two of them is hidden from the One they are asking.

phrases.translation: Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You
phrases.explanation:
The next request is explained as continuing the same report. This too is a report from Allah concerning Abraham and Ishmael, that they both raised the foundations while asking, so the supplication in this verse is joined to the one before it, and the sense of the words is that they ask that the two of them be made ones who submit.

A note is added on the wording of what follows. It has been mentioned that in one reading the clause about the rites is put in a different shape, and that reading is recorded because it bears on how the request later in the verse is understood, since the person shown the rites is then the offspring of the two of them and not the two of them themselves.

phrases.translation: and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you.
phrases.explanation:
The request concerning their offspring is then explained. By the words and from our offspring a community submitting to You, the sense is that the two of them asked for a group from among their descendants who submit to Allah.

It has been said that by this they meant the Arabs, and the report naming who said so is given. That statement is then answered, since its contrary is indicated by the outward meaning of the Book.

The word for community is explained as well. In this place it means a group of people, and another use of the same word in the Quran is cited as a witness for that sense.

phrases.translation: Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation:
The request about the rites is discussed first in the recitation. The reciters differ over the word, some reading it as a command addressed to Allah, show us our rites. The proponents of that reading then differed over what the rites are, some taking them one way and others saying they are the places of slaughter.

Others read the word differently again, and claimed its meaning is teach us, so the request concerns instruction rather than sight. The verb is then explained. By the word for showing, the sense is direct me to it and make its place known.

The word for the rites is explained. It is the plural of the singular, and that is the place where one offers sacrifice for Allah and draws near to Him by what pleases Him.

The request for the acceptance of repentance is explained, and the word for repentance is traced to the return from the detested to the beloved. The closing name names the One who returns to His servants with favor and grants repentance.

phrases.translation: Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations,
phrases.explanation:
The request for a messenger is explained first. The supplication is that of Abraham and Ishmael, and it concerns the Prophet in particular, since the Prophet used to say that he was the supplication of Abraham. A group of the people of interpretation concurred with this, and the reports naming them given.

The messenger asked for is then described as one from among them, so that he is of their own kind and speaks their tongue.

The reciting named in the request is then explained. By who recites to them Your signs, the sense is that he reads them out to those he is sent to, so the messenger's first work is carrying the signs to people rather than explaining them, and the sense given is that he recites the Book Allah reveals to him.

phrases.translation: teach them the Book and wisdom,
phrases.explanation:
The book named is explained first. By the book, Allah means the Quran, and why the Quran is called a book was explained earlier, so the point is referred to rather than argued again.

The wisdom joined to it is then discussed. The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning of the wisdom that Allah mentions here. Some of them said that it is the practice of the Prophet, and the report naming who said that is given. Others said that the wisdom is the knowledge of the religion and the deep understanding of it, and that is the sense which the word carries in the verse, since the Book is what is recited and the wisdom is what is understood and acted upon.

phrases.translation: and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”
phrases.explanation:
The view preferred about the wisdom is then stated. The correct view of the statement, in our opinion, is that it is knowledge of the ordinances Allah has laid down, and the reasoning for that reading is given, since it explains why wisdom is named separately from the book even though both are taught by the same messenger.

The interpretation of the whole verse is then put together. Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves who recites to them Your signs and teaches them the book and the wisdom and purifies them.

The purifying named last is explained from what was shown earlier, that its meaning is cleansing, and the discussion of what the messenger cleanses them from is given.

phrases.translation: And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life,
phrases.explanation:
The question at the head of the verse is explained first. Who turns away from the religion of Abraham, and the discourse on the interpretation of the saying is given at length, since the question is not asked for information but to rule the turning away out.

The exception that follows is then explained. Except him who makes a fool of himself, and the discourse on that saying is given in turn, since it names the only person of whom the turning away can be said.

A point of grammar is added about the form of the sentence. The word for himself stands in the accusative according to the meaning of specification, and the reason for that shape is explained, with the grammatical discussion given at length.

phrases.translation: and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous
phrases.explanation: The second half of the verse is explained as well. In the hereafter he is among the righteous, and the discourse on that is given in turn, so the verse joins what Allah did for Abraham in this world to the standing he has in the next, and the two are stated together as one description of him. The word for the righteous is then explained, and the sense given is that they are those who have been made upright by their own striving, so that the standing in the hereafter answers the choosing in this world, since the one who was chosen here is the one who stands there.

phrases.translation: When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained first. When his Lord said to him, submit, the statement concerning the explanation of those words is given, including the grammar of the form used for the command, and the sense is that the Lord said to him, submit to Me.

The answer is then explained. He said, I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds, so the response names the one submitted to and covers everything other than Him, and the account of what that submission consists of is given with it, namely that the whole of what a person does is turned to Allah, so that nothing remains for another. The answer is that of Abraham, who is the one addressed, and it is the same submission the verse has already asked for on behalf of his son.

phrases.translation: This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”
phrases.explanation:
The enjoining at the head of the verse is explained. By his words that he enjoined this, he enjoined this word upon those addressed, and by his words that Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, he made it incumbent on them. The word that would introduce the speech is omitted, since disclosing with the tongue is speech.

The words enjoined are then explained. By Allah has chosen the religion for you, the sense given is set out, and the meaning is that Allah selected this religion for them. The command that follows is then explained. Do death and life belong to the children of Adam, such that one could not die except in one state? The answer is that they are to be in that state when death comes.

phrases.translation: Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?”
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained first. The verse is put as a question to those who deny the messenger and hold to what came before him, asking whether they were present when death came to Jacob, and the answer given is that they were not, so a claim built on something they never witnessed is set aside.

The setting of the verses is then described. They came down as a refutation of the Jews and the Christians in what they claimed, and the people of interpretation spoke in accordance with that account.

The question Jacob put to his sons is then explained, and the sense of it is set out, so the scene the verse calls up is given before the reply is quoted.

phrases.translation: They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God.
phrases.explanation:
The recitation of the reply is then discussed. Some of the earlier reciters read the words as the God of your father Abraham, and the reading is explained. Their supposition was that Ishmael, since he was an uncle of Jacob, was not permitted to be counted among the forefathers named.

The reading preferred is then given. The correct reading in our view is the God of your fathers, and the reason given is that it agrees with what the verse goes on to say, since the reply names Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac together and one father would not cover them. The agreement of the reciters upon this reading and the anomalousness of the other are also given as reasons for preferring it.

phrases.translation: And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”
phrases.explanation:
The way the words are joined is then explained. The better of the two ways of reading them is that they work as a qualifying circumstance, so the submission named is what the reply itself adds to the worship named before it, and the sense is that they will worship the God of their forefathers and to Him they submit.

The order of the two names is then addressed. It has been said that Ishmael was placed before Isaac only because Ishmael was the elder, and the report of that is given. The sense of the answer is that the two of them together are named because the worship is one and shared by them all.

phrases.translation: That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done
phrases.explanation:
The community meant is explained first, and the exposition of the interpretation of the saying is given.

The word used for one who has passed away is then examined. It is only said of a person who has died and gone, because of his separation from what was his company, and the reason is given at length.

The address that follows is then explained. The Jews and the Christians are told that what belongs to the prophets and messengers of Allah is theirs, and the sense of that is set out.

Those who attribute the doctrines of those communities to themselves are then told that they will not be called to account for what they have fabricated, so the saying is a warning that the deeds of the earlier community do not pass to them.

phrases.translation: The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.”
phrases.explanation:
The claim of the two groups is explained first. By and you will be rightly guided, the sense is that then you will hit upon the path of truth, and another saying in the Quran is cited as a witness for that.

The reply that follows is then introduced, and the wording of it is set out.

The word for religion is then explained. It is the way of faith, so the two are not two separate things in the reply but one thing described in two words, and the sense of the reply is that the two groups each claim their own way for those who follow it.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham,
phrases.explanation:
The case of the word for Abraham's religion is then explained. In these words the noun stands in the accusative, and the reason for that is given.

A second way of accounting for it is then given. The accusative is taken to be caused by a verb that is left unexpressed but understood as we follow.

It is also possible, the reading continues, that it stands in the accusative as an exhortation, that is as an urging toward following the religion of Abraham.

Some of those who recite the Quran read the words in the nominative, and the explanation of that reading is given according to the reciters themselves.

phrases.translation: the upright—who was not a polytheist.”
phrases.explanation:
The uprightness named in the reply is explained. Allah advanced on behalf of His messenger the most eloquent and most concise of speech, and the wording is set out. The sense of the statement is then given, that the reply declares the religion of Abraham is followed, that it is upright, and that the speaker was not among those who associated partners.

The word for uprightness is examined. It means the straight of everything, and it has been said of the person whose one faith covers all of him.

And others said the word means the follower, as described earlier. Others said the sense is the sincerely devoted, and others said the uprightness here is Islam itself, so that everyone who takes Abraham as an example is counted among the upright.

The preferred view is given. The uprightness is steadfastness upon the religion of Abraham and the following of him. If it meant the pilgrimage to the House, then the Arabs would be counted among the upright, and the same holds for circumcision, for if it meant circumcision then the Jews would be counted among the upright, and Allah has excluded them.

A further question is then answered. If the uprightness is simply obedience to Allah, then the prophets before Abraham and their followers were also steadfast upon what they were commanded, and the answer is that they were all upright, but Allah made none of them a leader for the people, whereas Abraham was made one.

The closing words are explained. As for his saying that he was not among the polytheists, he was not among those who adhere to the religion of worshipping images and idols, nor among the Jews and Christians.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us;
phrases.explanation:
The address is explained first. The command to say is directed to the believers, and it is to be said to the Jews and the Christians who are being addressed, since they had told them to be Jews or Christians to be guided.

The meaning of faith is then given. It is holding for true, so believing here means accepting as true what is named, and the sense of the phrase is that they hold for true the Book Allah sent down to their Prophet.

The second item of the creed is then explained. What has been sent down to us is the Book Allah sent down, and the sense is that the believers hold it for true as well, and the address about the sending down is turned toward them.

phrases.translation: and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”
phrases.explanation:
The earlier scriptures are then named in turn. What was sent down to Abraham is the same thing as what was sent down to us, so the believers hold it for true as well.

What was given to Moses and to Jesus is then explained. It is the Torah that Allah gave to Moses and the Gospel that He gave to Jesus, and the believers likewise believe in both, so what the verse lists is a set of books rather than a set of persons.

The closing clause is then explained. By we are submitted to Him, the sense is that the believers submit to Allah, and the explanation of that is given with the rest of the sentence.

phrases.translation: So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided.
phrases.explanation:
The condition is explained first. If they believe in the like of that in which you believe, then they have been rightly guided, and the sense given is set out at length.

What the verse establishes is then stated. It shows that Allah accepts no deed from anyone except those who believe in this way, so the condition is the test that decides whose work is taken.

A reading that has been transmitted is then noted. It comes from one of the companions and the copies of the Muslims have taken it, and the reading is given.

The interpretation of that reading is then addressed. It does not rest on the meaning toward which the reading was directed, and what it actually means is set out.

phrases.translation: But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺.
phrases.explanation:
The warning is then explained. And if they turn away, the sense given is that if they turn away from what they have been given, then the consequence of that is stated.

The rest of the clause is then set out, and the account of it explains what is left for those who turn away and what is not. The state of division is named as the outcome, and the sense is that the people are in disagreement and enmity over the matter, so that they are split among themselves and against the truth that was set before them, and that they hold themselves apart from one another over it.

phrases.translation: But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation:
The word for division is then explained. Its origin, according to us, comes from the saying of a person who splits something in two, and the account of that is given.

The assurance that closes the verse is then explained. So Allah will suffice you against them, the sense is that the believers need no helper against those who turn away, because Allah deals with them, and the explanation of that is given at length. Allah did that with them at once and fulfilled His promise, for He gave His messenger power over them until some of them were killed and the rest were driven out and subdued.

phrases.translation: This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?
phrases.explanation:
The word for coloring is explained first. By it, the meaning is the coloring of Islam, so what the verse refers to is the way of life the believers are in, The reply is then introduced, since it is said to the people addressed when they told the believers to be Jews or Christians in order to be guided.

The case of the word is then discussed. Whoever reads it in the accusative places it there as a connection to the creed, so it is joined to what it qualifies. It is also permissible to place it in the nominative in a different manner, namely as the beginning of a new sentence. And it is also permissible to place it in the accusative in a manner other than as a connection to the creed, and the reason for that is explained.

In accordance with what has been said about the meaning of the word, a group of the exegetes have spoken, and the report naming who said that is given. Some of them said that the coloring of Allah is the religion of Allah, and others said that it is the original natural disposition of Allah, and whoever holds that view means that they follow the original natural disposition of Allah and His creed.

phrases.translation: And we worship ˹none but˺ Him
phrases.explanation:
The closing words are explained. By and we are worshippers of Him, the sense is that they alone are worshipped, and the rest of the clause is set out, the words being placed at the end of the sentence to seal it.

The sentence is then identified as a command from Allah to His messenger, so what is said in it is what the messenger is to declare, and the account of that is given. He is told to say it to the Jews and Christians who were addressed before, so that the declaration of the worship of Allah alone closes the reply and leaves them with nothing but that.

phrases.translation: Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained first. Do you dispute with us about Allah, and the sense given is that the address is to say to them, do you contend with us and argue about Him, when He is our Lord and your Lord.

The two claims that follow are then set out. Our deeds are ours and your deeds are yours, and no one is responsible for the deeds of another.

The closing clause is then explained. And we are sincerely devoted to Him alone means that we are devoted to Him alone, with no partner joined to Him.

The whole passage is then placed. It is a rebuke to the Jews and an argument on behalf of the people of faith, and the account of that is given.

phrases.translation: Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do
phrases.explanation:
The recitation of the opening question is discussed first. There are two possibilities in the recitation, and the first is with the letter that makes it read as you say, so the question is put to those addressed.

The other possibility is given. It is with the letter that makes it read as they say, and whoever recites it that way takes the question to be about what others have said rather than about what the speakers themselves have said.

Some linguists have asserted that when it is recited with the second letter and what follows is a command, the sense is that it is being said to the people addressed that their companions say so.

The reading preferred is then stated. The correct view in our opinion is the first, and the reason is given at length.

The question itself is then explained. It refers to the Jews and the Christians who said to the messenger and his companions that they should be Jews or Nazarenes for the way to be followed.

Others said that what is meant is the question about the one who conceals a testimony, and the report naming who said that is given.

The view already stated is then preferred, and the reason is given, since what the verse says points to it.

phrases.translation: That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done
phrases.explanation:
The sense of the verse is given at length. It is said to the messenger to those who dispute with him about Allah among the Jews and the Christians, that if they conceal the testimony they hold about Abraham and about the fact that they were Muslims, then truly Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the patriarchs were a community that has passed away, meaning that it has gone its way and returned to its Lord.

What belongs to that community is then set out. It has with Allah what it earned of good and what it earned of evil, and nothing benefits it except its good deeds and nothing harms it except its bad deeds. The consequence for those addressed is then drawn, since they are the ones in whom they take pride.

phrases.translation: The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?”
phrases.explanation:
The claim of the ignorant is explained. The foolish will say, and the sense is that the ignorant ones will ask about what they consider a matter.

It has been said that the foolish are the hypocrites, and the report naming who said that given. The reason for the word used is explained. Allah called them foolish only because they held the truth to be folly, so the word describes their judgement, not their understanding.

The question itself is explained. What has turned them away from their prayer direction, and the sense given is what thing has turned away and diverted the faces of these people from the place they faced.

The word for prayer direction is examined. The prayer direction of each thing is that which its face faces toward, and the form of the word is given with its derivation. The whole sentence is set out. The question is put to the believers when they turn their faces away from the prayer direction of the Jews.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”
phrases.explanation:
The reply is explained first. To Allah belongs the east and the west, and the sense is that the dominion covers what lies between the two extremities of the place of sunrise and of its place of sunset, and what is between them of the world.

The guidance named in it is then explained. He guides whom He wills of His creatures, meaning that He aids him onto the right way and leads him to the straight path, and the straight path is the prayer direction of Abraham, whom He made a leader for the people. And He forsakes whom He wills of them, and leads him astray from the way of truth.

The occasion of the question is given. The messenger prayed in the direction of Jerusalem for a period, and the account of how long that period lasted is given, with the reports naming who said what recorded. Some said it came by the choice of the messenger himself, others that it was on the basis of a prior instruction.

The occasion for the question is stated. It arose when the people who asked why they had been turned away saw the change of direction, and the reason for the prayer in that direction in the first place is given.

The wording of the reply is then explained. Say to Allah belongs the east and the west, He guides whom He wills to a straight path, and the sense given is that the messenger is to say this to those who said to him and his companions what has turned you away from your prayer direction of Jerusalem toward the sacred mosque.

phrases.translation: And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you.
phrases.explanation:
The phrase made upright community is explained. The sense is that just as the believers have been guided by the messenger and what he brought from Allah, so too they have been favoured above others as an upright community.

The word for community was explained earlier, meaning the generation of people and their grouping. The word for upright is examined. In the language of the Arabs it means the best and the choicest.

The meaning of upright is given as just and equitable, since the choicest among people are their just ones.

The witnessing named next is explained. The sense is that the community has been made upright and just so that it may be witnesses for the prophets concerning the conveyance of the message, and the messenger a witness over the believers.

phrases.translation: We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith.
phrases.explanation:
The reason the former prayer direction was appointed is then explained. The sense is that the appointment of that direction, and the turning away from it toward the sacred house, was to distinguish the one who follows the messenger from the one who turns back on his heels, and the direction meant is the one they used to face before the turn toward the house.

A point of grammar is then added. The mention of the turning away from it was omitted because the indication of the earlier part of the statement toward the intended meaning was enough, as in the other comparable cases already mentioned, and the same holds for the rest of the wording in the verse.

phrases.translation: It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah.
phrases.explanation:
The reasoning behind the testing is given. The trial the companions of the messenger underwent came when the direction changed from Jerusalem to the house, until some converted apostatised and hypocrites revealed themselves,

A question of wording is addressed. He ascribed the asking and the visiting to Himself, while in reality it concerned another, and by that We might distinguish the sense is that His protected ones might distinguish.

This is then set aside as far-fetched, since seeing stands in place of knowing, so knowledge may be indicated by the mention of seeing, but not seeing by the mention of knowing.

Others said it means only that His protected ones might distinguish.

The two sides of the testing are explained. The one who follows the messenger follows him in what Allah commands, and the one who turns back on his heels apostatises or opposes.

What was grave is discussed. Some said the word means the turning away from Jerusalem toward the sacred house, others that it means the prayer direction itself.

The interpretation preferred is given, that it is the turning of the face of the messenger from the first direction that fell grave upon them.

The change was weighty except for the one to whom Allah granted success.

phrases.translation: And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith.
phrases.explanation:
